questions.e: V = n × Vm = 0.25 × 22.4 = 5.6 L. 89.6 L divides 22.4 by 0.25 instead of multiplying, and 11.2 L is the volume of 0.5 mol.

questions.s: 4 g of sodium hydroxide is dissolved to make 100 mL of solution. What is its concentration? (H = 1, O = 16, Na = 23)
questions.e: n = 4/40 = 0.1 mol and V = 0.100 L, so c = 0.1/0.1 = 1 mol/L. 0.1 mol/L gives the amount, not the concentration, and 0.04 mol/L divides grams by millilitres.

questions.s: 5 g of sugar is dissolved in 95 g of water. What is the mass fraction of sugar in the solution?
questions.e: w = 5/(5 + 95) = 5/100 = 5 %. 5.3 % divides by the mass of water only (5/95), not by the mass of the solution.

questions.s: The molar mass of a substance is numerically equal to which quantity?
o: the mass of one molecule, in g
its relative molecular mass, in kg/mol
the Avogadro constant divided by its relative molecular mass
its relative molecular mass, in g/mol
questions.e: Molar mass in g/mol has the same number as the relative molecular (or formula) mass; for example Mr(H₂O) = 18 and M = 18 g/mol. In kg/mol the number would be 1000 times smaller, and one molecule has a mass of only about 10⁻²³ g.

questions.s: 10 mL of 6 mol/L hydrochloric acid is diluted with water to 60 mL. What is the new concentration?
questions.e: c₂ = c₁V₁/V₂ = 6 × 10/60 = 1 mol/L. 36 mol/L multiplies by the volume ratio instead of dividing, and 0.6 mol/L assumes a tenfold dilution.

questions.s: 2.4 g of magnesium burns completely in oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. What mass of magnesium oxide forms? (O = 16, Mg = 24)
questions.e: n(Mg) = 0.1 mol gives 0.1 mol MgO (2 : 2), and M(MgO) = 40 g/mol, so m = 4.0 g. 2.0 g wrongly halves the amount by reading the 2 : 1 ratio of Mg to O₂ as Mg to MgO.

questions.s: How many electrons are present in 1.8 g of water? (H = 1, O = 16; NA is the Avogadro constant)
questions.e: n(H₂O) = 1.8/18 = 0.1 mol, and each molecule has 8 + 1 + 1 = 10 electrons, so n(e⁻) = 1 mol = NA. 0.3 NA counts atoms instead of electrons.

questions.s: Equal masses of methane, CH₄, and oxygen, O₂, are compared. What is the ratio of the number of CH₄ molecules to the number of O₂ molecules? (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.e: For equal masses, n ∝ 1/M, so n(CH₄) : n(O₂) = 32 : 16 = 2 : 1. 1 : 2 is the ratio of molar masses, the inverse of the molecule ratio, and 5 : 1 is the ratio of atoms.

questions.s: At STP, 0.56 L of a gas has a mass of 1.1 g. What is the molar mass of the gas? (Use the molar volume 22.4 L/mol at STP.)
questions.e: n = 0.56/22.4 = 0.025 mol, so M = 1.1/0.025 = 44 g/mol. 24.6 g/mol multiplies the mass by 22.4 without using the measured volume, and 22 g/mol halves the correct value.

questions.s: A solution contains 0.1 mol/L K₂SO₄ and 0.1 mol/L KCl. What is the concentration of K⁺ ions?
questions.e: K₂SO₄ gives 2 × 0.1 = 0.2 mol/L K⁺ and KCl gives 0.1 mol/L, so c(K⁺) = 0.3 mol/L. 0.2 mol/L forgets the subscript 2 in K₂SO₄.

questions.s: What amount of gas is present in 8.3 L at 100 kPa and 400 K? (R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
questions.e: n = pV/(RT) = (1.00 × 10⁵ Pa × 8.3 × 10⁻³ m³)/(8.3 × 400) = 830/3320 = 0.25 mol. 250 mol keeps the volume in litres with the pressure in pascals.

questions.s: At the same temperature and pressure, 2 L of gas X₂ reacts exactly with 1 L of gas Y₂ to form 2 L of a single gaseous compound Z. What is the formula of Z?
questions.e: Volume ratio = mole ratio, so 2X₂ + Y₂ → 2Z. The atoms are 4 X and 2 Y in 2 Z, so Z = X₂Y. XY₂ swaps the roles of X and Y.

questions.s: 4.48 L of ammonia, measured at STP, is dissolved in water to make 250 mL of solution. What is the concentration of the solution? (Use the molar volume 22.4 L/mol at STP.)
questions.e: n(NH₃) = 4.48/22.4 = 0.2 mol, so c = 0.2/0.250 = 0.8 mol/L. 17.9 mol/L divides the gas volume by the solution volume without converting the gas to moles, and 0.2 is the amount, not the concentration.

questions.s: A mixture of 2 g of hydrogen and 8 g of oxygen is ignited: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. What mass of water forms? (H = 1, O = 16)
questions.e: n(H₂) = 1 mol and n(O₂) = 0.25 mol; 0.25 mol O₂ needs only 0.5 mol H₂, so O₂ is limiting and gives 0.5 mol H₂O = 9 g. 18 g assumes all the hydrogen reacts, and 10 g simply adds the masses even though hydrogen is left over.

questions.s: 16 g of iron(III) oxide is reduced, Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, and 8.4 g of iron is obtained. What is the percentage yield? (O = 16, Fe = 56)
questions.e: n(Fe₂O₃) = 16/160 = 0.1 mol, so the theoretical iron is 0.2 mol = 11.2 g and yield = 8.4/11.2 = 75 %. 150 % forgets that each Fe₂O₃ gives 2 Fe, and 52.5 % divides product mass by reactant mass.

questions.s: What volume of 2 mol/L hydrochloric acid reacts exactly with 13 g of zinc? (Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂; Zn = 65)
questions.e: n(Zn) = 13/65 = 0.2 mol needs 0.4 mol HCl, so V = 0.4/2 = 0.2 L = 200 mL. 100 mL uses a 1 : 1 ratio and ignores the coefficient 2 of HCl.

questions.s: Physiological saline is 0.9 % sodium chloride by mass. What mass of NaCl is in 500 g of saline?
questions.e: m(NaCl) = 500 × 0.9/100 = 4.5 g. 0.45 g and 45 g are slips in converting the percentage, and 9.0 g would be the mass in 1000 g of saline.

questions.s: Take the average molar mass of air as 29 g/mol. A hydrocarbon gas is 2 times as dense as air at the same temperature and pressure. Which could it be? (H = 1, C = 12)
questions.e: At the same T and p, density ∝ molar mass, so M = 2 × 29 = 58 g/mol, which is butane C₄H₁₀ (48 + 10). Propane (44) is denser than air but only about 1.5 times as dense.

questions.s: 200 mL of 0.5 mol/L calcium nitrate, Ca(NO₃)₂, is diluted with water to 500 mL. What is the nitrate-ion concentration in the diluted solution?
questions.e: n(NO₃⁻) = 2 × 0.5 × 0.200 = 0.2 mol in 0.500 L, so c = 0.4 mol/L. 0.2 mol/L is the Ca(NO₃)₂ (or Ca²⁺) concentration after dilution, and 1 mol/L is the nitrate concentration before dilution.

questions.s: A rigid, sealed steel tank contains gas at 27 °C and 300 kPa. It is warmed to 127 °C. What is the new pressure?
questions.e: At constant n and V, p/T is constant with T in kelvin: p₂ = 300 × 400/300 = 400 kPa. 1411 kPa uses the Celsius ratio 127/27, and 225 kPa inverts the temperature ratio.

questions.s: 1.6 g of methane burns completely: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. What volume of CO₂ is produced at STP? (H = 1, C = 12; use the molar volume 22.4 L/mol at STP.)
questions.e: n(CH₄) = 1.6/16 = 0.1 mol gives 0.1 mol CO₂ = 2.24 L. 4.48 L is the volume of oxygen used (0.2 mol), not the CO₂ formed.

questions.s: At STP, 11.2 L of a mixture of CO and CO₂ has a mass of 18 g. What is the mass of CO₂ in the mixture? (C = 12, O = 16; use the molar volume 22.4 L/mol at STP.)
questions.e: n(total) = 0.5 mol. With a mol CO and b mol CO₂: a + b = 0.5 and 28a + 44b = 18, so 14 + 16b = 18 and b = 0.25 mol. m(CO₂) = 0.25 × 44 = 11 g. 7 g is the mass of CO, and 9 g just halves the total mass.

questions.s: Concentrated hydrochloric acid is 36.5 % HCl by mass with a density of 1.2 g/mL. What volume of it is needed to prepare 600 mL of 1 mol/L HCl? (H = 1, Cl = 35.5)
questions.e: c(conc.) = 1000 × 1.2 × 0.365/36.5 = 12 mol/L. The dilute acid needs 1 × 0.600 = 0.6 mol, so V = 0.6/12 = 0.050 L = 50 mL. 60 mL ignores the density and takes the stock as 10 mol/L.

questions.s: NA is the Avogadro constant. Which statement is correct? (N = 14)
o: At STP, 11.2 L of SO₃ contains 0.5 NA molecules
1 L of 0.1 mol/L acetic acid contains 0.1 NA H⁺ ions
1 mol of hydroxide ions, OH⁻, contains 10 NA electrons
28 g of nitrogen gas, N₂, contains NA atoms
questions.e: OH⁻ has 8 + 1 + 1 = 10 electrons, so 1 mol contains 10 NA. SO₃ is a solid at STP, so 22.4 L/mol does not apply; acetic acid is a weak acid and is only partly ionised; 28 g of N₂ is 1 mol of molecules but 2 NA atoms.

questions.s: 1.8 g of a metal M that forms M³⁺ ions reacts completely with excess dilute acid and releases 2.24 L of H₂ at STP. What is the relative atomic mass of M? (Use the molar volume 22.4 L/mol at STP.)
questions.e: n(H₂) = 0.1 mol. From 2M + 6H⁺ → 2M³⁺ + 3H₂, n(M) = 0.1 × 2/3 = 1/15 mol, so Ar = 1.8 × 15 = 27 (aluminium). 18 assumes the metal forms M²⁺ ions (1 mol M per mol H₂).

questions.s: A container holds equal masses of hydrogen, H₂, and helium, He. What fraction of the total pressure is due to the helium? (H = 1, He = 4)
questions.e: For mass m: n(H₂) = m/2 and n(He) = m/4, so He makes up (m/4)/(m/2 + m/4) = 1/3 of the moles and hence 1/3 of the pressure. 1/2 assumes equal masses mean equal amounts, which is wrong since the molar masses differ.

questions.s: 16.8 g of sodium hydrogencarbonate is heated, 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂, and the solid left has a mass of 13.7 g. What percentage of the NaHCO₃ has decomposed? (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16, Na = 23)
questions.e: Complete decomposition of 0.2 mol NaHCO₃ would lose 0.1 mol of (H₂O + CO₂) = 0.1 × 62 = 6.2 g. The actual loss is 16.8 − 13.7 = 3.1 g, so 3.1/6.2 = 50 % has decomposed. 18.5 % is just the mass loss as a percentage of the sample.

questions.s: In a school laboratory, how is a small stock of sodium metal normally stored?
o: In a stoppered bottle of water
In a stoppered bottle of ethanol
In an open, dry glass beaker
questions.e: Sodium reacts with oxygen and water vapour in air, so it is kept under kerosene, which does not react with it and keeps air away; sodium is denser than kerosene and stays covered. Water reacts violently with sodium, and ethanol also reacts with sodium to release hydrogen, so neither can be used.

questions.s: A small piece of sodium is dropped into a beaker of water containing a few drops of phenolphthalein. Which observation is NOT made?
o: Sodium floats on the water surface
Sodium melts into a small shiny ball
The solution turns pink around the moving sodium
Sodium sinks and burns with a blue flame
questions.e: Sodium (density about 0.97 g/cm³) floats, melts into a ball because the reaction 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ is strongly exothermic and sodium has a low melting point, and the NaOH formed turns phenolphthalein pink. It does not sink, and any flame seen from burning sodium is yellow, not blue.

questions.s: A small piece of sodium is added to dilute copper(II) sulfate solution. What is observed?
o: Red copper is deposited on the sodium
A blue precipitate forms and a gas is given off
Red copper forms and the solution turns colourless
A black precipitate of CuO forms and no gas appears
questions.e: Sodium reacts with the water first: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂, so gas is released. The OH⁻ then precipitates the copper ions: Cu²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Cu(OH)₂, a blue solid. Sodium does not displace copper metal from aqueous solution because it reacts with water much faster.

questions.s: Sodium is heated in air until it burns. Which describes the flame colour and the main solid product?
o: Yellow flame; white sodium oxide, Na₂O
questions.e: Burning sodium gives the yellow flame typical of sodium, and on burning the product is sodium peroxide, 2Na + O₂ → Na₂O₂, a pale yellow solid. White Na₂O forms when sodium slowly oxidises in air at room temperature, not when it burns. Lilac is the flame colour of potassium and brick-red that of calcium.

questions.s: What is the ratio of the number of cations to the number of anions in solid sodium peroxide, Na₂O₂?
questions.e: Na₂O₂ is made of Na⁺ ions and peroxide ions O₂²⁻; each formula unit contains 2 Na⁺ and only one O₂²⁻ anion, so the ratio is 2 : 1. Answering 1 : 1 comes from treating the two oxygen atoms as two separate O⁻ anions.

questions.s: Sodium peroxide reacts with carbon dioxide: 2Na₂O₂ + 2CO₂ → 2Na₂CO₃ + O₂. How many moles of electrons are transferred when 0.2 mol Na₂O₂ reacts completely?
questions.e: Oxygen in Na₂O₂ is −1; in the reaction, half of these O atoms go to −2 (in Na₂CO₃) and half go to 0 (in O₂). For 2 mol Na₂O₂, 1 mol O₂ forms, so 2 mol electrons are transferred: 1 mol e⁻ per mol Na₂O₂, giving 0.2 mol. Answering 0.4 mol counts the electrons lost and gained separately.

questions.s: 15.6 g of Na₂O₂ reacts completely with excess carbon dioxide: 2Na₂O₂ + 2CO₂ → 2Na₂CO₃ + O₂. By how much does the mass of the solid increase? (Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.e: n(Na₂O₂) = 15.6/78 = 0.2 mol. Solid goes from 2 × 78 = 156 g to 2 × 106 = 212 g per 2 mol, an increase of 56 g, i.e. 28 g per mol (the mass of one 'CO'). So the increase is 0.2 × 28 = 5.6 g. Answering 8.8 g is the mass of CO₂ absorbed, forgetting the 3.2 g of O₂ released.

questions.s: Which sodium compound is used as a source of oxygen in submarines and breathing masks, because it releases O₂ when it absorbs exhaled CO₂ and water vapour?
questions.e: Sodium peroxide reacts as 2Na₂O₂ + 2CO₂ → 2Na₂CO₃ + O₂ and 2Na₂O₂ + 2H₂O → 4NaOH + O₂, so it removes CO₂ and supplies O₂. Na₂O only forms Na₂CO₃ or NaOH with no oxygen released, and NaOH absorbs CO₂ but gives no O₂.

questions.s: Which simple test distinguishes solid sodium carbonate from solid sodium hydrogencarbonate?
o: Heat each solid and pass any gas into limewater
Carry out a flame test on each solid
Add excess hydrochloric acid to each and look for gas
questions.e: On heating, 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂, and the CO₂ turns limewater milky, while Na₂CO₃ is stable to heat. Both give a yellow sodium flame, both solutions are alkaline and turn phenolphthalein pink, and both release CO₂ with excess acid, so the other tests do not distinguish them.

questions.s: Which statement comparing sodium carbonate and sodium hydrogencarbonate is correct?
o: At the same temperature, NaHCO₃ is more soluble in water than Na₂CO₃
Na₂CO₃ decomposes on heating more easily than NaHCO₃
With hydrochloric acid of equal concentration, NaHCO₃ gives off gas faster
Equal masses of the two give the same mass of CO₂ with excess acid
questions.e: HCO₃⁻ releases CO₂ in one step (HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O), while CO₃²⁻ must first take up one H⁺, so NaHCO₃ reacts faster. Na₂CO₃ is the more soluble and the more heat-stable salt. Equal masses do not give equal CO₂: 84 g NaHCO₃ and 106 g Na₂CO₃ each give 1 mol CO₂, so NaHCO₃ gives more per gram.

questions.s: 10.0 g of a mixture of Na₂CO₃ and NaHCO₃ is heated to constant mass, and the mass falls by 3.1 g. What mass of NaHCO₃ was in the mixture? (Na = 23, H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.e: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂: 2 × 84 = 168 g of NaHCO₃ loses 18 + 44 = 62 g. So m(NaHCO₃) = 168 × 3.1/62 = 8.4 g. Answering 4.2 g uses 84 g instead of 168 g, forgetting that 2 mol NaHCO₃ are needed per mole of H₂O and CO₂ lost.

questions.s: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added drop by drop, with stirring, to sodium carbonate solution until the acid is in excess. What is observed?
o: No gas at first, then bubbles appear
Bubbles at once, then stopping about halfway
questions.e: While carbonate is in excess, the acid only converts it to hydrogencarbonate: CO₃²⁻ + H⁺ → HCO₃⁻, with no gas. After all CO₃²⁻ is used, further acid gives HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O and bubbles appear. Bubbles at once would be seen if the carbonate were added to the acid instead.

questions.s: A solution of Na₂CO₃ contains a little NaHCO₃ as an impurity. What is the best way to remove it?
o: Add excess dilute hydrochloric acid, then evaporate
Add the right amount of NaOH solution
questions.e: NaOH converts the impurity into the wanted salt: HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ → CO₃²⁻ + H₂O, adding nothing new. Passing CO₂ does the opposite (Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → 2NaHCO₃), hydrochloric acid destroys both salts, and limewater precipitates the carbonate as CaCO₃.

questions.s: Flame tests are carried out on a sodium salt and a potassium salt (the potassium flame is viewed through blue cobalt glass). Which pair of colours is correct?
questions.e: Sodium gives an intense yellow flame and potassium a lilac (pale violet) flame; the blue cobalt glass filters out the yellow light from traces of sodium so the lilac can be seen. Brick-red belongs to calcium, green to copper and crimson to lithium.

questions.s: A piece of freshly cut sodium is left exposed to moist air for many days. What white powder is finally obtained?
questions.e: The sequence is Na → Na₂O (dull surface) → NaOH (absorbs water, becomes wet) → reacts with CO₂ to form Na₂CO₃·10H₂O → loses water of crystallisation to give Na₂CO₃ powder. NaOH is only an intermediate, because it keeps absorbing CO₂ from the air.

questions.s: 2.3 g of sodium is added to 97.8 g of water and reacts completely. What is the mass fraction of NaOH in the resulting solution? (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)
questions.e: n(Na) = 0.1 mol, giving 0.1 mol NaOH (4.0 g) and 0.05 mol H₂ (0.1 g), which escapes. Solution mass = 2.3 + 97.8 − 0.1 = 100.0 g, so the mass fraction is 4.0 %. Answering 4.1 % divides by the mass of water alone, and 2.3 % uses the mass of sodium instead of NaOH.

questions.s: A burning magnesium ribbon is lowered into a jar of carbon dioxide and keeps burning. What are the products?
questions.e: Magnesium is a strong enough reducing agent to remove oxygen from CO₂: 2Mg + CO₂ → 2MgO + C, giving white MgO and black specks of carbon. This is why CO₂ extinguishers must not be used on burning magnesium. No hydrogen is present, so Mg(OH)₂ cannot form.

questions.s: Magnesium is burned in pure nitrogen, and water is then added to the solid product. Which gas is given off?
questions.e: 3Mg + N₂ → Mg₃N₂ (magnesium nitride). The nitride ion is hydrolysed by water: Mg₃N₂ + 6H₂O → 3Mg(OH)₂ + 2NH₃, so ammonia is released. Hydrogen would come from unreacted magnesium in hot water, not from the nitride.

questions.s: Industrially, magnesium is obtained by electrolysing molten MgCl₂ rather than molten MgO. What is the main reason?
o: MgO has a very high melting point
MgCl₂ is easily reduced by carbon
questions.e: Both compounds are ionic and conduct when molten, but MgO melts at about 2800 °C, which would make electrolysis extremely costly, whereas MgCl₂ melts at about 714 °C. MgO is not covalent, solid ionic compounds do not conduct, and carbon is not used to reduce MgCl₂.

questions.s: Magnesium is extracted from seawater by: adding lime to precipitate Mg(OH)₂; dissolving it in hydrochloric acid; crystallising and drying MgCl₂; and electrolysing molten MgCl₂. Which step is a redox reaction?
questions.e: Only in electrolysis do oxidation states change: MgCl₂ → Mg + Cl₂, with Mg going from +2 to 0 and Cl from −1 to 0. Precipitation and neutralisation are ionic exchange reactions, and drying only removes water, so no electrons are transferred in those steps.

questions.s: Equal masses of magnesium and aluminium react separately with excess hydrochloric acid. What is the ratio of the volumes of hydrogen (Mg : Al) at the same conditions? (Mg = 24, Al = 27)
questions.e: Take 24 g of each. Mg: 1 mol Mg gives 1 mol H₂. Al: 24/27 = 8/9 mol Al gives 8/9 × 3/2 = 4/3 mol H₂. Ratio = 1 : 4/3 = 3 : 4. Answering 2 : 3 is the ratio for equal numbers of moles of the two metals, not equal masses.

questions.s: Which substance is suitable as an antacid to relieve excess stomach acid?
questions.e: Mg(OH)₂ is a weak, only slightly soluble base that neutralises HCl gently: Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O. NaOH and CaO are strongly caustic and would damage tissue, and BaCO₃ dissolves in stomach acid to release poisonous Ba²⁺ ions.

questions.s: Which statement about magnesium and its compounds is correct?
o: Magnesium does not burn in nitrogen
Magnesium is less reactive than aluminium
Mg reacts with hot water, turning phenolphthalein pink
questions.e: Mg + 2H₂O(hot) → Mg(OH)₂ + H₂, and the slightly soluble Mg(OH)₂ makes the water alkaline enough to turn phenolphthalein pink. Magnesium does burn in nitrogen to form Mg₃N₂, MgO is a basic oxide (unlike Al₂O₃), and Mg is above Al in reactivity.

questions.s: 4.8 g of magnesium burns completely in air, forming a mixture of MgO and Mg₃N₂ only. Which value could be the mass of the solid product? (Mg = 24, N = 14, O = 16)
questions.e: n(Mg) = 0.2 mol. If all became MgO: 0.2 × 40 = 8.0 g. If all became Mg₃N₂: 0.2/3 × 100 ≈ 6.7 g. A mixture must lie between 6.7 g and 8.0 g, so only 7.5 g is possible. 8.2 g is above the all-MgO limit, which some students miss by assuming more oxygen means a heavier product without bound.

questions.s: Aluminium reacts with both hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution. Which statement is correct?
o: Aluminium does not react with NaOH solution because it is a metal
Aluminium gives twice as much H₂ with NaOH as with HCl
Equal amounts of Al give equal volumes of H₂ with either excess reagent
Aluminium acts as the oxidising agent in both reactions
questions.e: In both reactions each Al atom loses 3 electrons and 2 Al give 3 H₂ (2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂; 2Al + 2NaOH + 6H₂O → 2Na[Al(OH)₄] + 3H₂), so equal moles of Al give equal H₂ when the acid or alkali is in excess. Aluminium is the reducing agent, and it does react with NaOH solution.

questions.s: Which oxide reacts with both dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution?
questions.e: Al₂O₃ is amphoteric: Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O and Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2Na[Al(OH)₄]. MgO, Fe₂O₃ and CuO are basic oxides: they dissolve in acids but not in NaOH solution.

questions.s: Which reagent is best for preparing a good yield of Al(OH)₃ from aluminium chloride solution?
questions.e: Al³⁺ + 3NH₃·H₂O → Al(OH)₃ + 3NH₄⁺, and Al(OH)₃ does not dissolve in the weak base ammonia, so excess does no harm. With excess NaOH, the amphoteric Al(OH)₃ dissolves again as [Al(OH)₄]⁻, so the amount of NaOH would have to be controlled exactly.

questions.s: Sodium hydroxide solution is added drop by drop to aluminium chloride solution until the NaOH is in large excess. What is observed?
o: A white precipitate forms, then dissolves
A white precipitate forms and remains
No change at first, then a white precipitate
A gas is given off, then a white precipitate
questions.e: First Al³⁺ + 3OH⁻ → Al(OH)₃, a white precipitate; once all Al³⁺ is precipitated, more OH⁻ dissolves it: Al(OH)₃ + OH⁻ → [Al(OH)₄]⁻, giving a colourless solution. 'No change at first, then a precipitate' is what happens in the reverse order, adding AlCl₃ to NaOH.

questions.s: A solution contains 0.1 mol AlCl₃. NaOH solution is added and 3.9 g of Al(OH)₃ precipitate is obtained. Which amount of NaOH could have been added? (Al = 27, O = 16, H = 1)
questions.e: n(Al(OH)₃) = 3.9/78 = 0.05 mol. Either NaOH was insufficient: 3 × 0.05 = 0.15 mol, or it was in excess: 0.3 mol to precipitate all 0.1 mol Al³⁺, then 0.05 mol more to dissolve 0.05 mol Al(OH)₃, total 0.35 mol. Of the options only 0.35 mol fits; 0.30 mol would leave all 7.8 g of precipitate.

questions.s: Cold concentrated nitric acid can be transported in aluminium tanks. Why?
o: Aluminium is less reactive than hydrogen in the series
Concentrated nitric acid is not an oxidising acid
A thin, dense oxide layer forms and protects the metal
Aluminium does not react with any acid
questions.e: Cold concentrated nitric acid (and concentrated sulfuric acid) passivates aluminium and iron: it oxidises the surface to a dense oxide film that stops further reaction. Aluminium is actually a reactive metal above hydrogen, it does react with dilute acids, and concentrated nitric acid is a strong oxidising acid.

questions.s: In the thermite reaction, 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe, used to weld railway lines, which statement is correct?
o: Al is the reducing agent and the reaction is strongly exothermic
The reaction absorbs heat, so it needs continuous strong heating
questions.e: Al goes from 0 to +3, so it is oxidised and acts as the reducing agent, while Fe₂O₃ (Fe +3 → 0) is the oxidising agent. Once started by a fuse, the reaction releases so much heat that the iron formed is molten. Saying aluminium is 'reduced' mixes up loss and gain of electrons.

questions.s: In the industrial electrolysis of aluminium oxide, cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) is added. What is its main purpose?
o: To lower the melting temperature of the electrolyte
To act as a catalyst for the decomposition
To react with the oxygen produced at the anode
To supply extra aluminium ions for discharge at the cathode
questions.e: Pure Al₂O₃ melts at about 2050 °C; dissolved in molten cryolite it can be electrolysed at about 950 °C, saving a great deal of energy. Cryolite is not consumed and is not a catalyst, and the oxygen formed at the anode reacts with the carbon anodes, not with cryolite.

questions.s: Why must sodium hydroxide never be melted in a crucible made of aluminium oxide?
o: Al₂O₃ melts at a lower temperature than NaOH
NaOH reduces Al₂O₃ to aluminium metal
Al₂O₃ is amphoteric and reacts with the molten NaOH
Al₂O₃ conducts heat too poorly to melt NaOH
questions.e: Al₂O₃ shows acidic as well as basic behaviour, so it reacts with hot alkali: Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O, and the crucible would be eaten away. Al₂O₃ actually melts at about 2050 °C, far above NaOH (about 318 °C), and NaOH is not a reducing agent; an iron crucible is used instead.

questions.s: Which of these sodium salts reacts with both dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution?
questions.e: The hydrogencarbonate ion can lose or gain H⁺: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O and HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ → CO₃²⁻ + H₂O. Na₂CO₃ reacts with acid but not with NaOH, and NaCl and Na₂SO₄ react with neither.

questions.s: Two solutions, one containing 0.3 mol HCl and the other 0.3 mol NaOH, each react with excess aluminium. What is the ratio of the amounts of hydrogen produced (HCl : NaOH)?
questions.e: 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂: 0.3 mol HCl gives 0.15 mol H₂. 2Al + 2NaOH + 6H₂O → 2Na[Al(OH)₄] + 3H₂: 0.3 mol NaOH gives 0.45 mol H₂. Ratio 0.15 : 0.45 = 1 : 3. Answering 1 : 1 applies the 'equal aluminium' rule, but here the aluminium is in excess and the acid and alkali are limiting.

questions.s: Aluminium is a reactive metal, yet aluminium window frames do not corrode noticeably in air. Why?
o: A dense surface layer of Al₂O₃ protects the metal
Aluminium is below hydrogen in the reactivity series
Aluminium does not react with oxygen at room temperature
Air contains too little oxygen to attack aluminium
questions.e: Aluminium reacts with oxygen at once, but the thin Al₂O₃ layer formed is dense and sticks firmly, so it stops oxygen and water reaching the metal underneath (unlike porous rust on iron). It is precisely because aluminium does react with oxygen that the protective layer forms.

questions.s: 5.1 g of a magnesium-aluminium alloy reacts with excess hydrochloric acid, giving 5.6 L of hydrogen measured at STP (22.4 L/mol). What mass of aluminium is in the alloy? (Mg = 24, Al = 27)
questions.e: n(H₂) = 0.25 mol. Let x = n(Mg), y = n(Al): 24x + 27y = 5.1 and x + 1.5y = 0.25. Substituting x = 0.25 − 1.5y gives 6 − 9y = 5.1, so y = 0.1 mol and m(Al) = 2.7 g. The value 2.4 g is the mass of magnesium (0.1 mol), not aluminium.

questions.s: Which ionic equation is correct?
questions.e: Al(OH)₃ dissolves in strong base as Al(OH)₃ + OH⁻ → [Al(OH)₄]⁻, balanced in atoms and charge. The first equation is unbalanced (the correct form is 2Al + 2OH⁻ + 6H₂O → 2[Al(OH)₄]⁻ + 3H₂), Al(OH)₃ does not dissolve in ammonia, and soluble AlCl₃ must be written as Al³⁺.

questions.s: Which pair of properties makes aluminium alloys widely used for aircraft bodies and drink cans?
o: High density and a very high melting point
It is magnetic and very hard
It is the most reactive common metal
Low density and resistance to corrosion
questions.e: Aluminium has a low density (about 2.7 g/cm³) and its protective oxide layer resists corrosion; alloying makes it strong as well. It is not magnetic, it has a fairly low density rather than a high one, and high reactivity alone would be a drawback, not an advantage.

questions.s: Both NaHCO₃ and Al(OH)₃ are used as antacids. Why is Al(OH)₃ preferred for a patient with a stomach ulcer?
o: NaHCO₃ releases CO₂ gas, which may worsen the ulcer
Al(OH)₃ is a strong base that acts faster
NaHCO₃ does not react with hydrochloric acid
questions.e: NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂: the gas swells the stomach and may risk perforating an ulcer, while Al(OH)₃ + 3HCl → AlCl₃ + 3H₂O gives no gas. Al(OH)₃ is a weak, insoluble base, which is why it acts gently.

questions.s: Which equation correctly shows iron reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.e: H⁺ is only a weak oxidising agent, so it oxidises iron only to Fe²⁺: Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂ (pale green solution). FeCl₃ forms with strong oxidising agents such as Cl₂. The third equation is not balanced in charge, and chlorine cannot be formed because Cl⁻ is not oxidised here.

questions.s: Hot iron wire is plunged into a jar of chlorine, with the iron in excess. What is the product?
o: A mixture of FeCl₂ and FeCl₃
questions.e: Chlorine is a strong oxidising agent, so dry iron burns in it to give brown smoke of FeCl₃: 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃, whatever the ratio of reactants. Excess iron cannot reduce Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ here because there is no solution for the two to react in.

questions.s: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to freshly made iron(II) sulfate solution and the mixture is left in air. What is observed?
o: A red-brown precipitate that later turns white
A white precipitate that turns grey-green, then red-brown
A blue precipitate that turns black on standing
A green precipitate that dissolves again in the excess alkali
questions.e: Fe²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₂, a white solid, which is quickly oxidised by air: 4Fe(OH)₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4Fe(OH)₃, passing through grey-green to red-brown. A blue precipitate turning black is copper(II) hydroxide changing to CuO.

questions.s: Which reagent and observation identify Fe³⁺ ions in a solution?
questions.e: Fe³⁺ forms an intensely red complex with thiocyanate: Fe³⁺ + 3SCN⁻ → Fe(SCN)₃. BaCl₂ tests for sulfate, AgNO₃ for chloride, and starch for iodine, so those observations say nothing about Fe³⁺.

questions.s: A solution may contain Fe²⁺. Which procedure proves that Fe²⁺ is present and that the solution does not already contain Fe³⁺?
o: Add KSCN: no colour; then add chlorine water: it turns red
Add chlorine water first, then KSCN: it turns red
Add KSCN: it turns blood-red at once
Add NaOH: a red-brown precipitate forms at once
questions.e: No red colour with KSCN first shows there is no Fe³⁺; turning red after Cl₂ is added shows Fe³⁺ was formed by 2Fe²⁺ + Cl₂ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2Cl⁻, so Fe²⁺ was there. Adding chlorine water first cannot tell whether the Fe³⁺ was present originally.

questions.s: A little iron powder is added to a bottle of iron(II) sulfate solution kept in the laboratory. Why?
o: Iron makes the solution more acidic to stop hydrolysis
Iron keeps the sulfate ions in solution
Iron reduces any Fe³⁺ formed back to Fe²⁺
Iron precipitates any copper ions present
questions.e: Air slowly oxidises Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺; iron powder converts it back by 2Fe³⁺ + Fe → 3Fe²⁺ without adding a new metal ion. Iron does not make the solution more acidic (it consumes acid), and the purpose is not removing copper.

questions.s: Printed circuit boards are etched with FeCl₃ solution, which dissolves copper: 2FeCl₃ + Cu → 2FeCl₂ + CuCl₂. Which statement is correct?
o: Copper is more reactive than iron
The products are iron metal and copper(II) chloride
Fe³⁺ is a stronger oxidising agent than Cu²⁺
questions.e: In the reaction Fe³⁺ (oxidising agent) is reduced to Fe²⁺ and Cu (reducing agent) is oxidised to Cu²⁺, so Fe³⁺ is a stronger oxidising agent than the product Cu²⁺. No iron metal forms, and copper remains less reactive than iron: Fe³⁺ is reduced only to Fe²⁺, not to Fe.

questions.s: 0.15 mol of iron powder is added to a solution containing 0.2 mol FeCl₃ and 0.1 mol CuCl₂, and the mixture is stirred until reaction stops. What mass of solid remains? (Fe = 56, Cu = 64)
questions.e: Fe³⁺ is the stronger oxidising agent, so it reacts first: 2Fe³⁺ + Fe → 3Fe²⁺ uses 0.1 mol Fe. The remaining 0.05 mol Fe then reacts with Cu²⁺: Fe + Cu²⁺ → Fe²⁺ + Cu, giving 0.05 mol Cu = 3.2 g, with no iron left. 6.4 g comes from letting all the Cu²⁺ react first and ignoring Fe³⁺.

questions.s: What is the main component of the red-brown rust that forms on iron in moist air?
questions.e: Iron rusts when both oxygen and water are present, forming hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O, which is red-brown and porous. Fe₃O₄ and FeO are black oxides, and FeCO₃ is not the product of rusting.

questions.s: Red-hot iron reacts with steam. What are the products?
questions.e: 3Fe + 4H₂O(g) → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂ at high temperature; the black magnetic oxide Fe₃O₄ forms, not Fe₂O₃. Hydroxides are not stable at red heat, and oxygen cannot be released because iron is the reducing agent and water is reduced to H₂.

questions.s: Small sachets of fine iron powder are sealed inside packets of biscuits and mooncakes. What is their main purpose?
o: To add iron to the food as a nutrient
To absorb oxygen and so slow down spoilage
To release heat and keep the food warm
To neutralise acids formed in the food
questions.e: Iron powder reacts slowly with oxygen and moisture in the packet (it rusts), removing the oxygen that would make fats go rancid and help microbes grow; it acts as an antioxidant (deoxidiser). It is not eaten, so it adds no nutrient, and the slow reaction releases too little heat to warm anything.

questions.s: The order of reducing power is I⁻ > Fe²⁺ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻. A small amount of chlorine is passed into FeBr₂ solution. Which ion is oxidised first?
o: Both ions at the same time
Neither; Cl₂ only reacts with the water
questions.e: Chlorine first reacts with the stronger reducing agent: 2Fe²⁺ + Cl₂ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2Cl⁻. Only after all Fe²⁺ is oxidised does Cl₂ oxidise Br⁻ to Br₂. Choosing Br⁻ ignores the given order of reducing power.

questions.s: The order of reducing power is I⁻ > Fe²⁺ > Br⁻. Exactly 0.1 mol Cl₂ is passed into a solution containing 0.1 mol FeI₂. Which ionic equation describes the reaction?
questions.e: I⁻ is oxidised first. The solution has 0.2 mol I⁻, which needs exactly 0.1 mol Cl₂ (2I⁻ + Cl₂ → I₂ + 2Cl⁻), so all the chlorine is used up before any Fe²⁺ reacts. The equation with 3Cl₂ is for excess chlorine, which would need 0.15 mol.

questions.s: In the blast furnace, iron ore (Fe₂O₃), coke and limestone are added. What is the main role of the limestone?
o: To remove sandy impurities (SiO₂) as slag
To act as the main reducing agent for the ore
To lower the melting point of the iron
To oxidise excess carbon in the molten iron
questions.e: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, and the basic CaO combines with acidic SiO₂: CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃, a molten slag that floats on the iron and is run off. The reducing agent is carbon monoxide from the coke: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂.

questions.s: Which iron compound is a red-brown powder used as a red pigment in paints?
questions.e: Iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃, is red-brown and stable, so it is used as a red pigment (and is the main part of haematite ore). FeO and Fe₃O₄ are black, and FeSO₄·7H₂O is pale green crystals.

questions.s: Galvanised iron is coated with zinc. Even where the coating is scratched, the iron underneath does not rust quickly. Why?
o: Zinc is less reactive than iron, so it shields the iron
Zinc makes iron passive in the same way nitric acid does
Zinc and iron form an alloy that cannot be oxidised
Zinc is more reactive, so it corrodes instead of the iron
questions.e: Zinc is above iron in reactivity, so where both are exposed zinc loses electrons in preference to iron (sacrificial protection), and the iron stays unoxidised. If zinc were less reactive, a scratch would make the iron corrode faster, as happens with tin-plated iron.

questions.s: Which reagent can NOT distinguish FeCl₂ solution from FeCl₃ solution?
questions.e: Both solutions contain Cl⁻, so AgNO₃ gives the same white AgCl precipitate with each. NaOH gives white Fe(OH)₂ (turning red-brown) versus red-brown Fe(OH)₃; KSCN turns only FeCl₃ red; copper dissolves only in FeCl₃ (2Fe³⁺ + Cu → 2Fe²⁺ + Cu²⁺).

questions.s: A mixture of Fe and Fe₂O₃ containing 0.1 mol Fe₂O₃ dissolves completely in hydrochloric acid, giving 0.1 mol H₂. The solution gives no red colour with KSCN. How many moles of Fe metal were in the mixture?
questions.e: Fe₂O₃ gives 0.2 mol Fe³⁺, and since no Fe³⁺ remains, it was all reduced: 2Fe³⁺ + Fe → 3Fe²⁺ uses 0.1 mol Fe. Another 0.1 mol Fe gave the hydrogen: Fe + 2H⁺ → Fe²⁺ + H₂. Total Fe = 0.2 mol. Answering 0.1 mol counts only the iron that released hydrogen.

questions.s: Copper does NOT react with which of these acids, even on warming?
questions.e: Copper is below hydrogen in reactivity, so H⁺ in dilute sulfuric acid cannot oxidise it. Concentrated sulfuric acid (on heating) and nitric acid of any concentration dissolve copper because the sulfate or nitrate part acts as a strong oxidising agent, releasing SO₂, NO or NO₂ instead of H₂.

questions.s: In the reaction Cu + 2H₂SO₄(conc) → CuSO₄ + SO₂ + 2H₂O, what role does the sulfuric acid play?
questions.e: Of the 2 H₂SO₄, one is reduced to SO₂ (S +6 → +4) and acts as the oxidising agent; the other supplies SO₄²⁻ to form the salt CuSO₄, showing acidic properties. Dehydration means removing H and O from a compound as water, as with sugar, which does not happen here.

questions.s: 1.92 g of copper dissolves completely in excess dilute nitric acid. What volume of NO gas is formed, measured at STP (22.4 L/mol)? (Cu = 64)
questions.e: 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO + 4H₂O. n(Cu) = 1.92/64 = 0.03 mol, so n(NO) = 0.03 × 2/3 = 0.02 mol, V = 0.448 L = 448 mL. 672 mL assumes 1 mol NO per mol Cu, and 1344 mL assumes NO₂ from concentrated acid (2 mol per mol Cu).

questions.s: In the reaction 3Cu + 8HNO₃(dilute) → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO + 4H₂O, what fraction of the nitric acid is reduced?
questions.e: Only the nitrogen that ends up in NO (+5 → +2) is reduced: 2 of the 8 HNO₃, which is 1/4. The other 6 HNO₃ remain as NO₃⁻ in Cu(NO₃)₂ and act only as an acid. 3/4 is the fraction that acts as an acid, not the fraction reduced.

questions.s: Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is used to test for water. What colour change shows that water is present?
questions.e: Anhydrous CuSO₄ is a white powder; with water it forms blue CuSO₄·5H₂O: CuSO₄ + 5H₂O → CuSO₄·5H₂O. Blue to white is the reverse change, seen when blue crystals are heated and lose their water of crystallisation.

questions.s: Copper roofs slowly turn green as basic copper carbonate, Cu₂(OH)₂CO₃, forms. Which substances from the air take part in this change?
questions.e: 2Cu + O₂ + H₂O + CO₂ → Cu₂(OH)₂CO₃. The formula itself shows the elements needed: Cu is oxidised by O₂, while the OH and CO₃ groups come from water and carbon dioxide. Nitrogen does not appear in the product, so it plays no part.

questions.s: A blue precipitate of Cu(OH)₂ is filtered off and heated strongly. What is formed?
questions.e: Insoluble hydroxides decompose on heating to the oxide and water: Cu(OH)₂ → CuO + H₂O, so the blue solid turns black. Heating alone does not reduce copper(II) to copper metal or Cu₂O, which needs a reducing agent such as H₂, C or CO.

questions.s: Aqueous ammonia is added drop by drop to copper(II) sulfate solution until it is in excess. What is observed?
o: A light blue precipitate forms, then dissolves to a deep blue solution
A white precipitate forms and remains in the excess
A light blue precipitate forms and stays unchanged in the excess
The blue solution slowly turns colourless with no precipitate
questions.e: First Cu²⁺ + 2NH₃·H₂O → Cu(OH)₂ + 2NH₄⁺ (light blue precipitate); excess ammonia then forms the soluble deep blue complex ion [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺. With NaOH instead of ammonia the precipitate would stay, which is the tempting wrong choice.

questions.s: Copper is heated separately in chlorine and with sulfur. What are the two products?
questions.e: Chlorine is a strong oxidising agent and gives copper(II): Cu + Cl₂ → CuCl₂ (brown-yellow smoke). Sulfur is a weaker oxidising agent and only gives copper(I): 2Cu + S → Cu₂S. In the same way iron gives FeCl₃ with chlorine but FeS with sulfur.

questions.s: Which method of making copper(II) sulfate from copper uses the least sulfuric acid and releases no polluting gas?
o: Heat copper with concentrated sulfuric acid
Warm copper with dilute sulfuric acid
Dissolve copper in dilute nitric acid, then add sulfuric acid
Heat copper in air to CuO, then dissolve it in dilute sulfuric acid
questions.e: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO, then CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O: 1 mol H₂SO₄ per mol CuSO₄ and no gas. Cu + 2H₂SO₄(conc) needs twice the acid and releases toxic SO₂; the nitric acid route releases NO; and copper does not react with dilute sulfuric acid at all.

questions.s: Which description of chlorine at room temperature is correct?
o: A colourless gas, less dense than air
A red-brown liquid with a choking smell
A pale yellow solid with no smell
A yellow-green gas, denser than air
questions.e: Chlorine is a yellow-green, poisonous gas with a choking smell; its molar mass (71 g/mol) is much larger than that of air (about 29 g/mol), so it is denser than air and is collected by upward displacement of air. Red-brown liquid describes bromine.

questions.s: Several tests are done on freshly prepared chlorine water. Which conclusion is correct?
o: Its pale yellow-green colour shows that HClO is present
Blue litmus turns red and stays red, so it contains only acid
AgNO₃ gives a white precipitate, showing that Cl⁻ is present
NaHCO₃ gives gas, showing that HClO is a strong acid
questions.e: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO, so Cl⁻ is present and gives white AgCl. The colour comes from dissolved Cl₂ molecules, not HClO; litmus turns red and is then bleached by HClO; and the gas with NaHCO₃ is due to HCl, since HClO is weaker than carbonic acid.

questions.s: Dry chlorine is passed over a dry piece of coloured cloth and then over a damp piece. Only the damp cloth is bleached. What does this show?
o: Chlorine gas itself is the bleaching agent
Hydrochloric acid is the bleaching agent
Oxygen from the air is the bleaching agent
HClO formed with water is the bleaching agent
questions.e: Dry Cl₂ has no effect, so chlorine molecules do not bleach. In the damp cloth, Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO, and hypochlorous acid, a strong oxidising agent, destroys the dye. Hydrochloric acid is not a bleach, as dilute HCl does not decolourise dyes.

questions.s: A bottle of chlorine water is left in sunlight for several days. Which change takes place?
o: The pH rises as chlorine gas escapes
Its bleaching power grows as more HClO forms
It becomes more acidic and loses its bleaching power
questions.e: In light, 2HClO → 2HCl + O₂; removing HClO pulls Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO to the right until the chlorine is used up, leaving dilute hydrochloric acid. The solution becomes more acidic (pH falls), colourless and no longer bleaches, which is why chlorine water is stored in brown bottles.

questions.s: Household bleach is made by passing chlorine into cold sodium hydroxide solution. What is its active ingredient?
questions.e: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O. Sodium hypochlorite, NaClO, is the oxidising, bleaching and disinfecting ingredient; NaCl formed at the same time has no bleaching action. NaClO₃ forms only with hot concentrated alkali.

questions.s: Excess MnO₂ is heated with concentrated hydrochloric acid containing 0.4 mol HCl: MnO₂ + 4HCl(conc) → MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O. How much chlorine is obtained?
o: Exactly 0.1 mol, since 4 mol HCl give 1 mol Cl₂
Exactly 0.2 mol, since half of the HCl is oxidised
More than 0.1 mol, because MnO₂ is in excess
Less than 0.1 mol, as the acid becomes too dilute
questions.e: 0.4 mol HCl could give at most 0.1 mol Cl₂, but as the reaction proceeds the acid becomes dilute, and dilute HCl does not reduce MnO₂; some HCl also evaporates on heating. So less than 0.1 mol Cl₂ forms. Only 2 of every 4 HCl are oxidised, but they still give 1 Cl₂, so 0.2 mol is impossible.

questions.s: Chlorine made from MnO₂ and concentrated hydrochloric acid contains HCl gas and water vapour. In what order should it be passed through washing bottles to obtain pure, dry chlorine?
o: Concentrated H₂SO₄, then saturated NaCl solution
Saturated NaCl solution, then concentrated H₂SO₄
Saturated NaHCO₃ solution, then soda lime
questions.e: Saturated brine dissolves HCl but very little Cl₂; drying with concentrated H₂SO₄ must come last, otherwise the gas picks up water again from the brine. NaOH, NaHCO₃ and soda lime all react with chlorine itself, so they cannot be used to purify it.

questions.s: The oxidising power of the halogens decreases in the order Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂. Which reaction does NOT occur in aqueous solution?
questions.e: A halogen can only oxidise the halide ions of the halogens below it. I₂ is the weakest oxidising agent of the three, so it cannot oxidise Cl⁻ to Cl₂. The other three reactions all have a stronger halogen displacing a weaker one.

questions.s: A jet of burning hydrogen is lowered into a jar of chlorine. What is observed?
o: It explodes at once with a bright blue flash
It burns quietly with a pale flame; white mist forms at the jar mouth
It burns with a yellow flame, giving clouds of brown smoke
It goes out, since chlorine does not support burning
questions.e: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl: hydrogen keeps burning quietly in chlorine with a pale flame, and the HCl formed meets moist air to give a white mist of hydrochloric acid droplets. This shows that burning does not always need oxygen. Brown smoke is seen when iron or copper burns in chlorine.

questions.s: Bleaching powder (active ingredient Ca(ClO)₂) loses its effect if it is stored in an open container. Why?
o: CaCl₂ in it absorbs water and slowly turns into hydrochloric acid
Nitrogen in the air reduces Ca(ClO)₂ to CaCl₂ over time
Ca(ClO)₂ reacts with CO₂ and water to give HClO, which then decomposes
Ca(ClO)₂ slowly evaporates at room temperature into the air
questions.e: Ca(ClO)₂ + CO₂ + H₂O → CaCO₃ + 2HClO, and then 2HClO → 2HCl + O₂ in light. So the active hypochlorite is used up. This works because carbonic acid is stronger than hypochlorous acid; nitrogen is far too unreactive to reduce hypochlorite.

questions.s: Chlorine can be made at room temperature by 2KMnO₄ + 16HCl → 2KCl + 2MnCl₂ + 5Cl₂ + 8H₂O. When 0.5 mol Cl₂ is produced, how many moles of HCl are oxidised?
questions.e: Of the 16 HCl, 10 are oxidised to 5Cl₂ and 6 end up as Cl⁻ in KCl and MnCl₂. Each Cl₂ needs 2 HCl oxidised, so 0.5 mol Cl₂ needs 1.0 mol HCl oxidised. 1.6 mol is the total HCl consumed (0.5 × 16/5), including the acid that is not oxidised.

questions.s: Which liquid is best for absorbing excess chlorine at the end of a laboratory experiment?
questions.e: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O, which removes chlorine quickly and completely. Chlorine is only moderately soluble in water and even less in brine, which is why brine is used to wash HCl out of chlorine, and concentrated H₂SO₄ only dries it.

questions.s: ClO₂ is used instead of Cl₂ to disinfect drinking water. If both are reduced to Cl⁻, how many times as many electrons does 1 mol ClO₂ accept as 1 mol Cl₂?
questions.e: In ClO₂ chlorine is +4, so each ClO₂ accepts 5 electrons going to Cl⁻. Each Cl₂ accepts 2 electrons (2 × 1). Ratio = 5/2 = 2.5. Answering 5 forgets that one Cl₂ contains two chlorine atoms, each accepting one electron.

questions.s: Bleaching powder works because Ca(ClO)₂ + CO₂ + H₂O → CaCO₃ + 2HClO. Which of these acids is the weakest?
questions.e: A stronger acid displaces a weaker acid from its salt; here carbonic acid releases HClO from hypochlorite, so HClO is weaker than H₂CO₃. HCl and H₂SO₄ are strong acids. Choosing H₂CO₃ overlooks what the given equation shows.

questions.s: Sulfur is burned in excess pure oxygen. What is the product?
questions.e: S + O₂ → SO₂, with a bright blue-violet flame in oxygen. Even with excess oxygen, burning sulfur does not give SO₃; converting SO₂ to SO₃ needs a catalyst such as V₂O₅ and controlled heating, as in the contact process.

questions.s: Magenta (fuchsine) dye solution is decolourised by SO₂, and the colourless solution is then heated. What happens, and why?
o: It stays colourless; SO₂ oxidises the dye permanently
The red colour returns; SO₂ forms an unstable colourless compound with the dye
The red colour returns; SO₂ is a strong oxidising agent
It stays colourless; heating drives the dye off as vapour
questions.e: SO₂ bleaches by combining with the dye to form an unstable colourless compound, which breaks down on heating, so the colour comes back. Chlorine water (HClO) bleaches by oxidation, which is permanent. SO₂ in this reaction is not acting as an oxidising agent.

questions.s: SO₂ is passed into purple acidified potassium permanganate solution, which becomes colourless. Which property of SO₂ does this show?
questions.e: 5SO₂ + 2MnO₄⁻ + 2H₂O → 5SO₄²⁻ + 2Mn²⁺ + 4H⁺: sulfur goes from +4 to +6, so SO₂ is the reducing agent. This is not bleaching, since bleaching refers to organic dyes; SO₂ likewise decolourises bromine water by reduction.

questions.s: Equal numbers of moles of SO₂ and Cl₂ are mixed and passed into a solution of a dye. What is observed?
o: The dye is bleached much more strongly than by either of the gases alone
The dye is bleached, but the colour returns on heating
The dye turns black because sulfur is precipitated
The dye is not bleached, because the gases react to form H₂SO₄ and HCl
questions.e: SO₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O → H₂SO₄ + 2HCl. In a 1 : 1 mixture both bleaching agents are destroyed, and the products are acids with no bleaching action. Expecting a stronger effect assumes the two bleaches simply add together.

questions.s: In the reaction 2H₂S + SO₂ → 3S + 2H₂O, what is the ratio of the mass of sulfur formed by oxidation to the mass formed by reduction?
questions.e: Sulfur from H₂S (−2 → 0) is formed by oxidation; there are 2 such atoms. Sulfur from SO₂ (+4 → 0) is formed by reduction; there is 1. So the ratio is 2 : 1. Answering 1 : 2 swaps which reactant is oxidised and which is reduced.

questions.s: When concentrated sulfuric acid is added to sugar, the sugar turns black. Which property of the acid causes the blackening?
questions.e: Concentrated H₂SO₄ removes hydrogen and oxygen atoms from the sugar as water, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ → 12C + 11H₂O, leaving black carbon: this is dehydration. Hygroscopic means absorbing water that is already present as water, for example drying a gas. The swelling and choking smell that follow come from its oxidising action on carbon.

questions.s: Which gas can NOT be dried by passing it through concentrated sulfuric acid?
questions.e: Ammonia is basic and reacts with the acid: 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄, so it is dried with soda lime instead. Cl₂, SO₂ and CO₂ are acidic or neutral gases that do not react with concentrated sulfuric acid; SO₂ cannot be oxidised further by it because no intermediate oxidation state lies between +4 and +6.

questions.s: What is the safe way to dilute concentrated sulfuric acid?
o: Pour the acid slowly into water, stirring all the time
Pour the water quickly into the acid and then stir it well
Mix equal volumes of acid and water all at once
Warm the acid first, then add the water
questions.e: Dissolving concentrated H₂SO₄ releases a lot of heat. Adding acid to a large volume of water lets the water absorb the heat; adding water to the acid makes the small amount of water boil instantly and spit hot acid out of the container.

questions.s: 50 mL of 18 mol/L sulfuric acid is heated with excess copper until no further reaction occurs. How much H₂SO₄ is reduced?
questions.e: n(H₂SO₄) = 0.9 mol. In Cu + 2H₂SO₄(conc) → CuSO₄ + SO₂ + 2H₂O, only half of the acid is reduced, so at most 0.45 mol. But the acid becomes dilute as water forms and acid is used, and dilute sulfuric acid does not react with copper, so less than 0.45 mol is actually reduced.

questions.s: In the contact process, SO₃ is absorbed in 98.3 % sulfuric acid rather than in water. Why?
o: SO₃ does not react with water at all
Concentrated sulfuric acid catalyses the reaction
Water forms an acid mist with SO₃, so absorption is poor
Water would reduce SO₃ back to SO₂
questions.e: SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ releases so much heat that the water vaporises and forms a fine mist of acid droplets, which is hard to collect, so absorption is slow and incomplete. SO₃ does react readily with water, which is the very cause of the problem; water is not a reducing agent for SO₃.

questions.s: What catalyst is used industrially for 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ in the contact process?
questions.e: V₂O₅ is used at about 400-500 °C because it is effective and cheap and is not easily poisoned. Iron is the catalyst in the Haber process for ammonia, and platinum-rhodium gauze is used for oxidising ammonia to NO in nitric acid manufacture.

questions.s: A sample of acid rain is collected in a stoppered bottle. Its pH is 4.8 at first and 4.4 a few hours later. What is the main reason for the fall in pH?
o: Water evaporates and the acid becomes more concentrated
CO₂ from the air in the bottle dissolves in the rain
Nitrogen from the air in the bottle dissolves in the rain
Dissolved oxygen oxidises H₂SO₃ to the stronger acid H₂SO₄
questions.e: SO₂ in rain forms the weak acid H₂SO₃, which is slowly oxidised: 2H₂SO₃ + O₂ → 2H₂SO₄, a strong acid, so [H⁺] rises and pH falls. The bottle is stoppered, so evaporation is negligible, and rain is already saturated with CO₂, which by itself only brings pH down to about 5.6.

questions.s: Limestone is mixed with coal in power stations to reduce SO₂ emissions. In the presence of air, what calcium compound is finally formed from the sulfur?
questions.e: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, CaO + SO₂ → CaSO₃, and then 2CaSO₃ + O₂ → 2CaSO₄ in the hot air; overall 2CaCO₃ + 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2CaSO₄ + 2CO₂. CaSO₃ is only an intermediate, since sulfur(IV) is oxidised further by the oxygen present; the gypsum formed can be sold.

questions.s: H₂S gas is passed into copper(II) sulfate solution. A black precipitate forms and the solution becomes more acidic. Which statement explains this?
o: H₂S is a stronger acid than H₂SO₄, so it displaces sulfate from the salt
H₂S reduces Cu²⁺ to copper metal
SO₄²⁻ ions oxidise the H₂S to sulfur
CuS is so insoluble that it does not dissolve even in dilute H₂SO₄
questions.e: CuSO₄ + H₂S → CuS + H₂SO₄. A weak acid can form a strong acid here only because black CuS is extremely insoluble, even in dilute acid, which removes the ions from solution. H₂S remains much weaker than H₂SO₄, and dilute sulfate is not an oxidising agent.

questions.s: Why is nitrogen gas very unreactive at room temperature?
o: Nitrogen atoms already have a full outer shell
Nitrogen gas consists of single atoms
Nitrogen is almost insoluble in water
The N≡N triple bond is very strong
questions.e: The two N atoms in N₂ are joined by a triple bond that needs about 946 kJ/mol to break, so N₂ reacts only under harsh conditions (lightning, high temperature, catalysts). A nitrogen atom has 5 outer electrons, not a full shell, and N₂ is diatomic.

questions.s: NO₂ reacts with water: 3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO. What is the ratio of NO₂ oxidised to NO₂ reduced?
questions.e: Nitrogen is +4 in NO₂. Two NO₂ go to HNO₃ (+5), so they are oxidised; one NO₂ goes to NO (+2) and is reduced. The ratio is 2 : 1, a disproportionation. Answering 1 : 2 swaps the oxidised and reduced parts.

questions.s: A test tube full of NO₂ is turned upside down in a trough of water and left until no further change occurs. What fraction of the tube is filled by water?
questions.e: 3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO: every 3 volumes of NO₂ leave 1 volume of insoluble, colourless NO. So 1/3 of the tube is still gas and water rises to fill 2/3. The tube would fill completely only if enough oxygen were also present (4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃).

questions.s: A tube contains 30 mL of a mixture of NO₂ and O₂. It is inverted in water, and after the reaction 5 mL of a colourless gas remains, which relights a glowing splint. What was the original volume of NO₂?
questions.e: The remaining gas is O₂, so 25 mL of mixture reacted completely by 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃, in a 4 : 1 volume ratio: NO₂ = 20 mL, O₂ = 5 mL (plus 5 mL left over). Answering 25 mL treats all the reacting gas as NO₂.

questions.s: In the ammonia fountain experiment, water containing phenolphthalein rushes up into a flask of dry ammonia and turns pink. Which two properties of ammonia does this show?
o: Denser than air; acts as a reducing agent
Very soluble; acts as an oxidising agent
questions.e: Ammonia dissolves so readily (about 700 volumes per volume of water) that the pressure in the flask falls sharply and water is pushed in as a fountain. NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃·H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ makes the solution alkaline, so phenolphthalein turns pink. No redox reaction takes place.

questions.s: Which observation identifies ammonia gas?
o: It turns damp red litmus paper blue
It turns damp blue litmus paper red
questions.e: Ammonia is the only common alkaline gas: with water it gives OH⁻ ions, turning damp red litmus blue. Turning blue litmus red shows an acidic gas such as HCl or SO₂, relighting a glowing splint shows O₂, and turning limewater milky shows CO₂.

questions.s: Ammonia is prepared by heating NH₄Cl with Ca(OH)₂. How should the gas be dried and collected?
o: Dried with concentrated H₂SO₄; collected over water
Dried with soda lime; collected in a dry tube held mouth downwards
Dried with anhydrous CaCl₂; collected in a dry tube held mouth upwards
Dried with soda lime; collected over water
questions.e: Ammonia is basic, so it is dried with the basic drying agent soda lime; concentrated H₂SO₄ reacts with it, and CaCl₂ also absorbs it (forming CaCl₂·8NH₃). It is very soluble in water and less dense than air, so it is collected in a dry inverted tube by upward delivery, never over water.

questions.s: Why is heating solid NH₄Cl on its own NOT a good way to prepare ammonia?
o: NH₄Cl does not decompose when it is heated
Heating NH₄Cl gives only N₂ and H₂, with no ammonia formed at all
NH₄Cl explodes violently when it is heated
NH₃ and HCl recombine as NH₄Cl in the cooler part of the tube
questions.e: NH₄Cl → NH₃ + HCl on heating, but the two gases meet again in the cooler upper part of the tube and re-form white solid NH₄Cl, so almost no ammonia escapes. That is why NH₄Cl is heated with Ca(OH)₂, which keeps the chloride as CaCl₂.

questions.s: A farmer is told not to mix ammonium sulfate fertiliser with wood ash, which contains K₂CO₃ and is alkaline. Why?
o: The mixture becomes strongly acidic and burns roots
Ammonia gas is released, so nitrogen is lost
Potassium forms an insoluble salt that plants cannot use
A hard precipitate forms that blocks the soil
questions.e: Ammonium salts react with bases: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O. With alkaline wood ash, the nitrogen escapes as ammonia gas and the fertiliser loses its value. Potassium salts are soluble, so the potassium is not locked away.

questions.s: Which sequence of nitrogen compounds is used in the industrial manufacture of nitric acid from ammonia?
questions.e: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O (Pt-Rh catalyst), then 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂, then 3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO, with the NO recycled. Ammonia is not oxidised directly to NO₂, and N₂ is avoided because it is so unreactive.

questions.s: Concentrated nitric acid that has been left in light often looks yellow. Why?
o: It has absorbed iron(III) ions from the glass
It contains colloidal sulfur from impurities
It has reacted with N₂ in air to form N₂O₅
It decomposes, and NO₂ dissolves in it
questions.e: Light or heat decomposes concentrated nitric acid: 4HNO₃ → 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O, and the red-brown NO₂ dissolved in the acid gives a yellow colour. That is why it is stored in brown bottles in a cool, dark place.

questions.s: 3.84 g of copper dissolves completely in concentrated nitric acid. As the acid becomes dilute, the gas changes, and 2.24 L of a mixture of NO₂ and NO (measured at STP, 22.4 L/mol) is collected. How many moles of HNO₃ reacted? (Cu = 64)
questions.e: Nitrogen is conserved: it ends up in Cu(NO₃)₂ or in the gas. n(Cu) = 0.06 mol needs 0.12 mol NO₃⁻ in the salt, and n(gas) = 0.1 mol contains 0.1 mol N. Total HNO₃ = 0.12 + 0.10 = 0.22 mol. Answering 0.12 mol counts only the acid in the salt.

questions.s: Aqua regia, which can dissolve gold and platinum, is a mixture of which concentrated acids, in what ratio by volume?
questions.e: Aqua regia is 3 volumes of concentrated HCl to 1 volume of concentrated HNO₃. Nitric acid supplies the oxidising power and the chloride ions help by forming stable chloro complexes with the gold. The 1 : 3 ratio is the common slip of reversing the order.

questions.s: In which substance does nitrogen have an oxidation state of +3?
questions.e: In HNO₂: (+1) + x + 2(−2) = 0, so x = +3. In NO₂ nitrogen is +4, in N₂O it is +1, and in NH₄⁺ it is −3. Nitrous acid HNO₂ should not be confused with nitric acid HNO₃, where nitrogen is +5.

questions.s: In a car's catalytic converter, nitrogen monoxide and carbon monoxide react to form two harmless gases. What are they?
questions.e: 2NO + 2CO → N₂ + 2CO₂ on a platinum-group catalyst: CO is oxidised and NO is reduced. NO₂ is itself a pollutant, and no hydrogen is present to form NH₃.

questions.s: Dry ammonia is passed over hot black copper(II) oxide. Red copper, water and a colourless, unreactive gas are formed. Which statement is correct?
o: NH₃ is an oxidising agent and the gas is H₂
NH₃ is a reducing agent and the gas is N₂
NH₃ acts only as a base and the gas is NO
NH₃ is a reducing agent and the gas is NO₂
questions.e: 2NH₃ + 3CuO → 3Cu + N₂ + 3H₂O: nitrogen goes from −3 to 0, so ammonia is the reducing agent, and the unreactive gas is N₂. NO₂ is red-brown, not colourless, and NO would turn brown in air.

questions.s: Which property of graphite makes it suitable for making electrodes?
questions.e: In graphite each carbon atom uses three electrons in bonds within a layer, and the fourth is delocalised, so graphite conducts electricity; it is also cheap and inert. Graphite is soft and slippery (diamond is the hard allotrope) and is black and opaque.

questions.s: Carbon dioxide is bubbled into limewater for a long time. What is observed?
o: It stays milky until the end
It turns milky, then clear again
It stays clear all the time
questions.e: First Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O makes the limewater milky. Excess CO₂ then dissolves the precipitate: CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca(HCO₃)₂, which is soluble, so the liquid clears. Stopping too early shows only the first step.

questions.s: Why is carbon monoxide poisonous?
o: It dissolves in blood to form a strong acid
It oxidises and destroys the cells of the lungs
It displaces the nitrogen needed by the lungs
It binds to haemoglobin so blood carries less O₂
questions.e: CO binds to haemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than oxygen, so the blood cannot carry enough O₂ to the body's tissues. CO is almost insoluble in water and is not acidic; it is a reducing agent, not an oxidising agent.

questions.s: Excess CO₂ is passed into a saturated solution of sodium carbonate. What is observed?
o: Bubbles of CO₂ are given off from the solution
No change, since CO₂ does not react with Na₂CO₃
White crystals form, because NaHCO₃ is less soluble
A white precipitate of CaCO₃ forms
questions.e: Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → 2NaHCO₃. More mass of salt is formed (2 × 84 = 168 g from 106 g), water is used up, and NaHCO₃ is less soluble than Na₂CO₃, so crystals of NaHCO₃ separate. No calcium is present, so CaCO₃ cannot form.

questions.s: In Hou's process for making sodium carbonate, ammonia is dissolved in brine first, and then CO₂ is passed in, precipitating NaHCO₃. Why is ammonia added before CO₂?
o: NH₃ makes the brine alkaline, so much more CO₂ can be absorbed
CO₂ would otherwise react with NaCl to form a precipitate
NH₃ is less soluble in water than CO₂
NH₃ acts as a catalyst for the reaction of CO₂ with water
questions.e: CO₂ is only slightly soluble in neutral brine, but ammonia is very soluble and makes the solution alkaline, so it can absorb a lot of acidic CO₂: NaCl + NH₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → NaHCO₃ + NH₄Cl. NH₃ is far more soluble than CO₂, and it is used up in the reaction, so it is not a catalyst.

questions.s: Which equation shows how kettle scale forms when temporary hard water containing calcium hydrogencarbonate is boiled?
questions.e: On boiling, soluble Ca(HCO₃)₂ decomposes to insoluble CaCO₃, which deposits as scale. The third equation is the reverse process, by which CO₂-rich water dissolves limestone. CaCO₃ only decomposes to CaO at about 900 °C, far above the temperature in a kettle.

questions.s: Which gas is the main cause of the enhanced greenhouse effect from burning fossil fuels?
questions.e: Burning coal, oil and gas adds large amounts of CO₂, which absorbs infrared radiation from the Earth's surface and traps heat. N₂, O₂ and Ar make up most of the air but absorb almost no infrared radiation; methane is another important greenhouse gas.

questions.s: 0.15 mol CO₂ is absorbed completely by a solution containing 0.2 mol NaOH. What is the mole ratio Na₂CO₃ : NaHCO₃ in the product?
questions.e: The NaOH : CO₂ ratio 0.2 : 0.15 lies between 2 : 1 (all Na₂CO₃) and 1 : 1 (all NaHCO₃), so both form. Conserving C and Na: x + y = 0.15 and 2x + y = 0.2, so x = 0.05 mol Na₂CO₃ and y = 0.10 mol NaHCO₃, ratio 1 : 2. The answer 2 : 1 swaps the two salts.

questions.s: Which substance is used to make the optical fibres in communication cables?
questions.e: Optical fibres are made of very pure silicon dioxide (silica glass), which carries light by total internal reflection. Elemental silicon is the semiconductor used in computer chips and solar cells, a common mix-up between Si and SiO₂.

questions.s: Which acid is used to etch patterns on glass?
questions.e: Hydrofluoric acid attacks the silica in glass: SiO₂ + 4HF → SiF₄ + 2H₂O. This is why HF is stored in plastic bottles. Silica does not react with hydrochloric, nitric or sulfuric acid.

questions.s: Sodium hydroxide solution is stored in glass bottles with rubber stoppers, not ground-glass stoppers. Why?
o: NaOH reacts with SiO₂, forming Na₂SiO₃, which glues the stopper
NaOH slowly escapes as vapour through the gap around a glass stopper
Glass slowly reduces NaOH to sodium metal
Light passing through glass decomposes NaOH
questions.e: SiO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SiO₃ + H₂O. On the rough ground-glass surface this happens enough for sodium silicate (water glass, an adhesive) to glue the stopper in. The smooth inside of the bottle is attacked very little, so the bottle itself is fine.

questions.s: Crude silicon is made by heating silica with coke in an electric furnace. Which equation is correct?
questions.e: At the very high temperature (about 2000 °C) with excess carbon, the oxide formed is CO, not CO₂ (any CO₂ would react with carbon: CO₂ + C → 2CO). So SiO₂ + 2C → Si + 2CO. CO is not a strong enough reducing agent to reduce silica.

questions.s: CO₂ is passed into sodium silicate (Na₂SiO₃) solution. What is observed?
o: Bubbles of a colourless gas are given off
questions.e: Na₂SiO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → H₂SiO₃ + Na₂CO₃: carbonic acid is stronger than silicic acid, so it releases insoluble silicic acid as a white gel. This reaction shows that carbon is more non-metallic than silicon.

questions.s: Which element is the main material of computer chips and solar cells?
questions.e: Very pure silicon is a semiconductor: its conductivity lies between that of metals and insulators and can be controlled, so it is used for chips and solar cells. Aluminium and copper are metallic conductors used for wiring, not as semiconductors.

questions.s: Which of these materials is NOT a traditional silicate product?
questions.e: Glass, cement and ceramics such as porcelain are made from silica and silicate minerals, so they are called silicate materials. Steel is an alloy of iron with a little carbon, made in a completely different way.

questions.s: 2.8 g of silicon reacts completely with excess NaOH solution: Si + 2NaOH + H₂O → Na₂SiO₃ + 2H₂. What volume of hydrogen is formed at STP (22.4 L/mol)? (Si = 28)
questions.e: n(Si) = 2.8/28 = 0.1 mol, and the equation gives 2 mol H₂ per mol Si, so n(H₂) = 0.2 mol and V = 0.2 × 22.4 = 4.48 L. Silicon goes from 0 to +4, losing 4 electrons, which matches 2 H₂. Answering 2.24 L takes a 1 : 1 ratio.

questions.s: In which group does every substance react with both dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution?
questions.e: Aluminium and its oxide and hydroxide are amphoteric, and HCO₃⁻ reacts with both H⁺ and OH⁻. Magnesium and iron compounds are basic and dissolve only in acid; copper does not react with dilute HCl at all, and Na₂CO₃ does not react with NaOH.

questions.s: Which substance is normally used to treat acidic soil on farms?
questions.e: Slaked lime is a cheap base that neutralises excess acid in soil and is only slightly soluble, so it acts gently. NaOH is too caustic and costly, ammonium chloride is an acidic salt, and adding sulfuric acid would make the soil even more acidic.

questions.s: Which oxide is an acidic oxide?
questions.e: SiO₂ reacts with bases to form a salt and water (SiO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SiO₃ + H₂O), so it is acidic even though it does not dissolve in water. CO and NO form no salts with bases or acids (they are neutral oxides), and Na₂O is a basic oxide.

questions.s: Open beakers of concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid are left in air for a few days. What happens to their masses and concentrations?
o: HCl: mass rises, concentration falls; H₂SO₄: mass rises, concentration rises
HCl: mass falls, concentration falls; H₂SO₄: mass rises, concentration falls
HCl: mass falls, concentration rises; H₂SO₄: mass falls, concentration falls
HCl: mass unchanged, concentration falls; H₂SO₄: mass falls, concentration rises
questions.e: Concentrated HCl is volatile: HCl gas escapes, so mass and concentration both fall. Concentrated H₂SO₄ is hygroscopic: it absorbs water vapour, so its mass rises but its concentration falls. Both acids therefore become more dilute, for different reasons.

questions.s: A mixture of 0.2 mol sodium and 0.1 mol aluminium is added to excess water. What total volume of hydrogen is produced at STP (22.4 L/mol)?
questions.e: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ gives 0.1 mol H₂ and 0.2 mol NaOH. The NaOH (in excess) then dissolves all the aluminium: 2Al + 2NaOH + 6H₂O → 2Na[Al(OH)₄] + 3H₂, giving 0.15 mol H₂. Total 0.25 mol, 5.60 L. Answering 2.24 L forgets that aluminium reacts with the NaOH formed.

questions.s: NaOH solution is added slowly to a solution containing 0.1 mol MgCl₂ and 0.1 mol AlCl₃. What is the minimum amount of NaOH needed so that the precipitate is Mg(OH)₂ only?
questions.e: Precipitating everything needs 2 × 0.1 + 3 × 0.1 = 0.5 mol OH⁻ (giving Mg(OH)₂ and Al(OH)₃). Dissolving the 0.1 mol Al(OH)₃ as [Al(OH)₄]⁻ needs 0.1 mol more, so 0.6 mol in total leaves only Mg(OH)₂. 0.5 mol is the point of maximum precipitate, when Al(OH)₃ is still present.

questions.s: Rain is called acid rain when its pH is below which value?
questions.e: Normal rain is already slightly acidic, pH about 5.6, because dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid. Rain with pH below 5.6 contains extra acids, mainly from SO₂ and nitrogen oxides. Using 7.0 forgets the natural effect of CO₂.

questions.s: Which substances are mainly responsible for the thinning of the ozone layer?
questions.e: In the stratosphere, UV light breaks CFC molecules and releases chlorine atoms, which destroy ozone in a chain reaction. CO₂ is a greenhouse gas and SO₂ causes acid rain; neither is the main cause of ozone loss.

questions.s: A lake turns green with algae and its fish die from lack of oxygen (eutrophication). Which pollutants most likely caused this?
o: Dissolved carbon dioxide absorbed from the air above the lake
Nitrates and phosphates from farms and detergents
questions.e: Nitrates and phosphates are plant nutrients; in excess they make algae grow rapidly, and when the algae die, bacteria decomposing them use up dissolved oxygen, so fish die. Sand, chloride ions and CO₂ do not act as fertilisers in this way.

questions.s: Iodised table salt in many countries, including China and Pakistan, contains a small amount of which compound?
questions.e: Potassium iodate, KIO₃, is stable in storage and supplies iodine to prevent goitre. Elemental iodine is volatile and toxic in quantity, while KClO₃ and KMnO₄ contain no iodine and are strong oxidising agents.

questions.s: Which compound is used in baking powder to make cakes rise when heated?
questions.e: Sodium hydrogencarbonate releases CO₂ on heating (2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂) and with acids in the mixture, and the gas makes the dough rise. Na₂CO₃ is stable to heat and much more alkaline, so it would not release gas in the oven.

questions.s: Which measure would NOT reduce the amount of acid rain?
o: Removing sulfur from coal before it is burned
Building taller chimneys at power stations
Using more solar and wind power
questions.e: Taller chimneys only carry SO₂ and NOₓ further away; the same amount of acid-forming gas is released and the acid rain falls elsewhere. Desulfurisation, catalytic converters (which remove NOₓ) and replacing fossil fuels all reduce emissions.

questions.s: Sodium can be cut easily with a knife, and the shiny cut surface turns dull within seconds. What do these observations show?
o: It is hard and unreactive in air
It is hard and reacts readily with oxygen
It is soft and reacts readily with oxygen
It is soft and unreactive in air
questions.e: Being cut by a knife shows sodium is soft; the shiny surface tarnishing quickly shows it reacts readily with oxygen in air (4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O). A metal unreactive in air, such as gold, would stay shiny.

questions.s: Which statement about Na₂O and Na₂O₂ is correct?
o: Both form NaOH with water, but only Na₂O₂ also releases O₂
Oxygen has an oxidation state of −2 in both
questions.e: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH, while 2Na₂O₂ + 2H₂O → 4NaOH + O₂. Na₂O₂ is pale yellow, contains O₂²⁻ with oxygen at −1, and is not a basic oxide because it gives O₂ as well as salt and water with acids.

questions.s: 3.0 g of a mixture of CO and H₂ is burned completely in excess oxygen, and all the products are passed through excess Na₂O₂. By how much does the mass of the solid increase?
o: It depends on the CO : H₂ ratio
questions.e: 2Na₂O₂ + 2CO₂ → 2Na₂CO₃ + O₂: the solid gains the mass of 'CO' for each CO₂ absorbed. 2Na₂O₂ + 2H₂O → 4NaOH + O₂: it gains the mass of 'H₂' for each H₂O. So the gain equals the original mass of CO and H₂, 3.0 g, whatever the ratio; the O₂ used in burning is given back.

questions.s: A solution of NaHCO₃ contains a little Na₂CO₃. What is the best way to remove the Na₂CO₃?
o: Add the right amount of NaOH solution
questions.e: Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → 2NaHCO₃ turns the impurity into the wanted salt, and excess CO₂ does no harm. NaOH would do the opposite (turn NaHCO₃ into Na₂CO₃), heating decomposes NaHCO₃, and limewater precipitates both carbonate ions.

questions.s: Why is magnesium powder used in fireworks and flares?
o: It burns with a dazzling white light
It burns with a deep blue flame
It burns with a green flame
It burns with a yellow, smoky flame
questions.e: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO releases a lot of energy as a brilliant white light, so magnesium is used in flares and to make firework colours brighter. A green flame is typical of copper or barium, and a yellow one of sodium.

questions.s: 2.4 g of magnesium burns completely in carbon dioxide. What is the total mass of the solid products? (Mg = 24, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.e: 2Mg + CO₂ → 2MgO + C. n(Mg) = 0.1 mol gives 0.1 mol MgO (4.0 g) and 0.05 mol carbon (0.6 g), total 4.6 g. Answering 4.0 g forgets that the black carbon is also a solid product.

questions.s: Which metal is the most abundant in the Earth's crust?
questions.e: Aluminium makes up about 8 % of the crust by mass, ahead of iron (about 5 %). Even so, aluminium was rare and costly until electrolysis made extraction from bauxite practical, because Al³⁺ is hard to reduce.

questions.s: Aluminium chloride solution is added drop by drop to sodium hydroxide solution, with shaking, until the AlCl₃ is in excess. What is observed?
o: A white precipitate at once, which then dissolves
A white precipitate at once, which stays
No lasting precipitate at first, then a white precipitate that stays
questions.e: At first OH⁻ is in excess, so any Al(OH)₃ dissolves at once: Al³⁺ + 4OH⁻ → [Al(OH)₄]⁻. Later, added Al³⁺ reacts with the aluminate: Al³⁺ + 3[Al(OH)₄]⁻ → 4Al(OH)₃, a lasting white precipitate. 'Precipitate then dissolves' is the order seen when NaOH is added to AlCl₃.

questions.s: In a thermite reaction, 5.4 g of aluminium reacts completely with excess iron(III) oxide. What mass of iron is formed? (Al = 27, Fe = 56)
questions.e: 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe: 1 mol Fe per mol Al. n(Al) = 5.4/27 = 0.2 mol, so n(Fe) = 0.2 mol = 11.2 g. Answering 5.6 g assumes 2 Al per Fe, the reverse of the true ratio.

questions.s: Ba(OH)₂ solution is added to KAl(SO₄)₂ solution until all the sulfate is just precipitated as BaSO₄. In what form is the aluminium then present?
questions.e: 1 mol KAl(SO₄)₂ has 2 mol SO₄²⁻, needing 2 mol Ba(OH)₂, which also supplies 4 mol OH⁻. With 4 OH⁻ per Al³⁺: Al³⁺ + 4OH⁻ → [Al(OH)₄]⁻, so no Al(OH)₃ remains. Maximum Al(OH)₃ occurs earlier, at 3 OH⁻ per Al³⁺ (1.5 mol Ba(OH)₂).

questions.s: Why should acidic or salty foods not be stored for a long time in aluminium pans?
o: Aluminium is magnetic and spoils food
Aluminium melts at normal cooking temperatures
Aluminium reacts with pure water at room temperature
The oxide layer and the metal are attacked by acids and salt
questions.e: The protective Al₂O₃ film is amphoteric and dissolves in acids (and alkalis), and chloride ions also break it down; the exposed aluminium then dissolves, contaminating the food. Aluminium is not magnetic and melts at 660 °C, far above cooking temperatures.

questions.s: Which iron oxide is black and strongly magnetic?
questions.e: Fe₃O₄ (magnetite) is the black magnetic oxide, formed for example when iron burns in oxygen or reacts with steam. FeO is black but not strongly magnetic, Fe₂O₃ is red-brown, and Fe(OH)₃ is a red-brown hydroxide, not an oxide.

questions.s: An iron nail is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution. When it is removed, dried and weighed, its mass has increased by 0.8 g. What mass of copper was deposited? (Fe = 56, Cu = 64)
questions.e: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu: for each mole, 56 g Fe dissolves and 64 g Cu is deposited, a gain of 8 g. A gain of 0.8 g means 0.1 mol, so 6.4 g of copper was deposited. 5.6 g is the mass of iron that dissolved.

questions.s: An FeCl₂ solution contains a little FeCl₃. What is the best way to remove the FeCl₃?
o: Add excess iron powder, then filter
questions.e: 2FeCl₃ + Fe → 3FeCl₂ converts the impurity into the wanted compound, and the unused iron is filtered off. Copper would remove Fe³⁺ but add Cu²⁺ as a new impurity, chlorine would oxidise the FeCl₂, and NaOH precipitates both iron ions.

questions.s: An FeCl₃ solution contains a little FeCl₂. What is the best way to remove the FeCl₂?
o: Add excess iron powder, then filter
questions.e: 2FeCl₂ + Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃ turns the impurity into the wanted compound without adding new ions. Iron powder would do the reverse, KSCN only detects Fe³⁺, and copper reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ while adding Cu²⁺.

questions.s: Excess iron powder is added to dilute nitric acid containing 0.8 mol HNO₃, and the only gas formed is NO. How many moles of iron dissolve?
questions.e: With iron in excess, any Fe³⁺ formed is reduced by more iron (2Fe³⁺ + Fe → 3Fe²⁺), so the overall reaction is 3Fe + 8HNO₃ → 3Fe(NO₃)₂ + 2NO + 4H₂O. 0.8 mol HNO₃ dissolves 0.3 mol Fe. Answering 0.2 mol uses Fe + 4HNO₃ → Fe(NO₃)₃ + NO + 2H₂O, which applies only when acid is in excess.

questions.s: Which substances must both be present for iron to rust?
