questions.e: The negative electrode is the one that is oxidised by the electrolyte. Aluminium reacts with NaOH (Al + 4OH⁻ → [Al(OH)₄]⁻ + 3e⁻) but magnesium does not, so Al is negative even though Mg is the more reactive metal. In dilute acid the answer would be Mg.

questions.s: A zinc–copper cell uses CuSO₄ solution as the electrolyte. After 0.2 mol of electrons has passed through the external circuit, how have the electrode masses changed? (Zn = 65, Cu = 64)
o: Zn loses 6.5 g; Cu gains 6.4 g
Zn loses 13 g; Cu gains 12.8 g
Zn loses 6.5 g; Cu gains 3.2 g
Zn gains 6.5 g; Cu loses 6.4 g
questions.e: Each Zn and each Cu²⁺ transfers 2 electrons, so 0.2 mol electrons means 0.1 mol Zn dissolves (6.5 g) and 0.1 mol Cu is deposited (6.4 g). Using 0.2 mol of each metal forgets the factor 2 and gives 13 g and 12.8 g.

questions.s: A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell uses potassium hydroxide solution as the electrolyte. What is the reaction at the positive electrode?
questions.e: At the positive electrode oxygen is reduced, and in alkaline solution the product is OH⁻: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. The equation with 4H⁺ applies to an acidic electrolyte, and H₂ + 2OH⁻ → 2H₂O + 2e⁻ is the negative-electrode reaction.

questions.s: A steel nail in moist, nearly neutral air rusts by oxygen-absorption corrosion. Which reaction occurs at the positive (cathodic) regions of the metal surface?
questions.e: Iron is oxidised at the negative regions, and the electrons reduce dissolved oxygen at the positive regions: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. Hydrogen evolution needs a clearly acidic film, and 4OH⁻ → O₂ is an oxidation, so it cannot take place at the positive regions.

questions.s: Blocks of a metal are fixed to a ship's steel hull so that they corrode instead of the iron. Which metal is suitable?
questions.e: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it becomes the negative electrode and is oxidised while the iron is protected (sacrificial anode protection). Copper, tin and lead are less reactive than iron, so attaching them would make the iron corrode faster.

questions.s: Copper(II) chloride solution is electrolysed using inert carbon electrodes. What forms at the cathode?
questions.e: Cations move to the cathode and are reduced; Cu²⁺ is reduced much more easily than water, so Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Chlorine forms at the anode, where Cl⁻ is oxidised, not at the cathode.

questions.s: Concentrated sodium chloride solution containing a few drops of phenolphthalein is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which observation is made?
o: Sodium metal is deposited on the cathode
Oxygen is the main gas at the anode
Pink colour appears around the anode
Pink colour appears around the cathode
questions.e: At the cathode water is reduced: 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻, and the OH⁻ turns phenolphthalein pink. At the anode concentrated Cl⁻ is oxidised to Cl₂, so oxygen is not the main product, and Na⁺ is far harder to reduce than water, so no sodium forms.

questions.s: Copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes until about half of the Cu²⁺ has been used. Which substance, added in the right amount, restores the solution to its original composition?
questions.e: The overall reaction 2CuSO₄ + 2H₂O → 2Cu + O₂ + 2H₂SO₄ removes copper and oxygen in a 1:1 atom ratio, which is CuO; CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O then restores the solution. Cu(OH)₂ would add extra water, Cu does not react with dilute H₂SO₄, and adding CuSO₄ leaves the acid behind.

questions.s: Dilute copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which statement is correct?
questions.e: At the anode water is oxidised: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻, so H⁺ accumulates and the pH falls. Copper is deposited at the cathode, so the blue colour fades. An inert anode cannot dissolve; that happens only with a copper anode.

questions.s: An iron spoon is to be electroplated with silver. How should the cell be set up?
o: Spoon as anode, silver as cathode, AgNO₃ solution
Spoon as cathode, silver as anode, NaCl solution
Spoon as cathode, silver as anode, AgNO₃ solution
Spoon as anode, silver as cathode, NaCl solution
questions.e: Silver must be deposited on the spoon, so the spoon is the cathode where Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag. The silver anode dissolves to replace the Ag⁺, and the electrolyte must contain Ag⁺, such as AgNO₃. Making the spoon the anode would dissolve the spoon.

questions.s: Impure copper containing small amounts of Zn, Fe, Ag and Au is purified by electrolysis in CuSO₄ solution. Which statement is correct?
o: The Cu²⁺ concentration stays exactly constant
Silver and gold collect as anode mud
Zinc is deposited on the cathode
questions.e: The impure copper is the anode. Zn and Fe, being more reactive, dissolve as ions along with Cu, but Ag and Au are harder to oxidise and fall to the bottom as anode mud. Zn²⁺ stays in solution because Cu²⁺ is reduced in preference, and since Zn and Fe dissolve while only Cu deposits, the Cu²⁺ concentration slowly falls.

questions.s: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What is the ratio of the volume of gas at the cathode to that at the anode, measured under the same conditions?
questions.e: Cathode: 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂; anode: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻. For 4 mol electrons, 2 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂ form, so the ratio is 2:1. 1:2 swaps the electrodes.

questions.s: Copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes, and 6.4 g of copper is deposited. What volume of oxygen forms at the anode, measured at STP? (Cu = 64; molar volume 22.4 L/mol)
questions.e: 6.4 g Cu is 0.1 mol, needing 0.2 mol electrons. Each O₂ releases 4 electrons, so 0.2/4 = 0.05 mol O₂, which is 0.05 × 22.4 = 1.12 L. 2.24 L comes from assuming one O₂ per Cu.

questions.s: Which statement about electrolysis is correct?
o: Electrolysis is a spontaneous redox reaction
The cathode is joined to the negative pole
questions.e: The cathode is connected to the negative pole of the power supply, receives electrons and is where reduction occurs. Oxidation occurs at the anode, anions move towards the anode, and electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous reaction.

questions.s: Sodium is made by electrolysing molten sodium chloride, not sodium chloride solution. What is the reason?
o: Water is reduced more easily than Na⁺
Na⁺ ions are absent from the solution
Molten NaCl contains no chloride ions
Sodium forms but chlorine destroys it
questions.e: In aqueous solution water is reduced at the cathode (2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻) in preference to Na⁺, so no sodium is obtained. The solution certainly contains Na⁺, and molten NaCl contains both Na⁺ and Cl⁻; the problem is the competing reduction of water.

questions.s: Silver nitrate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. When the cathode has gained 2.16 g of silver, what volume of oxygen has formed at the anode, measured at STP? (Ag = 108; molar volume 22.4 L/mol)
questions.e: 2.16/108 = 0.02 mol Ag, which needs 0.02 mol electrons (Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag). Each O₂ releases 4 electrons, so 0.005 mol O₂ = 0.005 × 22 400 mL = 112 mL. 224 mL comes from using 2 electrons per O₂.

questions.s: Sodium sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which statement is correct?
o: Sodium is deposited at the cathode
Sulfur dioxide forms at the anode
Water is decomposed into H₂ and O₂
questions.e: Na⁺ is harder to reduce than water and SO₄²⁻ is harder to oxidise than water, so H₂ forms at the cathode and O₂ at the anode. The net change is 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂; Na₂SO₄ is unchanged in amount and only makes the solution conduct.

questions.s: A lead–acid battery discharges by the reaction Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O. Which statement about discharge is correct?
questions.e: Sulfuric acid is used up and water is formed, so its concentration falls. Pb (0 → +2) is oxidised at the negative electrode and PbO₂ (+4 → +2) is reduced at the positive electrode. Both electrodes become coated with insoluble PbSO₄, so both get heavier.

questions.s: When a lead–acid battery is recharged, its negative electrode is connected to which pole of the charger, and what process occurs at that electrode?
questions.e: Charging reverses discharge: the battery's negative electrode must now be a cathode, so it is joined to the charger's negative pole and PbSO₄ + 2e⁻ → Pb + SO₄²⁻ (reduction) takes place. Joining negative to positive would discharge the battery further.

questions.s: Which reaction could be used as the basis of a galvanic cell?
questions.e: A galvanic cell needs a spontaneous redox reaction so that electrons can be sent through a wire. Cu + 2Fe³⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Fe²⁺ transfers electrons from Cu to Fe³⁺. The other three reactions involve no change in oxidation state, even though they release energy.

questions.s: A galvanic cell is to be built using the reaction Cu + 2Fe³⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Fe²⁺. Which arrangement is correct?
o: Cu negative, graphite positive, FeCl₃ electrolyte
Cu positive, Zn negative, FeCl₃ electrolyte
Cu negative, Fe positive, CuSO₄ electrolyte
Graphite negative, Cu positive, FeCl₃ electrolyte
questions.e: Copper is oxidised, so it must be the negative electrode, and Fe³⁺ must be in the electrolyte to be reduced at an inert positive electrode such as graphite. With zinc as the negative electrode, zinc rather than copper would be oxidised, and CuSO₄ contains no Fe³⁺ to be reduced.

questions.s: Two metals A and B are joined by a wire and dipped into dilute sulfuric acid. Metal A gradually dissolves and bubbles of gas form on B. Which statement is correct?
o: Electrons flow from B to A
A is more reactive than B
questions.e: A dissolves, so it is oxidised and is the negative electrode, which means A is the more reactive metal. Electrons flow from A to B through the wire, and H⁺ is reduced to H₂ at B, so reduction occurs at B, not A.

questions.s: In which reaction is the same element both oxidised and reduced?
questions.e: In Na₂O₂ oxygen is −1; some of it goes to −2 (in NaOH) and some to 0 (in O₂), so oxygen is both oxidised and reduced. In the sodium and CuO reactions two different elements change, and decomposing NaHCO₃ involves no redox at all.

questions.s: Sodium peroxide is used in breathing apparatus: 2Na₂O₂ + 2CO₂ → 2Na₂CO₃ + O₂. How many moles of electrons are transferred when 1 mol Na₂O₂ reacts?
questions.e: 2 mol Na₂O₂ give 1 mol O₂: two O atoms go from −1 to 0, transferring 2 mol electrons (the other two O go from −1 to −2). So 1 mol Na₂O₂ transfers 1 mol electrons. 2 mol counts both the loss and the gain of the same electrons.

questions.s: Hydrogen is passed over heated copper(II) oxide: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O. Which substance is oxidised?
questions.e: Hydrogen goes from 0 to +1 in H₂O, so it loses electrons and is oxidised; it is the reducing agent. CuO is reduced (Cu +2 → 0), and Cu and H₂O are products, not substances that are oxidised.

questions.s: Which substance is commonly used as an oxidising agent in the laboratory?
questions.e: In KMnO₄ manganese is in its highest state, +7, so it readily gains electrons and acts as a strong oxidising agent. H₂, CO and Zn are typical reducing agents: they are easily oxidised.

questions.s: Sulfur dioxide is bubbled into acidified potassium permanganate solution, and the purple colour disappears as sulfate ions form. Which property of SO₂ does this show?
questions.e: Sulfur rises from +4 in SO₂ to +6 in SO₄²⁻ while MnO₄⁻ is reduced to almost colourless Mn²⁺, so SO₂ is a reducing agent. Its bleaching action is a separate effect on certain dyes such as magenta, and acidity alone cannot reduce permanganate.

questions.s: In which reaction does hydrogen peroxide act as a reducing agent?
questions.e: With Cl₂, the oxygen in H₂O₂ rises from −1 to 0 in O₂, so H₂O₂ is oxidised and acts as a reducing agent. In the other three reactions its oxygen falls from −1 to −2, so H₂O₂ is the oxidising agent, which is its more usual role.

questions.s: Which reaction is NOT a redox reaction?
questions.e: In Fe₂O₃ + 6HCl, iron stays +3, chlorine stays −1 and oxygen stays −2, so it is simply an acid reacting with a basic oxide. Each of the other reactions changes the oxidation state of iron and of chlorine or iodine.

questions.s: 1.92 g of copper dissolves completely in concentrated nitric acid, giving a mixture of NO₂ and NO. The gas is mixed with oxygen and absorbed in water so that all of it is converted back to HNO₃. What volume of O₂ at STP is needed? (Cu = 64; molar volume 22.4 L/mol)
questions.e: Nitrogen starts and ends at +5, so overall the electrons lost by copper are gained by oxygen. Cu: 1.92/64 = 0.03 mol, losing 0.06 mol electrons; O₂ gains 4 each, so 0.015 mol O₂ = 336 mL. 672 mL comes from using 2 electrons per O₂.

questions.s: Thiosulfate reacts with iodine to form the tetrathionate ion: 2S₂O₃²⁻ + I₂ → S₄O₆²⁻ + 2I⁻. What is the average oxidation state of sulfur in S₄O₆²⁻?
questions.e: 4S + 6(−2) = −2 gives 4S = +10, so the average is +2.5. Sulfur in S₂O₃²⁻ averages +2, so it is oxidised while iodine is reduced. Ignoring the ion's charge gives +3.

questions.s: What is the oxidation state of nitrogen in nitric acid, HNO₃?
questions.e: +1 + N + 3(−2) = 0 gives N = +5, the highest state of nitrogen. +3 is nitrogen in HNO₂ and +4 in NO₂.

questions.s: In copper smelting, 2Cu₂O + Cu₂S → 6Cu + SO₂ on heating. Which statement is correct?
o: Cu₂S is the reducing agent only
Cu₂S is both oxidising and reducing agent
Copper metal is the oxidation product
Forming 1 mol SO₂ transfers 3 mol electrons
questions.e: Copper is +1 in both Cu₂O and Cu₂S and falls to 0, so both are oxidising agents; sulfur in Cu₂S rises from −2 to +4, so Cu₂S is also the reducing agent. Each SO₂ formed means 6 electrons lost by S, gained by six Cu⁺. Copper is the reduction product, not the oxidation product.

questions.s: What happens to a reducing agent in a redox reaction?
o: It gains electrons and is reduced
It gains electrons and is oxidised
It loses electrons and is reduced
It loses electrons and is oxidised
questions.e: A reducing agent gives electrons to another substance, so it loses electrons and is itself oxidised. Gaining electrons and being reduced describes the oxidising agent; the other two options pair the electron change with the wrong process.

questions.s: Aluminium is extracted by electrolysing molten aluminium oxide. How many moles of electrons are needed to produce 54 g of aluminium? (Al = 27)
questions.e: 54/27 = 2 mol Al, and each Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al needs 3 electrons, so 6 mol electrons. 3 mol is the amount for only 1 mol (27 g) of aluminium.

questions.s: What is the oxidation state of phosphorus in phosphoric acid, H₃PO₄?
questions.e: 3(+1) + P + 4(−2) = 0 gives P = +5. +3 is phosphorus in H₃PO₃ or PCl₃; forgetting to count all three hydrogens gives a wrong value.

questions.s: Potassium ferrate, K₂FeO₄, is used to treat drinking water. What is the oxidation state of iron in it?
questions.e: 2(+1) + Fe + 4(−2) = 0 gives Fe = +6, an unusually high state that makes ferrate a strong oxidising agent. Assuming iron must be +2 or +3, as in its common salts, is the trap.

questions.s: In the reaction Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu, which species is reduced?
questions.e: Cu²⁺ gains two electrons and becomes Cu, so it is reduced. Fe is oxidised to Fe²⁺, and sulfate is a spectator ion whose oxidation states do not change.

questions.s: Which of these reactions involves electron transfer?
questions.e: Hydrogen goes from 0 to +1 and oxygen from 0 to −2, so electrons are transferred. In the other reactions every element keeps its oxidation state: they are combination and double decomposition reactions without redox.

questions.s: Magnesium burns in carbon dioxide: 2Mg + CO₂ → 2MgO + C. Which statement is correct?
questions.e: Carbon in CO₂ is +4 and becomes 0 in C, so CO₂ is reduced and is the oxidising agent. Mg (0 → +2) is oxidised and is the reducing agent, so MgO is the oxidation product and carbon is the reduction product.

questions.s: Which conversion can only be achieved by adding an oxidising agent?
questions.e: Iodine rises from −1 to 0, so electrons must be removed by an oxidising agent such as Cl₂. Cu²⁺ → Cu and H⁺ → H₂ are reductions, and CO₃²⁻ → CO₂ keeps carbon at +4 and needs only an acid.

questions.s: Iron reacts with hydrochloric acid: Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂. How many moles of electrons are transferred when 5.6 g of iron reacts? (Fe = 56)
questions.e: 5.6/56 = 0.1 mol Fe, and each Fe loses 2 electrons to become Fe²⁺, giving 0.2 mol. 0.15 mol would follow from assuming Fe³⁺, which dilute HCl does not produce.

questions.s: Which ionic equation is balanced in both atoms and charge?
questions.e: Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag has +2 on each side and two electrons lost by Cu equal two gained by Ag⁺. The others balance atoms but not charge: Cu + Ag⁺ (+1 vs +2), Fe³⁺ + Cu (+3 vs +4) and Al + 2H⁺ (+2 vs +3).

questions.s: When the equation Cr₂O₇²⁻ + Fe²⁺ + H⁺ → Cr³⁺ + Fe³⁺ + H₂O is balanced with the smallest whole numbers, what is the coefficient of H⁺?
questions.e: Two Cr gain 2 × 3 = 6 electrons, so 6Fe²⁺ are oxidised; the seven O atoms form 7H₂O, needing 14H⁺: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O. Charge: −2 + 12 + 14 = 24 = 6 + 18. 6 is the Fe²⁺ coefficient and 7 the water coefficient.

questions.s: Iodate oxidises iodide in acid: IO₃⁻ + 5I⁻ + 6H⁺ → 3I₂ + 3H₂O. What is the mass ratio of iodine formed by oxidation to iodine formed by reduction?
questions.e: Five I⁻ are oxidised from −1 to 0 and one I in IO₃⁻ is reduced from +5 to 0, so of the six I atoms in 3I₂, five come from oxidation and one from reduction: 5:1. 1:5 gives the ratio the wrong way round.

questions.s: A zinc strip and a copper strip in dilute sulfuric acid are joined by a wire. Which way do electrons flow in the wire?
questions.e: Zinc is more reactive, so it is oxidised and releases electrons, which flow through the wire to copper, where H⁺ is reduced to H₂. Inside the acid, charge is carried by ions, not electrons.

questions.s: Pairs of electrodes are dipped into dilute sulfuric acid and joined by a wire. Which pair gives no current?
questions.e: A galvanic cell needs a spontaneous redox reaction. Neither copper nor carbon reacts with dilute sulfuric acid, so no electrons are pushed round the circuit. In each other pair the more reactive metal (Zn or Fe) is oxidised and H₂ forms at the other electrode.

questions.s: A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell uses dilute sulfuric acid as the electrolyte. What is the reaction at the negative electrode?
questions.e: Hydrogen is oxidised at the negative electrode, and in acid the product is H⁺: H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻. The OH⁻ version applies to an alkaline electrolyte, and the O₂ equations describe the positive electrode.

questions.s: Copper(II) chloride solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. When 0.2 mol Cl₂ has formed at the anode, what mass of copper has been deposited at the cathode? (Cu = 64)
questions.e: Forming 0.2 mol Cl₂ releases 0.4 mol electrons, and each Cu²⁺ needs 2 electrons, so 0.2 mol Cu = 12.8 g is deposited. 25.6 g comes from using one electron per Cu²⁺.

questions.s: Tinplate is iron coated with tin; galvanised iron is iron coated with zinc. Which statement is correct once the coating is scratched through to the iron?
o: Scratched tinplate rusts faster than plain iron
Tin protects iron even after scratching
Zinc coating stops protecting once scratched
Iron is the positive electrode in scratched tinplate
questions.e: Iron is more reactive than tin, so at a scratch the iron becomes the negative electrode and corrodes even faster than it would alone. Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it keeps corroding sacrificially and protects the iron after scratching.

questions.s: Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the anode?
questions.e: Br⁻ ions move to the anode and are oxidised: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻. Lead forms at the cathode. There is no water in a molten salt, so hydrogen and oxygen cannot form.

questions.s: Both of these reactions occur: Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag and Fe + Cu²⁺ → Fe²⁺ + Cu. Which species is the strongest oxidising agent?
questions.e: An oxidising agent is stronger than the oxidised product it forms. The first reaction gives Ag⁺ > Cu²⁺ and the second gives Cu²⁺ > Fe²⁺, so Ag⁺ is strongest. Iron metal is the strongest reducing agent here, not an oxidising agent.

questions.s: Hydrogen sulfide reduces iron(III) ions: 2Fe³⁺ + H₂S → 2Fe²⁺ + S + 2H⁺. How many moles of electrons are transferred when 3.2 g of sulfur is formed? (S = 32)
questions.e: 3.2/32 = 0.1 mol S, and each S goes from −2 to 0, losing 2 electrons, so 0.2 mol electrons, gained by 0.2 mol Fe³⁺. 0.1 mol forgets that each sulfur atom loses two electrons.

questions.s: Passing 0.2 mol of electrons through a solution of a salt of metal M deposits 6.4 g of M at the cathode. The relative atomic mass of M is 64. What is the charge on the metal ion?
questions.e: 6.4/64 = 0.1 mol M needs 0.2 mol electrons, which is 2 electrons per ion, so the ion is M²⁺. Taking the electrons as equal to the moles of metal gives +1.

questions.s: Ozone is detected with moist potassium iodide: O₃ + 2KI + H₂O → 2KOH + I₂ + O₂. Which statement is correct?
questions.e: Only one O atom of each O₃ is reduced, from 0 to −2 (ending in KOH), so 1 mol O₃ gains 2 mol electrons, matching 2 I⁻ → I₂. The O₂ keeps oxidation state 0, so it is neither oxidation nor reduction product; 6 mol assumes all three O atoms are reduced.

questions.s: Which substance is an electrolyte?
questions.e: An electrolyte is a compound that conducts when molten or dissolved because it forms ions; NaCl gives Na⁺ and Cl⁻. Copper conducts by electrons but is an element, so it is neither an electrolyte nor a non-electrolyte; sucrose and ethanol dissolve as molecules.

questions.s: Which substance is a non-electrolyte?
questions.e: CO₂ itself does not ionise; its solution conducts only because some of it forms H₂CO₃, which ionises. Acetic acid is a weak electrolyte, and BaSO₄ and NaOH are strong electrolytes.

questions.s: Which statement about electrolytes and electrical conduction is correct?
o: BaSO₄ is insoluble but is a strong electrolyte
Copper conducts electricity, so it is an electrolyte
Solid NaCl does not conduct, so it is not an electrolyte
NH₃ solution conducts, so NH₃ is an electrolyte
questions.e: Whether a substance is a strong electrolyte depends on whether the part that dissolves (or the melt) is fully ionised, not on solubility; dissolved BaSO₄ is completely ionised. Copper is an element, solid NaCl is an electrolyte because it conducts when molten or dissolved, and NH₃ solution conducts because of NH₃·H₂O, not NH₃ itself.

questions.s: Hydrogen chloride gas and liquid hydrogen chloride do not conduct electricity, but hydrochloric acid does. Which statement is correct?
o: HCl ionises when it dissolves in water
questions.e: HCl is a covalent molecule; only when it dissolves does water pull it apart into H⁺ and Cl⁻, which then carry current. Because pure HCl has no free ions it cannot be ionic, and since the ionisation in water is complete, it is a strong electrolyte.

questions.s: Which equation correctly shows the dissociation of the substance in water?
questions.e: HSO₄⁻ comes from a strong acid and is fully ionised in water, so NaHSO₄ → Na⁺ + H⁺ + SO₄²⁻. HCO₃⁻ stays largely intact, so NaHCO₃ → Na⁺ + HCO₃⁻; acetic acid is weak and needs ⇌; and Ba(OH)₂ gives Ba²⁺ + 2OH⁻.

questions.s: Dilute sulfuric acid is added gradually to barium hydroxide solution until the acid is in excess. How does the electrical conductivity of the mixture change?
o: It falls steadily to zero and stays there
It falls to nearly zero, then rises
questions.e: Ba²⁺ + 2OH⁻ + 2H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄ + 2H₂O removes ions as a precipitate and water, so the conductivity drops to almost zero at the equivalence point. Extra H₂SO₄ then supplies H⁺ and SO₄²⁻, so it rises again; it does not stay at zero.

questions.s: Which solution conducts electricity best?
questions.e: Conductivity depends on the concentration and charge of the ions. CaCl₂ gives 0.1 mol/L Ca²⁺ and 0.2 mol/L Cl⁻, more ions and more charge than NaCl (0.1 + 0.1). Acetic acid is only slightly ionised, and ethanol gives no ions.

questions.s: Ammonia solution conducts electricity poorly. When an equal amount of acetic acid of the same concentration is added, the conductivity increases greatly. Why?
o: Both are strong electrolytes on their own
The salt formed is a strong electrolyte
Water forms and water conducts well
Ammonia gas escapes from the solution
questions.e: NH₃·H₂O + CH₃COOH → CH₃COONH₄ + H₂O, and the salt ammonium acetate is fully ionised, so the ion concentration rises sharply. NH₃·H₂O and CH₃COOH are both weak electrolytes, and water is an extremely poor conductor.

questions.s: Which statement about strong electrolytes is correct?
o: Their solutions always conduct better than weak ones
They must be soluble in water
They are fully ionised in aqueous solution
questions.e: A strong electrolyte is completely ionised in water. A very dilute strong electrolyte can conduct worse than a concentrated weak one, insoluble salts such as BaSO₄ are strong electrolytes, and HCl is a covalent strong electrolyte.

questions.s: Which reaction is correctly represented by the ionic equation H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O?
questions.e: NaOH and HNO₃ are a strong soluble base and a strong acid, and NaNO₃ is soluble, so only H⁺ and OH⁻ react. Ba(OH)₂ + H₂SO₄ also forms BaSO₄, acetic acid must be written as CH₃COOH, and insoluble Mg(OH)₂ must be written as a formula.

questions.s: Which reaction is correctly represented by the ionic equation CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O?
questions.e: K₂CO₃ is a soluble carbonate and HNO₃ a strong acid, so both are written as ions and only CO₃²⁻ and H⁺ react. CaCO₃ is insoluble, acetic acid is weak and NaHCO₃ supplies HCO₃⁻, so each of those needs a different equation.

questions.s: Which of these ionic equations is correctly written?
questions.e: CaCO₃ is insoluble so it keeps its formula, and atoms and charge (+2 each side) balance. Fe³⁺ + Fe → 2Fe²⁺ has charge +3 on the left and +4 on the right (correct: 2Fe³⁺ + Fe → 3Fe²⁺); the sodium equation is not balanced in H; and soluble CuCl₂ should be written as ions.

questions.s: What is the ionic equation for the reaction of barium hydroxide solution with dilute sulfuric acid?
o: Ba²⁺ + OH⁻ + H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄ + H₂O
questions.e: A precipitate and water form together, so all four ions must appear, in the 1 : 2 ratios fixed by the formulas Ba(OH)₂ and H₂SO₄. The version with one OH⁻ and one H⁺ breaks the formula ratio, and the two short equations each leave out one of the reactions.

questions.s: What is the ionic equation for the reaction of sodium hydrogencarbonate solution with hydrochloric acid?
questions.e: NaHCO₃ dissolves as Na⁺ and HCO₃⁻, and HCO₃⁻ is not split further, so HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O. Writing CO₃²⁻ treats it as sodium carbonate, and keeping NaHCO₃ whole ignores that it is a soluble, fully dissociated salt.

questions.s: Excess carbon dioxide is bubbled into sodium hydroxide solution. What is the overall ionic equation?
questions.e: With CO₂ in excess, the carbonate first formed reacts further (CO₃²⁻ + CO₂ + H₂O → 2HCO₃⁻), giving overall CO₂ + OH⁻ → HCO₃⁻. CO₂ + 2OH⁻ → CO₃²⁻ + H₂O applies when NaOH is in excess, and NaHCO₃ is soluble so it is written as ions.

questions.s: An iron nail is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution. What is the ionic equation?
questions.e: Iron displaces copper and forms Fe²⁺, not Fe³⁺: Fe + Cu²⁺ → Fe²⁺ + Cu, with charge +2 on each side. Fe + Cu²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + Cu is not even charge-balanced, and CuSO₄ is a soluble salt, so it is written as ions.

questions.s: Which equation correctly represents chlorine dissolving and reacting in water?
questions.e: HCl is a strong acid, so it is written as H⁺ + Cl⁻, but hypochlorous acid is weak and stays as HClO. Splitting HClO into H⁺ and ClO⁻ treats it as strong, and keeping HCl as a molecule ignores its complete ionisation.

questions.s: Copper reacts with dilute nitric acid to give copper(II) nitrate, nitrogen monoxide and water. What is the ionic equation?
questions.e: Cu loses 2 electrons and N gains 3 (+5 → +2), so 3Cu react with 2NO₃⁻; charge then needs 8H⁺ (8 − 2 = +6 = 3 × 2). Cu + 4H⁺ + NO₃⁻ is not charge-balanced (+3 vs +2), HNO₃ is a strong acid and must be written as ions, and copper does not release H₂ from nitric acid.

questions.s: A small amount of sodium hydroxide solution is added to excess calcium hydrogencarbonate solution. What is the ionic equation?
questions.e: Each OH⁻ turns one HCO₃⁻ into CO₃²⁻, and with Ca²⁺ in excess every CO₃²⁻ is precipitated: Ca²⁺ + HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ → CaCO₃ + H₂O. The equation with 2OH⁻ and leftover CO₃²⁻ applies when NaOH is in excess, and the other two leave out one step.

questions.s: Which ionic equation involving iron ions is correct?
questions.e: 2Fe³⁺ + Cu → 2Fe²⁺ + Cu²⁺ balances atoms, charge (+6 each side) and electrons. The first two equations are not charge-balanced (they need 2Fe³⁺ and 2Fe²⁺), and iron reacts with dilute acid to give Fe²⁺, not Fe³⁺.

questions.s: Silver nitrate solution is mixed with sodium chloride solution and a white precipitate forms. Which ions are spectator ions?
questions.e: Only Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl takes place; Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ stay dissolved and unchanged, so they are spectator ions and are left out of the ionic equation. Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ form the precipitate, so they are the reacting ions.

questions.s: Which pair of substances reacts according to the ionic equation Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄ and no other ionic reaction?
questions.e: In BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectators, so only BaSO₄ forms. With Ba(OH)₂, water or Cu(OH)₂ also forms, and BaCO₃ is a solid that must be written as a formula and also releases CO₂.

questions.s: When ionic equations are written, which substance must be written as its full formula rather than as separate ions?
questions.e: Insoluble substances, gases, water and weak electrolytes are written as formulas; CaCO₃ is insoluble. HNO₃, NaOH and KCl are soluble strong electrolytes, so they are written as ions.

questions.s: In an ionic equation, how is calcium hydroxide written when the reactant is clear limewater, and when it is milk of lime (a suspension)?
o: Ions for limewater; Ca(OH)₂ for milk of lime
Ca(OH)₂ for limewater; ions for milk of lime
questions.e: Ca(OH)₂ is only slightly soluble. In clear limewater it is all dissolved and ionised, so it is written as Ca²⁺ and OH⁻; in milk of lime most of it is undissolved solid, so it is written as Ca(OH)₂. Treating the two cases the same ignores whether the solid is present.

questions.s: What is the ionic equation for the reaction of sodium with water?
questions.e: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2Na⁺ + 2OH⁻ + H₂ balances H (4 = 2 + 2), O and charge (0 = +2 − 2). The first has 2 H on the left but 3 on the right, the third has charge 0 on the left but −1 on the right, and pure water is written as H₂O, not H⁺.

questions.s: Which pair of solutions does NOT react when mixed?
questions.e: Mixing KNO₃ and NaCl only gives a solution of K⁺, Na⁺, NO₃⁻ and Cl⁻; no precipitate, gas or weak electrolyte can form. The other pairs form AgCl, CO₂ and Cu(OH)₂ respectively.

questions.s: Which of the following is NOT a condition that makes an ionic double decomposition reaction take place in solution?
o: Water or another weak electrolyte forms
questions.e: Ionic reactions go when they remove ions from solution by forming a precipitate, a gas or a weak electrolyte such as water. A colour change on its own does not remove ions; many coloured ions, such as Cu²⁺, simply stay in solution.

questions.s: Which pair of solutions reacts by forming a weak electrolyte, with no gas and no precipitate?
questions.e: CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH forms weak, mostly un-ionised acetic acid, which drives the reaction. Na₂SO₄ and BaCl₂ give a precipitate, Na₂CO₃ and H₂SO₄ give CO₂ gas, and NaCl and KNO₃ do not react.

questions.s: Ammonium chloride solution is warmed with sodium hydroxide solution. What is the ionic equation?
questions.e: Both NH₄Cl and NaOH are soluble strong electrolytes, so only NH₄⁺ and OH⁻ appear, and warming drives off ammonia gas: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O. Keeping NH₄Cl or NaOH as formulas is wrong, and no H⁺ is involved.

questions.s: Which group of ions can be present together in large amounts in a solution?
questions.e: No two of Na⁺, K⁺, NO₃⁻ and Cl⁻ form a precipitate, gas or weak electrolyte. Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ give AgCl, Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ give BaSO₄, and H⁺ and CO₃²⁻ give CO₂ and water.

questions.s: Which group of ions can be present in large amounts in a colourless, strongly acidic solution?
questions.e: Mg²⁺, NH₄⁺, SO₄²⁻ and Cl⁻ are colourless and none reacts with H⁺ or with each other. Cu²⁺ is blue, HCO₃⁻ reacts with H⁺ to give CO₂, and OH⁻ is neutralised by H⁺.

questions.s: Which group of ions can be present in large amounts in a strongly alkaline solution?
questions.e: Na⁺, K⁺, CO₃²⁻ and NO₃⁻ do not react with OH⁻. NH₄⁺ forms NH₃·H₂O, Mg²⁺ precipitates as Mg(OH)₂, and HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ → CO₃²⁻ + H₂O.

questions.s: Which group of ions cannot be present together in large amounts because a redox reaction occurs between them?
questions.e: NO₃⁻ in acid is a strong oxidising agent and oxidises Fe²⁺: 3Fe²⁺ + 4H⁺ + NO₃⁻ → 3Fe³⁺ + NO + 2H₂O. The other groups also cannot coexist, but for non-redox reasons: BaSO₄ precipitates, CO₂ is released, and NH₃·H₂O forms.

questions.s: Fe³⁺ cannot be present in large amounts together with which ion, because the two combine to form a complex?
questions.e: Fe³⁺ + 3SCN⁻ → Fe(SCN)₃ forms a blood-red complex, so the two ions cannot remain free together. Fe³⁺ salts of sulfate, nitrate and chloride are all common soluble compounds.

questions.s: Which group of ions can be present in large amounts in a colourless, transparent solution?
questions.e: Na⁺, Al³⁺, SO₄²⁻ and Cl⁻ are all colourless and do not react with one another. MnO₄⁻ is purple, Fe³⁺ yellow-brown and Fe²⁺ pale green, so those groups would be coloured even though their ions do not react.

questions.s: A solution turns methyl orange red. Which group of ions can be present in it in large amounts?
questions.e: Methyl orange is red, so the solution is acidic and contains much H⁺; Na⁺, NH₄⁺, Cl⁻ and NO₃⁻ are all stable in acid. ClO⁻ forms weak HClO (and Cl₂ with Cl⁻), SO₃²⁻ releases SO₂, and MnO₄⁻ oxidises Fe²⁺ in acid.

questions.s: In an acidic solution containing a large amount of I⁻, which ion cannot also be present in large amounts?
questions.e: Fe³⁺ oxidises iodide: 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂, so the two cannot coexist. K⁺, SO₄²⁻ and Cl⁻ neither oxidise I⁻ nor form a precipitate with it.

questions.s: Which ion can remain in large amounts both in a strongly acidic and in a strongly alkaline solution?
questions.e: SO₄²⁻ reacts with neither H⁺ nor OH⁻. HCO₃⁻ reacts with both, NH₄⁺ reacts with OH⁻ to form NH₃·H₂O, and Al³⁺ is precipitated by OH⁻, so each of these survives in at most one of the two solutions.

questions.s: A solution contains 0.2 mol/L Na⁺, 0.25 mol/L Mg²⁺ and 0.4 mol/L Cl⁻, and the only other ion present is SO₄²⁻. What is the concentration of SO₄²⁻?
questions.e: The solution is electrically neutral: 0.2 × 1 + 0.25 × 2 = 0.4 × 1 + 2c(SO₄²⁻), so 0.7 = 0.4 + 2c and c = 0.15 mol/L. 0.30 mol/L forgets to divide by the charge of 2.

questions.s: In a solution of aluminium sulfate, c(SO₄²⁻) = 0.3 mol/L. What is c(Al³⁺), ignoring any reaction of Al³⁺ with water?
questions.e: Al₂(SO₄)₃ gives Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ in the ratio 2 : 3, so c(Al³⁺) = 0.3 × 2/3 = 0.2 mol/L. Using the ratio upside down gives 0.45 mol/L.

questions.s: Excess BaCl₂ solution is added to 25 mL of sodium sulfate solution, and 2.33 g of BaSO₄ precipitate forms. What is the concentration of Na⁺ in the original solution? (BaSO₄ = 233)
questions.e: 2.33/233 = 0.01 mol BaSO₄, so 0.01 mol SO₄²⁻ and 0.02 mol Na⁺ were present. c(Na⁺) = 0.02/0.025 = 0.8 mol/L. 0.4 mol/L is the sulfate concentration, not the sodium concentration.

questions.s: Excess BaCl₂ solution is added to 100 mL of a solution of Na₂CO₃ and Na₂SO₄, giving 6.27 g of precipitate. After excess dilute nitric acid is added, 2.33 g of precipitate remains. What is the concentration of CO₃²⁻ in the original solution? (BaCO₃ = 197, BaSO₄ = 233)
questions.e: BaCO₃ dissolves in the acid but BaSO₄ does not, so the mass of BaCO₃ was 6.27 − 2.33 = 3.94 g, which is 3.94/197 = 0.02 mol. c(CO₃²⁻) = 0.02/0.1 = 0.2 mol/L. 0.1 mol/L is the sulfate concentration (2.33/233 = 0.01 mol).

questions.s: Sodium hydroxide solution is added drop by drop to a solution containing HCl, MgCl₂ and NH₄Cl. In which order do the ions react with OH⁻?
questions.e: H⁺ reacts first, because any Mg(OH)₂ or NH₃·H₂O formed would react with the acid. Mg²⁺ reacts before NH₄⁺, because NH₃·H₂O formed earlier would itself precipitate Mg²⁺ as Mg(OH)₂. So the order is H⁺, Mg²⁺, NH₄⁺.

questions.s: Which reagents are used to test a solution for chloride ions?
questions.e: Cl⁻ gives a white precipitate of AgCl with Ag⁺ that does not dissolve in dilute nitric acid. BaCl₂ with HCl tests for sulfate, warming with NaOH tests for ammonium, and KSCN tests for Fe³⁺.

questions.s: When a solution is tested for Cl⁻ with AgNO₃ solution, dilute nitric acid is also added. What is the purpose of the nitric acid?
o: To make the silver chloride precipitate dissolve
To oxidise the Cl⁻ to chlorine
To convert all of the chloride into HCl gas
To exclude CO₃²⁻, which also precipitates Ag⁺
questions.e: Ag₂CO₃ is also a white precipitate, but it dissolves in dilute HNO₃ while AgCl does not, so the acid prevents a false positive from carbonate. Nitric acid does not dissolve AgCl, and dilute nitric acid neither oxidises Cl⁻ nor drives off HCl.

questions.s: Which procedure is the most reliable test for sulfate ions in an unknown solution?
o: Add BaCl₂ solution only and look for a white precipitate
Add excess dilute HCl, then BaCl₂: white precipitate
Add dilute HNO₃, then Ba(NO₃)₂: white precipitate
Add BaCl₂, then dilute HNO₃: precipitate remains
questions.e: Adding HCl first removes CO₃²⁻ and SO₃²⁻ and would show Ag⁺ (as AgCl) before BaCl₂ is added; a white precipitate then must be BaSO₄. BaCl₂ alone also precipitates carbonate, and nitric acid oxidises SO₃²⁻ to SO₄²⁻, giving a false positive; AgCl from Ag⁺ would also remain undissolved.

questions.s: BaCl₂ solution is added to an unknown solution and a white precipitate forms that does not dissolve when dilute nitric acid is added. Which conclusion is correct?
o: Ag⁺ or SO₃²⁻ could explain it
questions.e: AgCl (from Ag⁺ and the Cl⁻ of BaCl₂) does not dissolve in nitric acid, and nitric acid oxidises BaSO₃ to insoluble BaSO₄, so SO₄²⁻ is not proved. BaCO₃ would dissolve in the acid with bubbles, so carbonate cannot be the cause.

questions.s: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a white solid, and a colourless, odourless gas is given off that turns limewater milky. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.e: The gas is CO₂, which both carbonates and hydrogencarbonates release with acid, so this test cannot tell them apart. SO₂ also turns limewater milky but has a choking smell, so an odourless gas rules out sulfite.

questions.s: Which reagent gives a white precipitate with sodium carbonate solution but not with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution?
questions.e: Ca²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → CaCO₃, while Ca(HCO₃)₂ is soluble, so dilute CaCl₂ precipitates only the carbonate. Limewater also contains OH⁻, which turns HCO₃⁻ into CO₃²⁻, so it precipitates both; NaOH gives no precipitate, and HCl gives gas with both.

questions.s: Which test confirms the presence of ammonium ions in a solution?
o: Warm with HCl; gas turns limewater milky
Warm with NaOH; gas turns damp blue litmus red
Warm with NaOH; gas turns damp red litmus blue
Add AgNO₃; a white precipitate appears
questions.e: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O on warming, and ammonia is an alkaline gas that turns damp red litmus blue. It cannot turn blue litmus red, the limewater test is for CO₂, and AgNO₃ tests for chloride.

questions.s: In the test for NH₄⁺, the mixture with NaOH is warmed and the red litmus paper is held damp at the mouth of the test tube. Why?
o: Warming oxidises NH₄⁺ to N₂; water dissolves the litmus dye
Warming drives out NH₃; NH₃ needs water to give OH⁻
Warming makes the gas acidic; water neutralises it
Warming forms N₂; water reacts with the N₂
questions.e: Ammonia is very soluble, so warming is needed to drive it out of the solution; the gas only turns litmus blue after dissolving in water: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. No N₂ is formed in this test, and ammonia is basic, not acidic.

questions.s: Which reagent can distinguish iron(II) chloride solution from iron(III) chloride solution by the colour of the precipitate formed?
questions.e: NaOH gives white Fe(OH)₂ (which soon turns grey-green and then red-brown) with Fe²⁺, but red-brown Fe(OH)₃ at once with Fe³⁺. AgNO₃ gives the same white AgCl with both chlorides, and BaCl₂ and HCl give no precipitate with either.

questions.s: NaOH solution is added to a pale green solution; a white precipitate forms, quickly turns grey-green and finally red-brown in air. Which equation shows the final change?
questions.e: Oxygen from the air oxidises white Fe(OH)₂ to red-brown Fe(OH)₃: 4Fe(OH)₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4Fe(OH)₃, balanced with 12 O and 12 H on each side. Water alone does not oxidise Fe(OH)₂ to give H₂, Fe(OH)₂ + O₂ → Fe(OH)₃ is unbalanced, and Fe²⁺ + 3OH⁻ is not charge-balanced.

questions.s: An iron(III) sulfate solution may contain some iron(II) sulfate as an impurity. Which reagent can show whether Fe²⁺ is present?
questions.e: Fe²⁺ reduces purple MnO₄⁻ in acid (MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O), so the purple colour fading shows Fe²⁺; Fe³⁺ has no effect. KSCN turns red with the Fe³⁺ already there, NaOH gives red-brown Fe(OH)₃ that hides any white Fe(OH)₂, and chlorine water causes no clear visible change.

questions.s: Which single reagent, with warming where needed, can distinguish the four solutions NH₄Cl, (NH₄)₂SO₄, Na₂SO₄ and NaCl from one another?
questions.e: With Ba(OH)₂: NH₄Cl gives only ammonia gas, (NH₄)₂SO₄ gives gas and a white BaSO₄ precipitate, Na₂SO₄ gives only the precipitate, and NaCl shows no change. NaOH cannot tell the two sulfate/chloride pairs apart, and BaCl₂ cannot detect ammonium.

questions.s: Which reagent can distinguish the three solutions Na₂CO₃, BaCl₂ and NaCl in a single step?
questions.e: Dilute H₂SO₄ gives CO₂ bubbles with Na₂CO₃, a white BaSO₄ precipitate with BaCl₂ and no change with NaCl. Dilute HCl gives no visible change with either BaCl₂ or NaCl, and AgNO₃ gives white precipitates with all three.

questions.s: A white solid X dissolves in water. Warming the solution with NaOH gives a gas that turns damp red litmus blue. Adding dilute HCl to a fresh sample gives no gas, and then adding BaCl₂ gives a white precipitate. What is X?
questions.e: The alkaline gas shows NH₄⁺, and a white precipitate with BaCl₂ after acidifying with HCl shows SO₄²⁻, so X is ammonium sulfate. NH₄Cl gives no precipitate, Na₂SO₄ gives no ammonia, and (NH₄)₂CO₃ would fizz with HCl.

questions.s: A colourless solution may contain K⁺, Cu²⁺, Ba²⁺, CO₃²⁻, SO₄²⁻ and Cl⁻. Excess dilute HCl gives bubbles of gas; BaCl₂ is then added and a white precipitate forms. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.e: The tests show CO₃²⁻ and SO₄²⁻; these exclude Ba²⁺ (it would precipitate with them), and Cu²⁺ is excluded because the solution is colourless. The solution must contain some cation, so K⁺ must be present. Cl⁻ cannot be decided, because HCl and BaCl₂ both added chloride.

questions.s: Silver nitrate solution is added to a tap-water sample and a white precipitate forms that does not dissolve in dilute nitric acid. Which ion does this show?
questions.e: Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl, a white solid that is insoluble in dilute HNO₃. Silver carbonate would dissolve in the acid, hydroxide is neutralised by it, and nitrate salts are all soluble.

questions.s: NaOH solution is added to a yellow-brown solution and a red-brown precipitate forms at once. What is the ionic equation?
questions.e: A yellow-brown solution and an immediate red-brown precipitate show Fe³⁺ forming Fe(OH)₃. Fe(OH)₂ is white at first, Cu(OH)₂ is blue, and Fe(SCN)₃ is a red solution formed with KSCN, not with NaOH.

questions.s: Crude salt solution contains Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ as impurities. They are removed with excess BaCl₂, NaOH and Na₂CO₃ solutions, filtration, and finally hydrochloric acid. Which order is correct?
questions.e: Na₂CO₃ must come after BaCl₂ so that it also removes the excess Ba²⁺ as BaCO₃, and HCl must be added after filtering so the precipitates (CaCO₃, BaCO₃, Mg(OH)₂) do not redissolve. Adding Na₂CO₃ before BaCl₂ leaves excess Ba²⁺ in the salt.

questions.s: Magnesium oxide dissolves in dilute hydrochloric acid. What is the ionic equation?
questions.e: MgO is a solid oxide, so it keeps its formula, while HCl is a strong acid written as H⁺ (Cl⁻ is a spectator). Splitting MgO into Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ is wrong for a solid, and keeping HCl as a molecule ignores its complete ionisation.

questions.s: Barium hydroxide solution is added to sodium hydrogensulfate solution until the mixture is exactly neutral. What is the ionic equation?
o: H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ + Ba²⁺ + OH⁻ → BaSO₄ + H₂O
questions.e: Neutral means all H⁺ is neutralised, so H⁺ : OH⁻ = 1 : 1, which needs 2NaHSO₄ per Ba(OH)₂: 2H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ + Ba²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → BaSO₄ + 2H₂O, leaving SO₄²⁻ in solution. The 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 equation describes adding Ba(OH)₂ until all the sulfate is precipitated, which leaves the mixture alkaline.

questions.s: Acetic acid is neutralised by sodium hydroxide solution. What is the ionic equation?
questions.e: Acetic acid is a weak electrolyte, so it is written as CH₃COOH, while NaOH is written as ions and Na⁺ cancels out: CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O. H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O wrongly treats acetic acid as a strong acid.

questions.s: Chlorine is passed into cold sodium hydroxide solution to make bleach. What is the ionic equation?
questions.e: Chlorine disproportionates into Cl⁻ and ClO⁻, and NaOH is a strong base written as OH⁻: Cl₂ + 2OH⁻ → Cl⁻ + ClO⁻ + H₂O. HClO cannot remain in an alkaline solution because OH⁻ neutralises it, free O atoms are not a product, and NaOH must be written as ions.

questions.s: Which pair of substances reacts according to the ionic equation Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl?
questions.e: AgNO₃ and HCl both dissolve completely, supplying free Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ that combine to form AgCl. Silver metal does not react with HCl, AgCl does not dissolve in HNO₃, and solid Ag₂O must be written as a formula.

questions.s: Which pair of ions reacts in solution to release a gas?
questions.e: H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → CO₂ + H₂O releases carbon dioxide. Ba²⁺ with SO₄²⁻ and Ag⁺ with Cl⁻ give precipitates, and H⁺ with OH⁻ gives water.

questions.s: Which pair of ions reacts in solution to form a weak electrolyte?
questions.e: H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ → CH₃COOH, a weak acid that stays mostly as molecules. Na⁺ with Cl⁻ and K⁺ with NO₃⁻ do not react, and Ba²⁺ with SO₄²⁻ gives a precipitate of BaSO₄, which is a strong electrolyte.

questions.s: A solution contains Ba²⁺, H⁺ and Cl⁻. Which ion can be added to it in large amounts without any reaction?
questions.e: Nitrate forms no precipitate, gas or weak electrolyte with Ba²⁺, H⁺ or Cl⁻. SO₄²⁻ precipitates Ba²⁺, CO₃²⁻ reacts with H⁺ (and Ba²⁺), and OH⁻ is neutralised by H⁺.

questions.s: Four students analysed four clear solutions and each reported the four ions present in large amounts. Which report must be wrong?
questions.e: Fe³⁺ oxidises I⁻ to I₂ (2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂), so both cannot be present in large amounts. In each other report no pair of ions forms a precipitate, gas or weak electrolyte, or reacts by redox.

questions.s: Mixing a bleach containing NaClO with a toilet cleaner containing hydrochloric acid releases a toxic yellow-green gas. What is the ionic equation?
questions.e: ClO⁻ (Cl +1) oxidises Cl⁻ (Cl −1) to Cl₂ in acid: ClO⁻ + Cl⁻ + 2H⁺ → Cl₂ + H₂O, with charge 0 on both sides. OH⁻ cannot be a product in acidic solution, HClO formation releases no gas, and HCl alone cannot oxidise itself to Cl₂.

questions.s: Hydrogen peroxide is added to an acidified solution of iron(II) sulfate. What is the ionic equation?
questions.e: Each H₂O₂ gains 2 electrons (O −1 → −2) and each Fe²⁺ loses 1, so 2Fe²⁺ react per H₂O₂; charge 4 + 2 = 6 = 2 × 3. The first and third options balance atoms but not charge, and the last is not charge-balanced either (+4 vs +8) and would have both reactants oxidised, which is impossible.

questions.s: NaOH solution is added drop by drop to a colourless solution. A white precipitate forms and then dissolves when the NaOH is in excess. Which ion is present?
questions.e: Al(OH)₃ is amphoteric: Al³⁺ + 3OH⁻ → Al(OH)₃, then Al(OH)₃ + OH⁻ → [Al(OH)₄]⁻. Mg(OH)₂ is white but does not dissolve in excess alkali, and Fe³⁺ and Cu²⁺ give coloured solutions and coloured precipitates.

questions.s: A solution contains both Cl⁻ and SO₄²⁻. Which order of tests correctly shows the presence of each?
questions.e: Testing for sulfate first with excess Ba(NO₃)₂ removes SO₄²⁻, which could otherwise form slightly soluble Ag₂SO₄ and confuse the chloride test; AgNO₃ then detects Cl⁻ in the filtrate. BaCl₂ would add Cl⁻ itself, and adding AgNO₃ first precipitates Ag₂SO₄ along with AgCl.

questions.s: A salt is either a carbonate or a sulfite. Dilute acid is added and a gas is given off. Which observation shows that it is a carbonate rather than a sulfite?
o: Gas has a sharp choking smell
questions.e: CO₂ and SO₂ both turn limewater milky, so that alone is not enough; CO₂ is odourless, while SO₂ has a choking smell and reduces (decolourises) acidified KMnO₄. An odourless gas that turns limewater milky must therefore be CO₂ from a carbonate.

questions.s: Which statement about sodium hydrogensulfate, NaHSO₄, is correct?
o: In water it gives Na⁺ and HSO₄⁻ only
When molten it gives Na⁺ and HSO₄⁻
When molten it gives Na⁺, H⁺ and SO₄²⁻
questions.e: Melting only separates the ions of the crystal, Na⁺ and HSO₄⁻; the covalent bonds inside HSO₄⁻ are not broken. In water HSO₄⁻ ionises fully to H⁺ and SO₄²⁻, so the solution is strongly acidic. Writing the molten case like the aqueous case is the usual mistake.

questions.s: Which of the following is a strong electrolyte?
questions.e: Potassium nitrate is a soluble salt that is completely ionised in water. Water, ammonia solution (NH₃·H₂O) and acetic acid are only slightly ionised, so they are weak electrolytes.

questions.s: A solution contains only K⁺, Fe³⁺, Cl⁻ and SO₄²⁻ (ignore H⁺ and OH⁻). The mole ratio n(K⁺) : n(Fe³⁺) : n(Cl⁻) = 3 : 2 : 1. What is the ratio n(Fe³⁺) : n(SO₄²⁻)?
questions.e: Positive charge: 3 × 1 + 2 × 3 = 9; negative charge: 1 × 1 + 2x = 9, so x = 4 mol SO₄²⁻. Then n(Fe³⁺) : n(SO₄²⁻) = 2 : 4 = 1 : 2. Forgetting the charges and balancing the numbers of ions gives wrong ratios such as 1:1.

questions.s: A solution containing 0.03 mol Ba(OH)₂ is mixed with a solution containing 0.02 mol H₂SO₄. Which ions remain in solution in significant amounts after the reaction?
questions.e: 0.02 mol SO₄²⁻ precipitates 0.02 mol Ba²⁺, leaving 0.01 mol Ba²⁺; 0.04 mol H⁺ neutralises 0.04 of the 0.06 mol OH⁻, leaving 0.02 mol OH⁻. Ba(OH)₂ is in excess, so no H⁺ or SO₄²⁻ is left, and Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ can never both remain.

questions.s: Iron(III) chloride solution contains some iron(II) chloride as an impurity. Which reagent removes the impurity without adding new ions?
questions.e: 2Fe²⁺ + Cl₂ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2Cl⁻ turns the impurity into the wanted FeCl₃ and adds only Cl⁻, which is already present. Iron powder would instead reduce Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺, copper adds Cu²⁺, and KMnO₄ adds K⁺ and Mn²⁺.

questions.s: Which of these conducts electricity because it contains freely moving ions?
questions.e: Melting NaCl frees its Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions to move and carry charge. Copper conducts by moving electrons, solid KCl has ions locked in a lattice, and ethanol contains no ions.

questions.s: What is the ionic equation for the reaction of hydrochloric acid with potassium hydroxide solution?
questions.e: HCl, KOH and KCl are all soluble strong electrolytes, so K⁺ and Cl⁻ cancel as spectators and only H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O remains. Keeping HCl or KOH as formulas ignores their complete ionisation, and KCl does not precipitate.

questions.s: Which pair of ions forms a precipitate when their solutions are mixed?
questions.e: Ba²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → BaCO₃, an insoluble white solid. All sodium, potassium and ammonium salts and all nitrates are soluble, so the other pairs stay in solution.

questions.s: Which dissociation equation is written correctly?
questions.e: Aluminium sulfate gives 2Al³⁺ and 3SO₄²⁻, and the charges balance (+6 and −6). Sulfuric acid gives 2H⁺, MgCl₂ gives 2Cl⁻, and ClO₃⁻ stays together as one ion rather than splitting into Cl⁻ and O²⁻.

questions.s: Which group of ions can be present together in large amounts?
questions.e: None of Cu²⁺, Na⁺, NO₃⁻ and SO₄²⁻ react with one another; the solution is blue, but colour does not stop ions coexisting. Mg²⁺ and OH⁻ form Mg(OH)₂, H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ form CO₂, and Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ form BaSO₄.

questions.s: A fertiliser is warmed with sodium hydroxide solution and gives off a pungent gas that turns damp red litmus paper blue. Which ion does the fertiliser contain?
questions.e: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O on warming, and ammonia is the only common alkaline gas. Nitrate, potassium and phosphate ions give no gas with NaOH.

questions.s: Marble chips (CaCO₃) react with dilute nitric acid. What is the ionic equation?
questions.e: CaCO₃ is insoluble, so it keeps its formula, while nitric acid is strong and is written as H⁺. Splitting CaCO₃ into ions is only allowed for soluble carbonates, and HNO₃ must not be kept as a molecule.

questions.s: Which ion cannot be present in large amounts in a solution of pH 1?
questions.e: pH 1 means a high H⁺ concentration, and CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O removes carbonate. NH₄⁺, SO₄²⁻ and Cl⁻ are all stable in acid.

questions.s: Which ion can be present in large amounts in a solution of pH 13?
questions.e: pH 13 means a high OH⁻ concentration, and nitrate does not react with OH⁻. Fe³⁺ forms Fe(OH)₃, NH₄⁺ forms NH₃·H₂O, and HCO₃⁻ is converted to CO₃²⁻ and water.

questions.s: Which of these ions gives a coloured aqueous solution?
questions.e: Fe²⁺ solutions are pale green. Al³⁺, Mg²⁺ and Zn²⁺ solutions are colourless, so these ions are allowed in a colourless solution.

questions.s: A few drops of dilute hydrochloric acid are added, with stirring, to a large volume of sodium carbonate solution. What is the ionic equation?
questions.e: With carbonate in large excess, each H⁺ is taken up by a CO₃²⁻ to form HCO₃⁻, so no gas is released at first. CO₂ forms only when the acid is in excess, and Na₂CO₃ and NaHCO₃ are soluble, so they are written as ions.

questions.s: When testing for sulfate, why is dilute hydrochloric acid added to the sample before BaCl₂ solution?
o: To exclude ions such as CO₃²⁻ and Ag⁺
To convert any sulfate into sulfuric acid
questions.e: Acid removes CO₃²⁻ (and SO₃²⁻) as gas and shows any Ag⁺ as AgCl first, so a white precipitate with BaCl₂ afterwards must be BaSO₄. BaSO₄ does not dissolve in HCl, and making sulfuric acid or adding Cl⁻ is not the purpose.

questions.s: A solution of FeCl₂ has been left open to the air for several days. A few drops of KSCN solution turn it red. What can be concluded?
o: Air has oxidised some Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺
All of the Fe²⁺ has turned into Fe³⁺
KSCN has oxidised Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺
Chloride ions give red with SCN⁻
questions.e: The red colour shows that Fe³⁺ is now present, formed by oxygen in the air: 4Fe²⁺ + O₂ + 4H⁺ → 4Fe³⁺ + 2H₂O. The test does not show that all the Fe²⁺ has gone; a separate test for Fe²⁺ would be needed. KSCN is not an oxidising agent and Cl⁻ gives no colour.

questions.s: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to freshly prepared iron(II) sulfate solution. What colour is the precipitate when it first forms?
questions.e: Fe²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₂, which is white when first formed and then turns grey-green and red-brown as air oxidises it. Red-brown at once is typical of Fe³⁺, and a blue precipitate is Cu(OH)₂.

questions.s: A solution contains 0.1 mol Na⁺, 0.2 mol Mg²⁺ and 0.3 mol Cl⁻, and the only other ion present is NO₃⁻. How many moles of NO₃⁻ does it contain?
questions.e: Positive charge: 0.1 × 1 + 0.2 × 2 = 0.5 mol; negative charge: 0.3 + n(NO₃⁻) = 0.5, so n(NO₃⁻) = 0.2 mol. Forgetting the 2+ charge of Mg²⁺ gives 0 mol, and simply adding the ions gives wrong values.

questions.s: Which pair of substances reacts according to the ionic equation Cu²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Cu(OH)₂ and no other ionic reaction?
questions.e: CuCl₂ and NaOH are soluble, and Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectators, so only Cu(OH)₂ forms. With Ba(OH)₂, BaSO₄ also precipitates; CuO does not react with NaOH, and solid CuCO₃ would have to be written as a formula.

questions.s: Which of these ionic equations, involving an oxide, a metal or a salt, is correct?
o: Ba²⁺ + OH⁻ + H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄ + H₂O
questions.e: Fe₂O₃ is a solid oxide written as a formula; atoms and charge (+6 each side) balance. Fe + Fe³⁺ → 2Fe²⁺ is not charge-balanced (+3 vs +4), copper does not react with dilute non-oxidising acid, and Ba(OH)₂ and H₂SO₄ react in a 2OH⁻ : 2H⁺ ratio.

questions.s: A colourless solution may contain Na⁺, Fe³⁺, NH₄⁺, CO₃²⁻ and SO₄²⁻. Warming with NaOH gives no gas. BaCl₂ gives a white precipitate that partly dissolves in excess dilute HCl with bubbles. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.e: No gas with NaOH rules out NH₄⁺, and the colourless solution rules out Fe³⁺. The precipitate partly dissolving with bubbles shows BaCO₃ and BaSO₄, so CO₃²⁻ and SO₄²⁻ are both present. A cation must balance their charge, and only Na⁺ remains, so it must be present.

questions.s: Which single reagent can distinguish NaCl, MgCl₂ and AlCl₃ solutions?
questions.e: Adding NaOH gradually: NaCl shows no change, MgCl₂ gives a white precipitate that stays in excess NaOH, and AlCl₃ gives a white precipitate that dissolves in excess. AgNO₃ gives white AgCl with all three chlorides, and HCl and BaCl₂ give no change.

questions.s: Barium hydroxide solution is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. What is the ionic equation?
questions.e: Two precipitates form at once, BaSO₄ and Cu(OH)₂, so all four ions react. Each short equation leaves out one of the precipitates, and Ba(OH)₂ is a soluble strong base that must be written as ions.

questions.s: How many neutrons are there in one atom of potassium-39 (atomic number 19)?
questions.e: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 39 − 19 = 20. The value 19 is the number of protons (and electrons), 39 is the total number of nucleons, and 58 comes from adding instead of subtracting.

questions.s: Which ion has the same number of electrons as a neon atom?
questions.e: Neon has 10 electrons. Mg has 12 electrons, so Mg²⁺ has 12 − 2 = 10. Cl⁻ (17 + 1), K⁺ (19 − 1) and Ca²⁺ (20 − 2) all have 18 electrons, the same as argon, not neon.

questions.s: For the ion ³²S²⁻ (sulfur, atomic number 16), what are the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons?
questions.e: Protons = Z = 16; neutrons = 32 − 16 = 16; the 2− charge means two extra electrons, so 16 + 2 = 18. The option with 14 electrons treats the negative charge as a loss of electrons, and 32 neutrons confuses the mass number with the neutron number.

questions.s: Isotopes of the same element always have the same
questions.e: Isotopes are atoms of one element, so they share the atomic number (number of protons) but differ in the number of neutrons. Because the neutron number differs, the mass number and properties that depend on mass, such as density, also differ.

questions.s: Natural boron consists of ¹⁰B and ¹¹B only, and its relative atomic mass is 10.8. What percentage of boron atoms are ¹⁰B?
questions.e: Let the fraction of ¹⁰B be x: 10x + 11(1 − x) = 10.8, so 11 − x = 10.8 and x = 0.2, i.e. 20 %. 80 % is the abundance of ¹¹B; a mean of 10.8 lies closer to 11, so the heavier isotope must be the more abundant one.

questions.s: What is the ground-state electron configuration of the chloride ion, Cl⁻ (chlorine has atomic number 17)?
questions.e: Cl⁻ has 17 + 1 = 18 electrons, filling 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s and 3p completely: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶. 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁵ is the neutral Cl atom, and 3p⁴ would mean an electron was removed instead of added.

questions.s: An atom has the ground-state electron configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p³. Where is this element in the periodic table?
questions.e: The highest shell is n = 3, so it is in period 3; it has 2 + 3 = 5 outer electrons in s and p subshells, so it is in group 15 (it is phosphorus). Period 5 wrongly uses the number of outer electrons as the period, and for p-block elements the group number is 10 + (s + p electrons), so 3s²3p³ gives group 15, not 13 or 3.

questions.s: Which of the following atoms has the largest atomic radius?
questions.e: Radius increases down a group (more shells) and decreases across a period (larger nuclear charge pulls the same shell closer). K is in period 4 with four occupied shells, so it is larger than Na, Mg and Cl, all in period 3. Na is the largest of the period 3 atoms but is still smaller than K.

questions.s: Which of the following atoms has the highest first ionisation energy?
questions.e: First ionisation energy generally rises across period 2, but N (2p³, half-filled with one electron in each 2p orbital) is higher than O. In O (2p⁴) one 2p orbital holds a pair of electrons, and the repulsion between them makes one electron easier to remove. So the order is N > O > C > B.

questions.s: Which of the following elements has the highest electronegativity?
questions.e: Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group. O is in period 2 and is the second most electronegative element (about 3.4), higher than Cl (about 3.2), which is in period 3. S is to the left of Cl and Br is below Cl, so both are lower than Cl.

questions.s: Elements in the same main group of the periodic table have the same
questions.e: A main group collects elements with the same number of outer (valence) electrons, which is why they react similarly. Elements in the same period, not group, have the same number of occupied shells; atomic mass and neutron number increase down a group.

questions.s: Which of the following ions has the smallest radius?
questions.e: All four ions have 10 electrons (1s²2s²2p⁶), so the radius depends on the nuclear charge: O (8) < F (9) < Na (11) < Mg (12). Mg²⁺ has the most protons pulling on the same 10 electrons, so it is the smallest, and O²⁻ is the largest.

questions.s: An ion X³⁺ has mass number 56 and its nucleus contains 30 neutrons. How many electrons does the ion have?
questions.e: Protons = 56 − 30 = 26, so the neutral atom has 26 electrons and X³⁺ has 26 − 3 = 23. 26 forgets the charge, 29 adds the three electrons instead of removing them, and 27 subtracts 3 from the neutron number.

questions.s: Which of the following hydroxides is the strongest base?
questions.e: Metallic character increases down a group and decreases across a period, and so does the basic strength of the hydroxides. K is below Na in group 1, so KOH is stronger than NaOH; Mg(OH)₂ is weaker, and Al(OH)₃ is amphoteric.

questions.s: Which of the following is the strongest acid?
questions.e: These are the highest oxoacids of Si, P, S and Cl, which lie in that order across period 3. Non-metallic character increases across the period, so acid strength increases: H₂SiO₃ < H₃PO₄ < H₂SO₄ < HClO₄. H₂SO₄ is a strong acid, but perchloric acid is stronger still.

questions.s: How many electrons are in the outermost shell of an aluminium atom (atomic number 13)?
questions.e: Aluminium has the configuration 2, 8, 3 (1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p¹), so its outer shell holds 3 electrons and it is in group 13. Answering 1 counts only the 3p electron, and 2 counts only the 3s electrons.

questions.s: Which pair of atomic numbers belongs to two elements in the same group of the periodic table?
questions.e: Z = 8 (O, 2,6) and Z = 16 (S, 2,8,6) both have 6 outer electrons, so both are in group 16. Z = 2 (He) and Z = 4 (Be) both have 2 outer electrons, but helium is a noble gas in group 18 and Be is in group 2; 8 and 17, and 11 and 12, are in different groups.

questions.s: The first five successive ionisation energies of element X, in kJ/mol, are 578, 1817, 2745, 11577 and 14842. In which group is X?
questions.e: The large jump comes between the third (2745) and fourth (11577) ionisation energies, so the fourth electron is removed from an inner, full shell. X therefore has 3 outer electrons and is in group 13 (it is aluminium). Group 2 would show the jump after the second value.

questions.s: What is the ground-state electron configuration of Fe³⁺ (iron has atomic number 26)?
questions.e: Fe is [Ar]3d⁶4s². When a transition metal forms ions, the 4s electrons are lost first, then 3d: Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶ and Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵. [Ar]3d³4s² removes the three electrons from 3d, which is the common mistake, and [Ar]3d⁶ is Fe²⁺.

questions.s: Which statement about subatomic particles is correct?
o: A neutron has a charge of +1
An electron has no charge at all
An electron weighs about as much as a proton
A proton and a neutron have nearly equal mass
questions.e: Protons and neutrons each have a mass of about 1 u, while an electron is about 1/1836 of that. The neutron is uncharged, the proton carries +1 and the electron −1, so the other statements are false.

questions.s: How many unpaired electrons does a ground-state nitrogen atom (atomic number 7) have?
questions.e: Nitrogen is 1s²2s²2p³. By Hund's rule, the three 2p electrons occupy the three 2p orbitals singly with parallel spins, so there are 3 unpaired electrons. 5 is the number of valence electrons, but the two 2s electrons are paired.

questions.s: In which ground-state atom are all the electrons paired?
questions.e: Mg is 1s²2s²2p⁶3s², with every occupied orbital full, so no electron is unpaired. Na (3s¹) and Al (3p¹) each have one unpaired electron, and O (2p⁴) has two unpaired electrons by Hund's rule.

questions.s: The ions X²⁺ and Y⁻ both have the same electron configuration as an argon atom. Which statement is correct?
o: The atomic number of X is smaller than that of Y
X²⁺ has a larger radius than Y⁻
X and Y are in different periods
questions.e: X²⁺ has 18 electrons, so X has 20 (calcium, period 4); Y⁻ has 18, so Y has 17 (chlorine, period 3). So X and Y are in different periods and Z(X) = 20 > Z(Y) = 17. With equal electron numbers, Ca²⁺ has more protons than Cl⁻, so Ca²⁺ is the smaller ion.

questions.s: Which noble gas is in period 3 of the periodic table?
questions.e: Argon (Z = 18, configuration 2, 8, 8) has three occupied shells, so it ends period 3. Helium ends period 1, neon ends period 2 and krypton ends period 4.

questions.s: Going down group 1 from lithium to caesium, which property increases?
questions.e: Each step down adds an electron shell, so the atomic radius increases. The outer electron is then further from the nucleus and better shielded, so ionisation energy and electronegativity fall. The metallic bonding also weakens, so melting points decrease (Li about 181 °C, Cs about 28 °C).

questions.s: X, Y, Z and W are elements of periods 1-3 with increasing atomic numbers. The outer shell of X holds twice as many electrons as its inner shell; Y is the most abundant element in the Earth's crust; Z has the largest atomic radius in period 3; W is in the same group as Y. Which statement is correct?
o: The hydride of Y is more stable than the hydride of W
The atomic radius of W is larger than that of Z
The highest oxide of X dissolves to give a strong acid
Z and Y can form only one compound
questions.e: X is carbon (2, 4), Y is oxygen, Z is sodium and W is sulfur. O is more non-metallic than S, so H₂O is more stable than H₂S. Na is larger than S, carbonic acid is weak, and Na and O form both Na₂O and Na₂O₂, so the other statements are false.

questions.s: Chlorine has two stable isotopes, ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl. How many different relative molecular masses can Cl₂ molecules have?
questions.e: The possible pairs are ³⁵Cl³⁵Cl (70), ³⁵Cl³⁷Cl (72) and ³⁷Cl³⁷Cl (74), so there are 3 masses. Answering 4 counts ³⁵Cl³⁷Cl and ³⁷Cl³⁵Cl separately, but they are the same molecule.

questions.s: Which electron configuration describes an atom in an excited state rather than the ground state?
questions.e: 1s²2s¹2p³ has 6 electrons (carbon), but one electron has moved from 2s to 2p while 2s is not full, so it is an excited state; ground-state carbon is 1s²2s²2p². The other three fill the subshells in order of energy, so they are ground states of Ne, F and Na.

questions.s: What is the maximum number of electrons that the shell with n = 3 can hold?
questions.e: A shell can hold at most 2n² electrons, so n = 3 holds 2 × 9 = 18 (3s², 3p⁶, 3d¹⁰). 8 is the most it holds as an outermost shell, and 9 is n² without the factor 2 for the two spins per orbital.

questions.s: What is the ground-state electron configuration of a copper atom (atomic number 29)?
questions.e: Copper is an exception to the simple filling order: a full 3d¹⁰ subshell is more stable, so one 4s electron moves into 3d, giving [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹. [Ar]3d⁹4s² follows the simple rule but is not the ground state; [Ar]3d¹⁰4s² has 30 electrons (zinc) and [Ar]3d¹⁰ is Cu⁺.

questions.s: Which pair of species contains the same total number of electrons?
questions.e: H₂O has 8 + 2 = 10 electrons and NH₄⁺ has 7 + 4 − 1 = 10. Na⁺ has 10 but Cl⁻ has 18; H₂S and HCl have 18 each, while NH₄⁺ and OH⁻ (8 + 1 + 1) have 10.

questions.s: The element with atomic number 12 belongs to which family?
questions.e: Z = 12 gives 2, 8, 2, so the element (magnesium) has 2 outer electrons and is in group 2, the alkaline earth metals. Alkali metals have 1 outer electron, halogens 7 and noble gases a full outer shell.

questions.s: Which order of first ionisation energy is correct for sodium, magnesium and aluminium?
questions.e: The values are about Na 496, Mg 738 and Al 578 kJ/mol. The general rise across the period is broken at Al because its outer electron is in 3p, which is higher in energy and shielded by 3s², so it is easier to remove than an electron from Mg's full 3s². Al > Mg > Na follows the general trend but ignores this exception.

questions.s: A water molecule is made from two ²H atoms and one ¹⁸O atom (oxygen has atomic number 8). What are its relative molecular mass and the total number of neutrons in it?
questions.e: Mass = 2 × 2 + 18 = 22. Each ²H has 1 neutron and ¹⁸O has 18 − 8 = 10, so the total is 2 + 10 = 12. 20 and 10 are the values for ²H₂¹⁶O, and 22 and 10 forgets the neutrons in the deuterium atoms.

questions.s: A neutral atom has 2 electrons in the first shell, 8 in the second and 7 in the third. What is the highest positive oxidation state the element shows in its compounds?
questions.e: The atom is chlorine (Z = 17) with 7 valence electrons, so its highest positive oxidation state is +7, as in HClO₄ and Cl₂O₇. −1 is its lowest oxidation state (in chlorides), not the highest positive one.

questions.s: Silver consists of ¹⁰⁷Ag and ¹⁰⁹Ag only. If its relative atomic mass is taken as 107.9, what is the ratio of the number of ¹⁰⁷Ag atoms to ¹⁰⁹Ag atoms?
questions.e: Let the fraction of ¹⁰⁷Ag be x: 107x + 109(1 − x) = 107.9 gives 2x = 1.1, so x = 0.55 and ¹⁰⁹Ag is 0.45. The ratio is 55 : 45 = 11 : 9. 9 : 11 has the isotopes swapped; since 107.9 is closer to 107, the lighter isotope must be the more common.

questions.s: The atomic number of an element is equal to the number of
o: protons in the nucleus of its atom
neutrons in the nucleus of its atom
nucleons in the nucleus of its atom
electrons in the outer shell of its atom
questions.e: The atomic number Z is the number of protons, which defines the element; in a neutral atom it also equals the total number of electrons. The number of nucleons is the mass number, and the outer-shell electrons decide the group, not Z.

questions.s: Which ground-state electron configuration belongs to a halogen atom?
questions.e: Halogens have 7 outer electrons (ns²np⁵); 1s²2s²2p⁵ is fluorine. 3s²3p⁶ is argon (noble gas), 3s¹ is sodium (alkali metal) and 3s²3p⁴ is sulfur (group 16).

questions.s: The first four successive ionisation energies of a period 3 element X, in kJ/mol, are 738, 1451, 7733 and 10543. What is the formula of the compound X forms with chlorine?
questions.e: The big jump is between the second (1451) and third (7733) values, so X has 2 outer electrons and forms X²⁺ (X is magnesium). With Cl⁻ the formula is XCl₂. XCl₃ would fit a jump after the third ionisation energy.

questions.s: Moving across period 3 from sodium to chlorine, which trend is correct?
questions.e: Across a period the nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same shell, so atoms shrink and hold electrons more strongly: electronegativity and ionisation energy increase overall. Atomic radius and metallic character therefore decrease, so the other statements are reversed.

questions.s: Which of the following elements is a metalloid (semimetal)?
questions.e: Silicon lies near the border between metals and non-metals in group 14 and has properties of both; it is a semiconductor. Sodium is a typical metal, while sulfur and chlorine are non-metals.

questions.s: Which order of ionic radius is correct?
questions.e: All four ions have 18 electrons (the argon configuration). The radius falls as the nuclear charge rises: S (16) > Cl (17) > K (19) > Ca (20). The first option reverses the trend, as if a larger nuclear charge made the ion bigger.

questions.s: Which of the following atoms has the highest second ionisation energy?
questions.e: After Na loses its single 3s electron, Na⁺ has the neon configuration, so the second electron must come from the full 2p subshell close to the nucleus, which needs a very large energy (about 4560 kJ/mol). For Mg, Al and Si the second electron still comes from the n = 3 shell. Si is tempting because its first ionisation energy is the highest of the four.

questions.s: Which element is in period 2 and group 14 of the periodic table?
questions.e: Period 2 means two occupied shells and group 14 means four outer electrons: 2, 4, which is carbon (Z = 6). Silicon is also in group 14 but in period 3; boron is group 13 and nitrogen group 15.

questions.s: Element X has atomic number 20. Which statement about X is correct?
o: It forms an ion X²⁺ that has 18 electrons
It is in period 3 of the periodic table
Its atom has 2 occupied electron shells
Its oxide is an acidic oxide
questions.e: Z = 20 is calcium, 2, 8, 8, 2: four shells, period 4, group 2. It loses its 2 outer electrons to form Ca²⁺ with 18 electrons. As a reactive metal it has a basic oxide, CaO; 2 is the number of outer electrons, not shells.

questions.s: The ions ᵃXᵐ⁺ and ᵇYⁿ⁻ have the same electron configuration, where a and b are the atomic numbers of X and Y. Which relation is correct?
questions.e: Xᵐ⁺ has lost m electrons, so it has a − m electrons; Yⁿ⁻ has gained n, so it has b + n. Equal configurations mean equal electron numbers: a − m = b + n. a − m = b − n treats the anion as if it had lost electrons.

questions.s: What is the ground-state electron configuration of a chromium atom (atomic number 24)?
questions.e: Chromium is an exception: the arrangement 3d⁵4s¹, with both subshells half-filled, is lower in energy than 3d⁴4s², so the ground state is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹. [Ar]3d⁴4s² is what the simple filling order predicts, and [Ar]3d⁵4s² has 25 electrons (manganese).

questions.s: Water molecules can be formed from the isotopes ¹H, ²H, ¹⁶O and ¹⁸O. How many different relative molecular masses can these water molecules have?
questions.e: The hydrogen pairs ¹H¹H, ¹H²H and ²H²H add 2, 3 or 4; with ¹⁶O this gives 18, 19, 20 and with ¹⁸O gives 20, 21, 22. There are 6 kinds of molecule, but ²H₂¹⁶O and ¹H₂¹⁸O both have mass 20, so only 5 different masses exist (18 to 22).

questions.s: Which hydrogen halide is the most thermally stable?
questions.e: The stability of hydrides follows the non-metallic character of the element, which falls down group 17: HF > HCl > HBr > HI. HI is the least stable and decomposes on heating to H₂ and purple iodine vapour.

questions.s: Which comparison is correct?
questions.e: Ca is below Mg in group 2, so it is more metallic and Ca(OH)₂ is the stronger base. Cl is smaller than S (same period, more protons), N is more non-metallic than P so HNO₃ is the stronger acid, and Na is more metallic than Mg.

questions.s: Natural magnesium contains 80 % ²⁴Mg, 10 % ²⁵Mg and 10 % ²⁶Mg by number of atoms. What is the relative atomic mass of magnesium?
questions.e: Ar = 0.80 × 24 + 0.10 × 25 + 0.10 × 26 = 19.2 + 2.5 + 2.6 = 24.3. 25.0 is the simple average of the three mass numbers, which ignores that ²⁴Mg is far more abundant.

questions.s: The outer-electron configuration of an element is 3d⁵4s¹. Where is it in the periodic table?
questions.e: The highest shell is n = 4, so it is in period 4. For a d-block element the group number is the number of (n−1)d plus ns electrons: 5 + 1 = 6, so group 6 (it is chromium). Group 1 counts only the 4s electron, and period 3 is taken from the 3d label.

questions.s: Selenium (Se) is in group 16, directly below sulfur. Which prediction about selenium is correct?
o: H₂Se is more thermally stable than H₂S
Se is more electronegative than S
The highest oxide of selenium is SeO₂
H₂SeO₄ is a weaker acid than H₂SO₄
questions.e: Going down group 16, non-metallic character decreases, so the highest oxoacid becomes weaker (H₂SeO₄ < H₂SO₄), the hydride becomes less stable and electronegativity falls. With 6 valence electrons the highest oxidation state is +6, so the highest oxide is SeO₃, not SeO₂.

questions.s: What is the shape of an s atomic orbital?
questions.e: An s orbital is spherically symmetric around the nucleus, so the chance of finding the electron depends only on the distance from the nucleus. p orbitals are dumbbell-shaped, with two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus.

questions.s: What are the numbers of protons and electrons in one hydronium ion, H₃O⁺ (H: Z = 1, O: Z = 8)?
questions.e: Protons = 3 × 1 + 8 = 11. A neutral H₃O would have 11 electrons, and the + charge means one fewer, so 10 electrons. The positive charge always means more protons than electrons, so 10 protons and 11 electrons is reversed.

questions.s: Which statement about ¹²C, ¹³C and ¹⁴C is correct?
o: They have almost the same chemical properties
They have different numbers of electrons
An atom of ¹⁴C contains 14 neutrons
questions.e: They are isotopes: each has 6 protons and 6 electrons, so the same electron configuration and almost identical chemistry. Allotropes are different structural forms of an element (diamond, graphite), not different nuclides, and ¹⁴C has 14 − 6 = 8 neutrons.

questions.s: How many periods (horizontal rows) does the modern periodic table have?
questions.e: There are 7 periods, one for each principal shell from n = 1 to n = 7 that is the outer shell of some element. 18 is the number of groups (vertical columns), not periods.

questions.s: X, Y and Z are period 3 elements. The hydroxide of X is a strong base; the hydroxide of Y reacts with both hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution; Z has the highest electronegativity in period 3. Which statement is correct?
o: Y and Z form an ionic compound with formula YZ
The first ionisation energy of X is higher than that of Y
The hydride of Z is less stable than H₂S
questions.e: X is Na (NaOH), Y is Al (amphoteric Al(OH)₃) and Z is Cl. Across the period radius falls, so Na > Al > Cl. Al and Cl form AlCl₃, not YZ; Na (496 kJ/mol) has a lower first ionisation energy than Al (578 kJ/mol); and HCl is more stable than H₂S.
