questions.s: Which ground-state atom has the greatest number of unpaired electrons?
questions.e: P is [Ne]3s²3p³; its three 3p electrons occupy separate orbitals, giving 3 unpaired electrons. C (2p²), Si (3p²) and O (2p⁴) each have only 2 unpaired electrons.

questions.s: How many atomic orbitals are there in the shell with n = 2?
questions.e: The n = 2 shell has one 2s orbital and three 2p orbitals, 4 in total (n² = 4). 8 is the maximum number of electrons in that shell (two per orbital), and 3 counts only the p orbitals.

questions.s: Where is almost all of the mass of an atom concentrated?
questions.e: Protons and neutrons, each about 1836 times heavier than an electron, are packed in the tiny nucleus, so the nucleus holds more than 99.9 % of the mass. The electron cloud fills almost all of the volume but contributes very little mass.

questions.s: Which ion has a completely filled 3d subshell? (Mn: Z = 25, Fe: Z = 26, Cu: Z = 29, Zn: Z = 30)
questions.e: Zn is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s² and loses its two 4s electrons to give Zn²⁺, [Ar]3d¹⁰. Cu²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁹ (Cu is 3d¹⁰4s¹ and loses the 4s and one 3d electron), Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶ and Mn²⁺ is 3d⁵.

questions.s: Going down group 17 from fluorine to iodine, which property of the elements increases?
questions.e: Larger halogen molecules have stronger intermolecular (van der Waals) forces, so melting points rise: F₂ and Cl₂ are gases, Br₂ a liquid and I₂ a solid. Electronegativity, oxidising strength and the vigour of reaction with hydrogen all decrease down the group.

questions.s: An atom of element X (atomic number below 20) has n occupied electron shells, 2n + 1 electrons in its outer shell and 2n² − 1 protons. Which statement about X must be true?
o: X forms an oxoacid with formula HXO₃
X forms a hydride with formula H₂X
questions.e: n = 2 gives 5 outer electrons and Z = 7 (nitrogen, 2, 5); n = 3 gives 7 outer electrons and Z = 17 (chlorine, 2, 8, 7); n = 1 is impossible. So X is N or Cl, both non-metals, and both form HXO₃ (HNO₃, HClO₃). Period 3 is only true for Cl, and their hydrides are NH₃ and HCl, not H₂X.

questions.s: Which element has the lowest first ionisation energy?
questions.e: Ionisation energy falls down a group and rises across a period, so it is lowest at the bottom left: caesium, whose outer 6s electron is far from the nucleus and well shielded. Helium has the highest first ionisation energy of all elements.

questions.s: Which element forms an oxide that is basic?
questions.e: Metals form basic oxides: CaO reacts with water to give Ca(OH)₂ and neutralises acids. Sulfur, phosphorus and carbon are non-metals whose oxides (SO₂, P₄O₁₀, CO₂) are acidic.

questions.s: Gallium consists of 60 % ⁶⁹Ga and 40 % ⁷¹Ga by number of atoms. What is its relative atomic mass?
questions.e: Ar = 0.60 × 69 + 0.40 × 71 = 41.4 + 28.4 = 69.8. 70.2 swaps the abundances, and 70.0 is the plain average of the two mass numbers.

questions.s: An atom has the ground-state electron configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶4s². Where is the element in the periodic table?
questions.e: The outermost shell is n = 4, so period 4, and there are 2 outer electrons in 4s with no d electrons, so group 2 (calcium, Z = 20). Group 12 would need a full 3d¹⁰ as well (zinc); period 3 comes from looking only at the 3p subshell.

questions.s: Which set of ions all have the same electron configuration as a neon atom?
questions.e: Al³⁺ (13 − 3), O²⁻ (8 + 2) and F⁻ (9 + 1) all have 10 electrons, like Ne. Cl⁻, K⁺ and Ca²⁺ have 18 electrons (argon), and Li⁺ has only 2 (helium).

questions.s: The first ionisation energy of an element is the energy needed to
o: add one electron to each atom in 1 mol of gaseous atoms
remove one electron from each atom in 1 mol of gaseous atoms
remove all outer electrons from 1 mol of gaseous atoms
break 1 mol of the element into separate gaseous atoms
questions.e: First ionisation energy is the energy for X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻ per mole: one electron removed from each gaseous atom. Adding an electron is described by electron affinity, and turning the element into gaseous atoms is atomisation.

questions.s: Strontium (Sr) is in group 2 and period 5. Which prediction about strontium is correct?
o: It reacts with water less vigorously than magnesium
Sr(OH)₂ is a stronger base than Ca(OH)₂
A strontium atom is smaller than a calcium atom
It forms Sr⁺ ions in its compounds
questions.e: Metallic character increases down group 2, so Sr is more reactive than Mg and Ca, and its hydroxide is the stronger base. Sr has more shells than Ca, so its atom is larger, and with 2 outer electrons it forms Sr²⁺.

questions.s: Which order of first ionisation energy is correct?
questions.e: Values (kJ/mol) are about Li 520, Be 900, B 801, C 1086, N 1402, O 1314. N exceeds O because N's 2p³ is half-filled, while O's fourth 2p electron is paired and repelled. B > Be is wrong for a similar reason: B's 2p electron is easier to remove than Be's 2s electrons.

questions.s: The first six successive ionisation energies of a period 3 element Y, in kJ/mol, are 1012, 1907, 2914, 4964, 6274 and 21267. What is the formula of the highest oxide of Y?
questions.e: The large jump is between the fifth (6274) and sixth (21267) values, so Y has 5 outer electrons and is in group 15 (phosphorus). Its highest oxidation state is +5, so the highest oxide is Y₂O₅ (written P₄O₁₀ for the real molecule). Y₂O₃ uses the +3 state, which is not the highest.

questions.s: Which of the following atoms contains exactly one proton and one neutron?
questions.e: Hydrogen has Z = 1, so every H atom has one proton; ²H (deuterium) has 2 − 1 = 1 neutron. ¹H has no neutron, ³H (tritium) has 2, and ⁴He has 2 protons and 2 neutrons.

questions.s: Which element has three occupied electron shells and six electrons in its outer shell?
questions.e: Three shells with 6 outer electrons is 2, 8, 6, i.e. Z = 16, sulfur (period 3, group 16). Oxygen also has 6 outer electrons but only 2 shells; chlorine has 7 and silicon 4.

questions.s: Which comparison of particle radii is correct?
questions.e: When Cl gains an electron, the extra electron–electron repulsion with the same nuclear charge makes the ion larger, so Cl⁻ > Cl. Cations are smaller than their atoms (Na⁺ loses the whole 3s shell), and Fe³⁺, with fewer electrons than Fe²⁺, is the smaller of the two iron ions.

questions.s: Uranium has atomic number 92. In one atom of ²³⁵U, by how many does the number of neutrons exceed the number of electrons?
questions.e: Neutrons = 235 − 92 = 143 and electrons = 92 in the neutral atom, so the difference is 143 − 92 = 51. 143 is the number of neutrons itself, not the difference.

questions.s: Which element is in the same period as potassium and the same group as nitrogen?
questions.e: Potassium is in period 4 and nitrogen in group 15; the period 4 member of group 15 is arsenic (Z = 33). Phosphorus is in group 15 but period 3, antimony is in period 5, and calcium is in period 4 but group 2.

questions.s: A main-group element X forms the hydride H₂X. In the highest oxide of X, X makes up 40 % of the mass. What is the relative atomic mass of X? (O = 16)
questions.e: H₂X shows X has a −2 state, so it is in group 16 and its highest oxidation state is +6, giving the oxide XO₃. Then X/(X + 48) = 0.40, so 0.6X = 19.2 and X = 32 (sulfur). Using XO₂ instead would not give a whole-number answer, and 16 is oxygen itself.

questions.s: Which statement about the structure of the periodic table is correct?
o: Every period begins with an alkali metal
The transition elements begin in period 2
questions.e: Period 3 runs from Na (Z = 11) to Ar (Z = 18), which is 8 elements. Period 1 begins with hydrogen, which is a non-metal although it sits in group 1, and the transition (d-block) elements first appear in period 4 (Sc to Zn).

questions.s: How many neutrons are in one atom of aluminium-27 (atomic number 13)?
questions.e: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 27 − 13 = 14. 13 is the number of protons and 27 is the total number of protons plus neutrons.

questions.s: How many electrons does the nitride ion, N³⁻, contain? (N: Z = 7)
questions.e: A nitrogen atom has 7 electrons and the 3− charge means it has gained 3 more, giving 10 (the neon configuration). 4 comes from subtracting the charge, as if the ion were positive.

questions.s: What is the ground-state electron configuration of a potassium atom (atomic number 19)?
questions.e: After 3p⁶ (18 electrons), the 4s subshell is lower in energy than 3d, so the 19th electron goes into 4s: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶4s¹. Putting it into 3d ignores the filling order, and 4s² would need 20 electrons.

questions.s: Copper consists of ⁶³Cu and ⁶⁵Cu only, and its relative atomic mass is 63.5. What percentage of copper atoms are ⁶³Cu?
questions.e: Let x be the fraction of ⁶³Cu: 63x + 65(1 − x) = 63.5, so 2x = 1.5 and x = 0.75, i.e. 75 %. 25 % is the share of ⁶⁵Cu; an average of 63.5 is much closer to 63, so ⁶³Cu must dominate.

questions.s: Which of the following atoms has the smallest atomic radius?
questions.e: All four are in period 2. Across a period the nuclear charge rises while electrons are added to the same shell, so the atoms get smaller; fluorine, furthest to the right, is the smallest and lithium the largest.

questions.s: Main-group elements whose outer electron configuration is ns²np⁴ belong to which group?
questions.e: ns²np⁴ means 6 outer electrons, which is group 16 (O, S, Se). For p-block elements the group number is 10 + the number of s and p outer electrons; group 6 is a d-block group (Cr, Mo) and group 14 has ns²np².

questions.s: Which order of electronegativity is correct?
questions.e: Electronegativity increases across period 2 because the nuclear charge increases while the atoms shrink, so F > O > N > C. Fluorine is the most electronegative element of all; C > N > O > F is the order reversed.

questions.s: The atom of element X has two electron shells with 5 electrons in the outer shell. What is the formula of the simplest hydride of X?
questions.e: 2, 5 is nitrogen (Z = 7). It needs 3 more electrons to complete its octet, so it forms three bonds to hydrogen: NH₃, i.e. XH₃. XH₂ fits group 16 and XH₄ fits group 14.

questions.s: Which of the following is a transition (d-block) element?
questions.e: Iron (Z = 26) is [Ar]3d⁶4s² and lies in the d-block in period 4. Potassium and calcium are s-block metals and aluminium is a p-block metal in group 13.

questions.s: How many electrons occupy the 3p subshell of a ground-state sulfur atom (atomic number 16)?
questions.e: Sulfur is 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁴: after 12 electrons fill up to 3s², the remaining 4 go into 3p. 6 is the capacity of a p subshell, and 2 is the 3s count.

questions.s: The first four successive ionisation energies of element X, in kJ/mol, are 419, 3052, 4420 and 5877. In which group is X?
questions.e: The big jump comes straight after the first value (419 to 3052), so only one electron is in the outer shell and the second comes from a full inner shell. X is in group 1 (it is potassium). A group 2 element would show the jump between the second and third values.

questions.s: Which pair consists of two isotopes?
questions.e: ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl have the same number of protons (17) and different numbers of neutrons (18 and 20), so they are isotopes. O₂ and O₃ are allotropes, H₂O and D₂O are compounds, and ⁴⁰K and ⁴⁰Ca have the same mass number but are different elements.

questions.s: The ions A²⁺, B⁺, C³⁻ and D⁻ all have the same electron configuration. Which order of atomic numbers (written a, b, c, d) is correct?
questions.e: Equal electron numbers mean a − 2 = b − 1 = c + 3 = d + 1, so a is the largest and c the smallest: a > b > d > c (for example Mg, Na, N, F). The reversed order c > d > b > a forgets that cations have lost electrons and so need more protons.

questions.s: Why are the group 18 elements (noble gases) very unreactive?
questions.e: Noble gases have a full outer shell (2 for He, ns²np⁶ for the others), which is very stable, so they have little tendency to gain, lose or share electrons. Atoms with one outer electron are the reactive alkali metals.

questions.s: Which of the following oxides is amphoteric?
questions.e: Aluminium lies between the metals and non-metals of period 3, and Al₂O₃ reacts with both acids (giving Al³⁺) and strong bases (giving aluminate). Na₂O and MgO are basic oxides, and SO₃ is an acidic oxide.

questions.s: Which order of atomic radius is correct?
questions.e: K is below Na in group 1, so it has an extra shell and is larger. Na, Mg and Al are in period 3, where radius falls from left to right. So K > Na > Mg > Al; the third option reverses both trends.

questions.s: How many unpaired electrons does a ground-state manganese atom (atomic number 25) have?
questions.e: Mn is [Ar]3d⁵4s². The 4s electrons are paired, and by Hund's rule the five 3d electrons occupy the five 3d orbitals singly, giving 5 unpaired electrons. 7 counts all the outer electrons, including the paired 4s pair.

questions.s: What is the maximum number of electrons the first shell (n = 1) can hold?
questions.e: The first shell has only the 1s orbital, which holds 2 electrons with opposite spins (2n² = 2). That is why period 1 has only hydrogen and helium.

questions.s: Hydrogen chloride molecules can be formed from the isotopes ¹H, ²H, ³H, ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl. How many different relative molecular masses are possible?
questions.e: There are 3 × 2 = 6 kinds of molecule, with masses 36, 37, 38 (with ³⁵Cl) and 38, 39, 40 (with ³⁷Cl). ³H³⁵Cl and ¹H³⁷Cl both have mass 38, so there are 5 different masses. 6 counts molecules rather than masses.

questions.s: How many electrons occupy p orbitals in a ground-state silicon atom (atomic number 14)?
questions.e: Silicon is 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p², so the p electrons are 2p⁶ plus 3p², giving 8. Answering 2 counts only the outer 3p electrons, and 6 only the 2p electrons.

questions.s: Which of the following elements is in the p-block of the periodic table?
questions.e: Sulfur's last electrons enter the 3p subshell (3s²3p⁴), so it is a p-block element in group 16. Sodium and calcium are s-block elements, and iron is a d-block element.

questions.s: For a main-group element R, the sum of its highest positive oxidation state and its lowest negative oxidation state is 4. Which element is R?
questions.e: For a group with g outer electrons (g ≥ 4), the highest state is +g and the lowest is g − 8, so the sum is 2g − 8 = 4, giving g = 6. Sulfur fits: +6 + (−2) = 4. Carbon gives +4 − 4 = 0, nitrogen +5 − 3 = 2 and chlorine +7 − 1 = 6.

questions.s: How many unpaired electrons does a ground-state Fe²⁺ ion have? (Fe: Z = 26)
questions.e: Fe is [Ar]3d⁶4s², and Fe²⁺ loses the two 4s electrons to give [Ar]3d⁶. Six electrons in five 3d orbitals: five go in singly, and the sixth pairs with one of them, leaving 4 unpaired. 6 forgets that one pair must form.

questions.s: The reactivity of group 1 metals with water increases down the group. What is the main reason?
o: The outer electron is lost more easily
The atoms gain electrons more easily
The number of outer electrons rises
questions.e: Down the group the outer electron is in a higher shell, further from the nucleus and better shielded, so it is lost more easily and the metal reacts faster. The nuclear charge actually increases down the group, and every group 1 atom has exactly one outer electron.

questions.s: What is the electron configuration of the aluminium ion, Al³⁺ (aluminium has atomic number 13)?
questions.e: Al is 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p¹; forming Al³⁺ removes the 3p¹ and both 3s electrons, leaving 10 electrons as 1s²2s²2p⁶. 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p¹ is the neutral atom, and 1s²2s²2p³ wrongly takes the 3 electrons off a 10-electron core.

questions.s: Which of the following compounds contains ionic bonds?
questions.e: Magnesium, a reactive metal, transfers two electrons to two chlorine atoms, giving Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held by ionic bonds. HCl, CO₂ and CH₄ are formed from non-metals only, which share electron pairs in covalent bonds; HCl is polar but still covalent.

questions.s: Which substance contains both ionic bonds and covalent bonds?
questions.e: NaOH is made of Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions (ionic bonding), and inside each OH⁻ ion the O and H are joined by a covalent bond. CaCl₂ and Na₂O contain only ionic bonds, and H₂O₂ contains only covalent bonds (O–H and O–O).

questions.s: What is the shape of a carbon dioxide molecule?
questions.e: In O=C=O the central carbon has two bonding regions (two double bonds) and no lone pairs, so they point in opposite directions: the molecule is linear with a 180° angle. Bent shapes, as in H₂O, need lone pairs on the central atom.

questions.s: Which molecule contains polar bonds but is non-polar overall?
questions.e: Each C–Cl bond is polar, but CCl₄ is a regular tetrahedron, so the four bond dipoles cancel and the molecule has no overall dipole. H₂O (bent) and NH₃ (pyramidal) have dipoles that do not cancel, and HCl has a single polar bond.

questions.s: What is the approximate H–N–H bond angle in an ammonia molecule?
questions.e: N has three bonding pairs and one lone pair, arranged roughly tetrahedrally. The lone pair repels the bonding pairs more strongly than they repel each other, squeezing the angle from 109.5° (as in CH₄) to about 107°.

questions.s: Water boils at 100 °C, while hydrogen sulfide, H₂S, boils at about −60 °C. What is the main reason for this difference?
o: O–H bonds are stronger than S–H bonds
Hydrogen bonds form between H₂O molecules
H₂O has a larger molar mass than H₂S
H₂O molecules are linear but H₂S are bent
questions.e: Boiling separates molecules, so it depends on intermolecular forces, not on the covalent O–H bonds inside each molecule. O is small and very electronegative, so H₂O molecules form hydrogen bonds, which are much stronger than the van der Waals forces in H₂S. H₂O actually has the smaller molar mass (18 versus 34), and both molecules are bent.

questions.s: Which solid is a covalent network (giant covalent) crystal?
questions.e: In SiO₂ every Si atom is covalently bonded to 4 O atoms and every O to 2 Si atoms in a continuous 3D network, with no separate molecules. Dry ice (CO₂) and iodine (I₂) are molecular crystals, and sodium chloride is an ionic crystal.

questions.s: How many lone pairs of electrons are on the nitrogen atom in an ammonia molecule, NH₃?
questions.e: N has 5 valence electrons; 3 are used in the three N–H bonds and the other 2 form one lone pair. Answering 3 confuses the number of bonding pairs with lone pairs.

questions.s: In which molecule does every atom have a complete outer shell of 8 electrons (2 for hydrogen)?
questions.e: In NCl₃, N has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair (8 electrons) and each Cl has 1 bond and 3 lone pairs (8 electrons). In BF₃ boron has only 6 electrons, while P in PCl₅ has 10 and S in SF₆ has 12.

questions.s: Which order of boiling points of the hydrogen halides is correct?
questions.e: For HCl, HBr and HI, van der Waals forces grow with molecular size, so HI > HBr > HCl (about −35, −67 and −85 °C). HF forms hydrogen bonds between molecules, which lifts its boiling point to about 20 °C, above all the others. HI > HBr > HCl > HF ignores hydrogen bonding.

questions.s: Which substance conducts electricity well in the solid state?
questions.e: Copper is a metal: its delocalised electrons move freely through the lattice and carry current. Solid sodium chloride has ions fixed in place and conducts only when molten or dissolved; sulfur and ice are molecular solids with no mobile charges.

questions.s: What is the shape of a boron trifluoride, BF₃, molecule?
questions.e: Boron has 3 valence electrons, all used in three B–F bonds, so there are 3 bonding pairs and no lone pair on B. They spread out at 120° in one plane: trigonal planar. Trigonal pyramidal (as in NH₃) needs a fourth, lone pair.

questions.s: How many σ (sigma) and π (pi) bonds are there in a nitrogen molecule, N₂?
questions.e: N≡N is a triple bond. The first bond between two atoms is always a σ bond formed by head-on overlap; the second and third are π bonds formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals. So N₂ has 1 σ and 2 π bonds; there can never be more than one σ bond between the same two atoms.

questions.s: Magnesium oxide melts at about 2850 °C, while sodium chloride melts at 801 °C. What is the main reason?
questions.e: Both are ionic crystals. Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry twice the charges of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (and are also smaller), so the electrostatic attraction and lattice energy are much greater. Larger ions would weaken the attraction, not strengthen it.

questions.s: Which description best fits metallic bonding?
o: Electron pairs shared by two atoms
Electrons transferred from metal to non-metal
Cations held in a sea of delocalised electrons
questions.e: In a metal, atoms release their outer electrons into a shared, delocalised 'sea', and the attraction between the cations and these electrons holds the lattice together. Sharing pairs is covalent bonding, transfer is ionic bonding, and attractions between molecules are intermolecular forces.

questions.s: Which of the following molecules is polar?
questions.e: S in SO₂ has two bonding regions and one lone pair, so the molecule is bent and the two S=O bond dipoles do not cancel. CO₂ is linear, BF₃ trigonal planar and CH₄ tetrahedral, so their bond dipoles cancel by symmetry.

questions.s: Which substance has the highest melting point?
questions.e: Diamond is a covalent network: melting means breaking strong C–C covalent bonds throughout the crystal, so it melts above 3500 °C. Sodium chloride (801 °C) is ionic, sodium (98 °C) is a soft metal and iodine (114 °C) is a molecular solid.

questions.s: Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats. What is the explanation?
o: Hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice
The O–H bonds become longer when water freezes
Ice contains lighter molecules than liquid water
Freezing breaks the hydrogen bonds between molecules
questions.e: In ice each H₂O molecule forms hydrogen bonds to 4 neighbours in a fixed tetrahedral arrangement, which leaves a lot of empty space. On melting, some hydrogen bonds break and molecules pack closer, so the liquid is denser. Freezing forms more hydrogen bonds, not fewer.

questions.s: Which order of bond energy is correct?
questions.e: Down group 17 the halogen atom gets larger, so the H–X bond gets longer and weaker: H–F > H–Cl > H–Br > H–I (about 568, 431, 366, 298 kJ/mol). Multiple bonds between the same atoms are stronger, so C≡C > C=C > C–C, and Cl–Cl (242 kJ/mol) is weaker than both H–Cl and H–H (436 kJ/mol).

questions.s: Which substance contains a coordinate (dative covalent) bond?
questions.e: In NH₄⁺ the lone pair on N in NH₃ is donated to an H⁺ ion, forming a coordinate bond (once formed it is identical to the other N–H bonds). CH₄ and H₂O have only ordinary covalent bonds, and NaCl is purely ionic.

questions.s: How many σ bonds and π bonds are there in one ethene molecule, CH₂=CH₂?
questions.e: Ethene has four C–H single bonds (4 σ) and one C=C double bond, which is 1 σ + 1 π. In total that is 5 σ and 1 π. 4 σ and 1 π forgets the σ part of the double bond, and 6 σ treats both halves of the double bond as σ.

questions.s: Which pair of species has the same shape?
questions.e: In both NH₃ and H₃O⁺ the central atom has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair, so both are trigonal pyramidal. BF₃ (no lone pair) is trigonal planar unlike NH₃; SO₂ has a lone pair and is bent while CO₂ is linear; H₂O is bent while CH₄ is tetrahedral.

questions.s: In the electron-dot structure of a nitrogen molecule, N₂, how many lone pairs of electrons are there in total?
questions.e: Each N has 5 valence electrons (10 in total). The N≡N triple bond uses 6, and the remaining 4 form one lone pair on each N, so there are 2 lone pairs. 3 is the number of shared pairs, not lone pairs.

questions.s: Substance X melts at about 1700 °C, is very hard, does not conduct electricity either as a solid or when molten, and does not dissolve in water. What type of crystal is X most likely to form?
questions.e: A very high melting point and hardness need strong bonds throughout the solid, and no conduction even when molten rules out ions and free electrons. That fits a covalent network crystal such as SiO₂. An ionic crystal would conduct when molten, and molecular crystals melt at low temperatures.

questions.s: Which order of melting points is correct?
questions.e: In ionic crystals with ions of the same charge, smaller ions give stronger attraction: F⁻ is smaller than Cl⁻ and Na⁺ smaller than K⁺, so NaF (993 °C) > NaCl (801 °C) > KCl (770 °C). Metallic bonding strengthens from Na to Al, so that order is reversed, and molecular CO₂ melts far below network SiO₂.

questions.s: Which of the following bonds is the most polar?
questions.e: Bond polarity grows with the electronegativity difference between the two atoms. F is the most electronegative element, so the difference with H is largest in H–F; it decreases from Cl to Br to I.

questions.s: What is the shape of a water molecule?
questions.e: O in H₂O has 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs arranged roughly tetrahedrally; with only the atoms counted, the shape is bent with an angle of about 104.5°. It is not linear because the lone pairs push the two O–H bonds together.

questions.s: In silicon dioxide each Si atom is bonded to 4 O atoms and each O atom to 2 Si atoms. How many moles of Si–O bonds are present in 1 mol of SiO₂?
questions.e: Each Si atom forms 4 Si–O bonds, and every Si–O bond has exactly one Si atom, so counting from Si gives 4 bonds per SiO₂ unit: 4 mol. Counting from O (2 O × 2 bonds) also gives 4. 2 mol comes from the formula's two O atoms, as if each O formed only one bond.

questions.s: Which of the following substances forms hydrogen bonds between its molecules?
questions.e: Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded directly to N, O or F; methanol has an O–H group, so its molecules hydrogen-bond to each other. In CH₄, HCl and H₂S, hydrogen is bonded to C, Cl or S, which are not electronegative and small enough, so only van der Waals forces act.

questions.s: Silicon dioxide melts at about 1700 °C, while carbon dioxide is a gas at room temperature. What is the main reason?
o: Si–O bonds are polar but C=O bonds are not
SiO₂ has a much larger molar mass than CO₂
SiO₂ is a covalent network but CO₂ is molecular
CO₂ molecules attract each other by hydrogen bonds
questions.e: Melting SiO₂ requires breaking strong Si–O covalent bonds in a giant 3D network, whereas CO₂ exists as small separate molecules held only by weak van der Waals forces. Both kinds of bond are polar, and CO₂ cannot form hydrogen bonds since it has no H atom.

questions.s: Which statement about ionic compounds is correct?
o: They are soft with low melting points
They are made of separate molecules
questions.e: When an ionic compound melts (or dissolves), its ions become free to move and carry current. In the solid the ions are locked in the lattice, so it does not conduct. Ionic compounds are hard and have high melting points, and they are lattices of ions rather than molecules.

questions.s: In which molecule is the central atom sp² hybridised?
questions.e: The central atom's hybridisation follows its number of electron domains (bonding pairs plus lone pairs). B in BF₃ has 3 domains and no lone pair, so it is sp² and the molecule is planar. C in CH₄, N in NH₃ and O in H₂O each have 4 domains (counting lone pairs), so they are sp³ even though NH₃ and H₂O are not tetrahedral in shape.

questions.s: Which order of boiling points is correct for the group 14 hydrides?
questions.e: These are all non-polar tetrahedral molecules with no hydrogen bonding, so only van der Waals forces act, and these grow with molecular size. Boiling point therefore rises steadily from CH₄ to SnH₄. Putting CH₄ first wrongly assumes hydrogen bonding, which C–H bonds cannot form.

questions.s: Which molecule contains a triple bond?
questions.e: In H–C≡N the carbon uses one electron pair for the bond to H and three pairs for the bond to N, completing the octets of C and N. O₂ and C₂H₄ have double bonds, and Cl₂ has a single bond.

questions.s: Which solid is a molecular crystal?
questions.e: Solid iodine is made of I₂ molecules held together by weak van der Waals forces, so it is soft and sublimes easily. Quartz (SiO₂) is a covalent network, potassium bromide is ionic and iron is metallic.

questions.s: Which set contains only non-polar molecules?
questions.e: CO₂ (linear), BF₃ (trigonal planar) and CCl₄ (tetrahedral) are symmetrical, so their bond dipoles cancel. Each other set contains a polar molecule: H₂O and NH₃ have lone pairs that make them asymmetrical, and HCl has a single polar bond.

questions.s: X, Y and Z are elements of periods 1-3. X has the smallest atomic radius of all elements; the outer shell of Y has three times as many electrons as its inner shell; Z is the period 3 metal with the largest atomic radius. Which statement is correct?
o: X₂Y₂ contains only polar covalent bonds
Z₂Y₂ contains ionic bonds and non-polar covalent bonds
The X–Y–X bond angle in X₂Y is 180°
questions.e: X is H, Y is O (2, 6) and Z is Na. Na₂O₂ consists of Na⁺ and O₂²⁻ ions, and inside O₂²⁻ the O–O bond is a non-polar covalent bond. H₂O₂ contains a non-polar O–O bond as well as polar O–H bonds, NaH is ionic (Na⁺ H⁻), and H₂O is bent (about 104.5°).

questions.s: The melting points of sodium, magnesium and aluminium are 98 °C, 650 °C and 660 °C. What explains the rise in melting point from sodium to aluminium?
o: More delocalised electrons and higher cation charge
Atomic radius increases from sodium to aluminium
The atoms have fewer and fewer valence electrons
Van der Waals forces between the atoms grow stronger
questions.e: Na, Mg and Al give 1, 2 and 3 electrons each to the electron sea and form cations of charge +1, +2, +3, which are also smaller. The attraction between cations and delocalised electrons, and so the metallic bond, gets stronger. The atomic radius actually decreases and the number of valence electrons increases across the period.

questions.s: In a sodium chloride crystal, how many Cl⁻ ions are nearest neighbours of each Na⁺ ion?
questions.e: In the rock-salt structure each Na⁺ sits at the centre of an octahedron of 6 Cl⁻ ions, and each Cl⁻ is likewise surrounded by 6 Na⁺. 8 is the coordination number in caesium chloride, where the larger Cs⁺ ion fits 8 neighbours.

questions.s: Ammonia is extremely soluble in water. Which factor is most important?
o: NH₃ has a larger molar mass than water
NH₃ forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules
NH₃ molecules have a linear, symmetrical shape
questions.e: NH₃ is polar and has N–H bonds and a lone pair on N, so it forms hydrogen bonds with H₂O molecules; polar dissolves in polar. NH₃ is actually polar and trigonal pyramidal, and its molar mass (17) is slightly smaller than that of water (18).

questions.s: Why does graphite conduct electricity?
o: Its layers slide easily over each other
Each C atom has one delocalised electron
questions.e: In graphite each carbon uses 3 of its 4 valence electrons in σ bonds within a flat layer; the fourth electron is delocalised over the whole layer and can move, carrying current. The sliding of layers explains why graphite is soft and slippery, not why it conducts.

questions.s: Which of the following processes breaks covalent bonds?
questions.e: Quartz is a covalent network, so melting it must break Si–O covalent bonds. Melting ice breaks hydrogen bonds between H₂O molecules, dissolving NaCl separates ions (ionic bonds), and subliming iodine overcomes van der Waals forces between I₂ molecules while the I–I bonds stay intact.

questions.s: What is the shape of the carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻?
questions.e: The central C forms bonds to three O atoms and has no lone pair (its 4 valence electrons plus the 2 extra electrons are all used in bonding to O), so there are 3 electron domains at 120°: trigonal planar. Trigonal pyramidal would require a lone pair on C, as on N in NH₃.

questions.s: Iodine dissolves much better in tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, than in water. What is the reason?
o: Both I₂ and CCl₄ are non-polar
I₂ forms hydrogen bonds with CCl₄
CCl₄ is a strongly polar solvent
questions.e: Like dissolves like: non-polar I₂ mixes easily with the non-polar solvent CCl₄, while water molecules hold each other strongly by hydrogen bonds and do not let I₂ in. Neither I₂ nor CCl₄ has H bonded to N, O or F, so no hydrogen bonds form between them.

questions.s: Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, and dimethyl ether, CH₃OCH₃, have the same molecular formula. Ethanol boils at 78 °C and dimethyl ether at −24 °C. Why?
o: Ethanol has a larger molar mass
Dimethyl ether molecules contain no polar bonds
Ethanol molecules hydrogen-bond to each other
questions.e: Ethanol has an O–H group, so its molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other; dimethyl ether has no H on oxygen, so it cannot. The molar masses are identical (both C₂H₆O), and dimethyl ether does contain polar C–O bonds, so those options are wrong.

questions.s: In diamond each carbon atom is covalently bonded to 4 other carbon atoms. How many moles of C–C bonds are there in 12 g of diamond? (C = 12)
questions.e: 12 g is 1 mol of C atoms. Each atom has 4 bonds, but each bond is shared by 2 atoms, so the number of bonds is 1 × 4 ÷ 2 = 2 mol. 4 mol counts every bond twice, and 1.5 mol is the value for graphite, where each C has only 3 bonds.

questions.s: What is the shape of the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻?
questions.e: The central S is bonded to 4 O atoms and has no lone pair, so the 4 electron domains point to the corners of a tetrahedron (angles about 109.5°). Square planar would need 2 extra lone pairs on S, and octahedral needs 6 domains.

questions.s: A covalent bond is formed by
o: transfer of electrons from one atom to another
sharing a pair of electrons between two atoms
questions.e: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons attracted by the nuclei of both atoms. Transfer of electrons followed by attraction between the ions is ionic bonding, and attraction between molecules is an intermolecular force, not a bond within a molecule.

questions.s: Aluminium is a metal, yet aluminium chloride is usually described as covalent. Which observation is the best evidence that AlCl₃ is covalent?
o: Molten AlCl₃ does not conduct electricity
questions.e: An ionic compound conducts when molten because its ions become mobile. Molten AlCl₃ does not conduct, so it contains no free ions: it is made of covalent molecules (it also sublimes at about 180 °C). Its solution conducts only because AlCl₃ reacts with water to form ions, which also happens with covalent HCl, so that is not evidence.

questions.s: Which of the following alkanes has the lowest boiling point?
questions.e: Pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane are isomers (C₅H₁₂); more branching makes the molecule more compact, reducing the contact area and van der Waals forces, so 2,2-dimethylpropane boils lowest (about 10 °C, against 28 °C and 36 °C). Hexane is larger still and boils highest.

questions.s: Which of the following compounds is covalent?
questions.e: CCl₄ contains only non-metals (C and Cl), which share electron pairs. KF, CaO and Na₂S are each formed from a reactive metal and a non-metal, which transfer electrons to form ions.

questions.s: In the electron-dot structure of carbon dioxide, O=C=O, how many lone pairs of electrons are there in the whole molecule?
questions.e: CO₂ has 4 + 6 + 6 = 16 valence electrons; the two double bonds use 8, leaving 8 electrons = 4 lone pairs, two on each O. The carbon has none, which is why answering 0 is tempting if only the central atom is considered.

questions.s: Which statement about hydrogen bonds is correct?
o: They are stronger than covalent bonds
They raise the boiling point of water
They form between H and any non-metal
questions.e: Hydrogen bonds between H₂O molecules must be overcome on boiling, which is why water boils at 100 °C rather than far below 0 °C. They are much weaker than covalent bonds, and they need H attached to N, O or F, so methane (C–H bonds) cannot form them.

questions.s: Which statement about the phosphorus trichloride molecule, PCl₃, is correct?
o: It is trigonal planar and non-polar
It is tetrahedral with no lone pair on P
The P atom has no lone pair of electrons
It is trigonal pyramidal and polar
questions.e: P has 5 valence electrons: 3 form P–Cl bonds and 2 form a lone pair, giving 4 electron domains and a trigonal pyramidal shape like NH₃. The bond dipoles do not cancel, so the molecule is polar. Trigonal planar would be correct only without the lone pair, as in BCl₃.

questions.s: Which compound has the greatest ionic character in its bonding?
questions.e: Ionic character grows with the electronegativity difference. Cs is the least electronegative of these metals and F the most electronegative element, so CsF has by far the largest difference (about 3.2). AlCl₃ and BeCl₂ are largely covalent, and LiI has a small difference because I is only moderately electronegative.

questions.s: Which statement comparing diamond and graphite is correct?
o: In graphite each C is bonded to 3 others
Diamond is soft because its layers slide
Diamond and graphite are isotopes of carbon
questions.e: In graphite each carbon is covalently bonded to 3 others in flat hexagonal layers; in diamond each is bonded to 4 in a 3D network. Graphite conducts and is soft (layers slide), while diamond is hard and does not conduct. They are allotropes, not isotopes.

questions.s: Which order of carbon–carbon bond length is correct?
questions.e: More shared electron pairs pull the two nuclei closer, so bond length decreases from single to double to triple: about 154, 134 and 120 pm. Bond strength follows the opposite order, which is why C≡C > C=C > C–C is a tempting mix-up.

questions.s: The boiling points of NH₃, PH₃ and AsH₃ are −33 °C, −88 °C and −62 °C. Which explanation is correct?
o: NH₃ has the strongest van der Waals forces of the three
The P–H bond is the weakest of the three covalent bonds
NH₃ forms hydrogen bonds; van der Waals forces rise from PH₃ to AsH₃
PH₃ is a non-polar molecule, so it boils lowest
questions.e: PH₃ and AsH₃ have no hydrogen bonding, so their boiling points rise with molecular size (stronger van der Waals forces). NH₃, the smallest, would boil lowest, but N–H bonds allow hydrogen bonding, raising it above both. NH₃ actually has the weakest van der Waals forces, and boiling does not break covalent bonds.

questions.s: When magnesium reacts with chlorine to form magnesium chloride, what happens to the electrons?
o: Each Mg atom shares two electron pairs with the Cl atoms
Each Cl atom loses one electron to Mg
Each Mg atom gains two electrons from Cl
Each Mg atom gives one electron to each of two Cl
questions.e: Mg (2, 8, 2) loses its 2 outer electrons, one to each Cl atom (2, 8, 7), giving Mg²⁺ and two Cl⁻ ions, all with full outer shells; hence the formula MgCl₂. A metal loses electrons rather than gaining them, and no electron pairs are shared in ionic bonding.

questions.s: Which molecule contains both polar and non-polar covalent bonds but is non-polar overall?
questions.e: Ethene has polar C–H bonds and a non-polar C=C bond, and its planar, symmetrical shape makes the dipoles cancel. H₂O₂ and N₂H₄ also contain non-polar O–O and N–N bonds, but their shapes are not symmetrical, so they are polar molecules. CO₂ is non-polar but has only polar C=O bonds.

questions.s: Which substance contains a non-polar covalent bond?
questions.e: In Cl₂ two identical atoms share the electron pair equally, so the bond is non-polar. HCl and H₂O have polar covalent bonds because Cl and O are more electronegative than H, and NaCl is ionic.

questions.s: What are the shape and bond angle of a methane molecule, CH₄?
questions.e: Carbon has 4 bonding pairs and no lone pair; they repel each other equally and point to the corners of a regular tetrahedron with angles of 109.5°. Trigonal pyramidal with 107° is the shape of NH₃, which has a lone pair.

questions.s: Which compound contains both ionic and covalent bonds?
questions.e: Ammonium nitrate consists of NH₄⁺ and NO₃⁻ ions held by ionic bonds, and the atoms inside each ion are joined by covalent bonds. MgO and KCl are purely ionic, and HNO₃ is a covalent molecule.

questions.s: Which of these molecules has an overall dipole moment?
questions.e: NH₃ is trigonal pyramidal because of the lone pair on N, so its three N–H bond dipoles add up to an overall dipole. CO₂ (linear), CCl₄ (tetrahedral) and BF₃ (trigonal planar) are symmetrical, so their bond dipoles cancel.

questions.s: Which group 16 hydride has the highest boiling point?
questions.e: H₂O molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, which makes its boiling point (100 °C) far higher than the others. Among H₂S, H₂Se and H₂Te the boiling point rises with molecular size, so H₂Te would be the answer only if hydrogen bonding were ignored.

questions.s: Which pair of substances forms the same type of crystal in the solid state?
questions.e: Dry ice (solid CO₂) and ice (solid H₂O) are both molecular crystals, made of separate molecules held by intermolecular forces. NaCl is ionic but HCl is molecular, SiO₂ is a covalent network but CO₂ is molecular, and Fe is metallic while FeCl₃ is not.

questions.s: How many electron pairs are shared between the two atoms in an oxygen molecule, O₂?
questions.e: Each O atom has 6 valence electrons and needs 2 more for an octet, so the two atoms share 2 pairs, forming the double bond O=O. 3 shared pairs is the triple bond of N₂.

questions.s: How many σ bonds and π bonds are there in a hydrogen cyanide molecule, H–C≡N?
questions.e: The H–C single bond is 1 σ. The C≡N triple bond is 1 σ + 2 π. Altogether there are 2 σ and 2 π bonds. 3 σ and 1 π treats the triple bond as two σ bonds, but only one σ bond can form between the same two atoms.

questions.s: What is the shape of the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺?
questions.e: When NH₃ accepts H⁺, its lone pair becomes the fourth N–H bonding pair. With 4 bonding pairs and no lone pair, the ion is a regular tetrahedron with 109.5° angles. Trigonal pyramidal is the shape of NH₃ before it gains H⁺.

questions.s: Which order of melting points of the alkali metals is correct?
questions.e: Down group 1 the atoms get larger while each still gives one electron to the electron sea, so the attraction between cations and delocalised electrons weakens. Melting points fall: Li (181 °C) > Na (98 °C) > K (63 °C).

questions.s: Which of the following substances is made of ions?
questions.e: Calcium chloride is formed from a metal and a non-metal: it is a lattice of Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. Sugar, ethanol and carbon dioxide are covalent molecular substances made only of non-metal atoms.

questions.s: White phosphorus consists of P₄ molecules in which the four P atoms sit at the corners of a tetrahedron, each bonded to the other three. How many moles of P–P bonds are there in 1 mol of P₄?
questions.e: A tetrahedron has 6 edges, and each edge is a P–P bond: 4 atoms × 3 bonds ÷ 2 = 6 bonds per molecule, so 6 mol per mole of P₄. 12 counts each bond from both ends, and 4 counts one bond per atom.

questions.s: Which properties are typical of a molecular crystal such as sulfur or ice?
o: Very high melting point and hardness
questions.e: In a molecular crystal only weak intermolecular forces hold the molecules together, so little energy is needed to separate them: melting points are low and the solids are soft. They contain no ions or free electrons, so they do not conduct as solids or liquids.

questions.s: Which of the following bonds is the least polar?
questions.e: Polarity depends on the electronegativity difference: C (2.5) and H (2.2) are close, so C–H is almost non-polar. The difference increases for N–H, O–H and is largest for F–H.

questions.s: Which order of bond angle is correct?
questions.e: All three central atoms have 4 electron domains. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, so each lone pair squeezes the bond angle: CH₄ (no lone pair) 109.5°, NH₃ (one) about 107°, H₂O (two) about 104.5°. The first option reverses this.

questions.s: Argon boils at −186 °C and neon at −246 °C. Why does argon have the higher boiling point?
o: Its atoms are joined by covalent bonds
Its atoms form hydrogen bonds with each other
Its larger atoms have stronger van der Waals forces
Its atoms are polar and attract each other as dipoles
questions.e: Noble gases are single, non-polar atoms held in the liquid only by van der Waals (dispersion) forces. Argon atoms have more electrons and are larger, so these forces are stronger and more energy is needed to boil it. Noble gas atoms form no covalent or hydrogen bonds.

questions.s: Which pair of substances are both covalent network crystals?
questions.e: Silicon has a diamond-like structure and silicon carbide (SiC) is a network of alternating Si and C atoms, both joined by covalent bonds throughout. Dry ice, iodine and sulfur are molecular, and sodium chloride is ionic.

questions.s: In the electron-dot structure of hydrogen chloride, HCl, how many lone pairs are on the chlorine atom?
questions.e: Cl has 7 valence electrons; one is shared with H in the H–Cl bond and the other 6 form 3 lone pairs, giving Cl 8 electrons in total. Hydrogen has no lone pair.

questions.s: X and Y are elements of periods 2 and 3. The ions X⁺ and Y²⁻ both have the same electron configuration as neon. Which statement is correct?
o: X and Y form only a covalent compound
The radius of X⁺ is larger than that of Y²⁻
The compound X₂Y₂ contains only ionic bonds
X₂Y is an ionic compound with a high melting point
questions.e: X⁺ with 10 electrons means X is Na; Y²⁻ with 10 electrons means Y is O. Na₂O is an ionic crystal with a high melting point. Na⁺ (11 protons) is smaller than O²⁻ (8 protons), and Na₂O₂ contains a covalent O–O bond inside the O₂²⁻ ion as well as ionic bonds.

questions.s: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but its aqueous solution does. Why?
o: Its ions can move only in solution
questions.e: Solid NaCl already consists of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, but they are held fixed in the lattice. In water the lattice breaks up and the hydrated ions can move, carrying current. Water does not supply free electrons, and no sodium metal forms.

questions.s: Marble chips (calcium carbonate) react with dilute hydrochloric acid. Which change increases the initial rate of reaction?
o: Using larger marble chips of the same mass
Using marble powder of the same mass
Cooling the acid to 10 °C before mixing
questions.e: Powder has a much larger surface area than chips of the same mass, so more acid particles collide with the solid per second and the rate rises. Larger chips reduce the surface area, more dilute acid lowers the frequency of collisions, and cooling lowers both collision frequency and the fraction of collisions with enough energy.

questions.s: Why does a catalyst increase the rate of a chemical reaction?
o: It raises the temperature of the reaction mixture
It provides a pathway with a lower activation energy
It makes the enthalpy change of the reaction larger
It shifts the equilibrium position towards the products
questions.e: A catalyst offers an alternative reaction route with a lower activation energy, so a larger fraction of collisions are successful at the same temperature. It does not change the temperature or ΔH, and because it speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally it does not move the equilibrium position.

questions.s: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) in a 2.0 L sealed vessel, the amount of N₂ falls from 2.0 mol to 1.4 mol in the first 2 min. What is the average rate of formation of NH₃ in this time?
questions.e: Δc(N₂) = 0.6 mol ÷ 2.0 L = 0.30 mol/L, so v(N₂) = 0.30 ÷ 2 min = 0.15 mol/(L·min). Rates are in the ratio of the coefficients, so v(NH₃) = 2 × 0.15 = 0.30 mol/(L·min). 0.15 is the rate for N₂, and 0.60 comes from forgetting to divide the amount by the volume.

questions.s: The reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) is run under four different sets of conditions, and the rates below are measured. In which case is the reaction fastest?
questions.e: Convert every rate to v(O₂) in mol/(L·min) by dividing by the coefficient: 0.4/2 = 0.2, 0.25, 0.45/2 = 0.225, and 0.01 mol/(L·s) × 60 = 0.6. The last case is fastest. Comparing the raw numbers without converting units or dividing by the coefficients would wrongly pick the SO₃ value.

questions.s: Which statement about an exothermic reaction is correct?
o: The products have less enthalpy than the reactants, so ΔH < 0
The products have more enthalpy than the reactants, so ΔH < 0
Heat is taken in from the surroundings, so ΔH > 0
Heat is given out to the surroundings, so ΔH > 0
questions.e: In an exothermic reaction energy is released to the surroundings, so the products lie lower in enthalpy than the reactants and ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) is negative. Taking in heat describes an endothermic reaction, and released heat always goes with a negative ΔH, not a positive one.

questions.s: Which of the following reactions is endothermic?
o: Neutralisation of hydrochloric acid by NaOH
Reaction of sodium metal with water
questions.e: CaCO₃ must be heated strongly and continuously to give CaO and CO₂; the reaction absorbs heat, so it is endothermic. Combustion, neutralisation and the reaction of sodium with water all release heat and are exothermic.

questions.s: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH < 0, which change increases the equilibrium yield of ammonia?
o: Raising the temperature of the mixture
Removing ammonia as it is formed
questions.e: Removing NH₃ lowers its concentration, so by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts right and more ammonia is produced. Raising the temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction, lowering pressure favours the side with more gas moles (the left), and a catalyst only helps equilibrium be reached faster.

questions.s: What is the equilibrium constant expression for C(s) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H₂(g)?
questions.e: K is products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient, and pure solids such as carbon are left out because their concentration is constant. So K = c(CO)·c(H₂)/c(H₂O). Including c(C) is the common mistake, and the inverted expressions belong to the reverse reaction.

questions.s: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) at a certain temperature, the equilibrium concentrations are c(H₂) = 0.10 mol/L, c(I₂) = 0.10 mol/L and c(HI) = 0.80 mol/L. What is K?
questions.e: K = c(HI)²/[c(H₂)·c(I₂)] = 0.80²/(0.10 × 0.10) = 0.64/0.010 = 64. Forgetting to square c(HI) gives 80, and 1/64 is K for the reverse reaction.

questions.s: Which statement about a reversible reaction at dynamic equilibrium is correct?
o: The forward and reverse reactions have both stopped
The forward and reverse rates are equal but not zero
The concentrations of reactants and products are equal
There is always more product than reactant present
questions.e: At dynamic equilibrium both reactions continue at the same rate, so the concentrations stay constant. The concentrations do not have to be equal, and the reactions have not stopped; the position of equilibrium may favour either side.

questions.s: The reaction 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g) is carried out in a sealed rigid container at constant temperature. NO₂ is brown and N₂O₄ is colourless. Which observation shows that equilibrium has been reached?
o: The colour of the gas mixture no longer changes
N₂O₄ forms at half the rate at which NO₂ is used up
The density of the gas mixture no longer changes
c(NO₂) : c(N₂O₄) has become equal to 2 : 1
questions.e: A constant colour means c(NO₂) is constant, which only happens at equilibrium. The 1 : 2 rate relation for the forward reaction is true at every moment; the density is always constant because mass and volume are fixed; and the concentration ratio at equilibrium need not match the coefficients.

questions.s: 1.0 mol of N₂O₄ is placed in a 1.0 L sealed flask and N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) comes to equilibrium. At equilibrium 20 % of the N₂O₄ has dissociated. What is K at this temperature?
questions.e: 0.20 mol/L of N₂O₄ reacts, leaving 0.80 mol/L and forming 2 × 0.20 = 0.40 mol/L of NO₂. K = 0.40²/0.80 = 0.16/0.80 = 0.20. Forgetting to square c(NO₂) gives 0.50, and taking c(NO₂) as 0.20 instead of 0.40 gives 0.25.

questions.s: Bond enthalpies (kJ/mol): H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 432. What is ΔH for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g)?
questions.e: ΔH = bonds broken − bonds formed = (436 + 243) − 2 × 432 = 679 − 864 = −185 kJ/mol. Counting only one H–Cl bond gives +247, and taking bonds formed minus bonds broken gives the wrong sign, +185.

questions.s: Given C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −393 kJ/mol, and CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −283 kJ/mol. What is ΔH for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g)?
questions.e: By Hess's law, subtract the second equation from the first: C + ½O₂ → CO, ΔH = −393 − (−283) = −110 kJ/mol. Adding the two values gives −676, and reversing the subtraction gives +110, which would wrongly make the partial combustion of carbon endothermic.

questions.s: On an energy profile for a one-step reaction, the activation energy of the forward reaction is the energy difference between which two points?
o: The reactants and the transition state
The products and the transition state
questions.e: The forward activation energy is the height of the energy barrier measured from the reactants up to the transition state. The reactant-to-product difference is ΔH, and the product-to-transition-state difference is the activation energy of the reverse reaction.

questions.s: A reaction has ΔH = −40 kJ/mol and a forward activation energy of 120 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?
questions.e: For an exothermic reaction the products lie 40 kJ/mol below the reactants, so the barrier seen from the products is 120 + 40 = 160 kJ/mol. Subtracting instead (120 − 40 = 80) would place the products above the reactants, which describes an endothermic reaction.

questions.s: Why does raising the temperature increase the rate of most reactions?
o: The activation energy of the reaction becomes smaller
A larger fraction of collisions have at least the activation energy
The number of particles per unit volume increases
The reaction becomes more exothermic at higher temperature
questions.e: At higher temperature more particles have energy equal to or above Ea, so a larger fraction of collisions succeed (collisions are also a little more frequent). Temperature does not change Ea (only a catalyst does), does not change the concentration of a solution, and does not make the reaction more exothermic.

questions.s: The equilibrium H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) is set up in a syringe. I₂ vapour is violet; H₂ and HI are colourless. The gas is compressed to half its volume at constant temperature. What happens?
o: The equilibrium shifts right and the colour fades
The position does not shift but the colour becomes darker
The equilibrium shifts left and the colour becomes darker
The position does not shift and the colour is unchanged
questions.e: There are 2 mol of gas on each side, so a pressure change does not move the position of equilibrium. However, halving the volume doubles the concentration of every gas, including I₂, so the violet colour becomes darker. The colour change is not evidence of a shift.

questions.s: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH < 0, what is the effect of raising the temperature?
o: K increases and the equilibrium shifts to the right
K is unchanged and the equilibrium shifts to the left
K decreases and the equilibrium shifts to the left
K decreases and the equilibrium shifts to the right
questions.e: Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, which here is the reverse reaction, so the equilibrium shifts left. For an exothermic reaction K therefore decreases as temperature rises. K is unchanged only for changes in concentration, pressure or catalyst, not temperature.

questions.s: Which change alters the value of the equilibrium constant K of a given reaction?
questions.e: K depends only on temperature for a given reaction. Adding reactant or changing pressure may shift the position of equilibrium, but the concentrations readjust so the ratio still equals the same K; a catalyst changes neither K nor the position.

questions.s: For A(g) + B(g) ⇌ 2C(g), K = 4 at a certain temperature. A mixture at this temperature has c(A) = 0.5 mol/L, c(B) = 2.0 mol/L and c(C) = 3.0 mol/L. Which statement is correct?
o: The net reaction goes forward because Q < K
The net reaction goes backward because Q < K
The mixture is already at equilibrium
The net reaction goes backward because Q > K
questions.e: Q = c(C)²/[c(A)·c(B)] = 9.0/(0.5 × 2.0) = 9. Since Q = 9 > K = 4, there is too much product, so the net reaction proceeds backward until Q falls to 4. Forgetting to square c(C) gives Q = 3 < 4 and the wrong direction.

questions.s: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −572 kJ/mol. How much heat is released when 1 mol of H₂ burns completely to liquid water?
questions.e: The ΔH value refers to the equation as written, in which 2 mol of H₂ burns and releases 572 kJ. For 1 mol of H₂ the heat released is 572 ÷ 2 = 286 kJ. Taking 572 kJ ignores the coefficient 2 in front of H₂.

questions.s: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890 kJ/mol. How much heat is released when 8 g of methane burns completely? (H = 1, C = 12)
questions.e: M(CH₄) = 16 g/mol, so 8 g is 0.5 mol, and the heat released is 0.5 × 890 = 445 kJ. Multiplying 890 by the mass in grams (8 × 890 = 7120) confuses mass with amount in moles.

questions.s: A catalyst is added to a gaseous reaction mixture that is already at equilibrium at constant temperature. What is the effect?
o: The forward rate increases but the reverse rate is unchanged
Both rates increase equally and the composition is unchanged
The position shifts so that more product is present
K increases so that the yield of product rises
questions.e: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount, so both rates increase equally and the system stays at the same equilibrium composition. K depends only on temperature, so it is not changed by a catalyst.

questions.s: Ammonia synthesis, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, is exothermic, yet industry runs it at about 450 °C rather than at a much lower temperature. What is the main reason?
o: At 450 °C the equilibrium yield is higher than at 200 °C
At low temperatures the reaction is too slow to be economical
At 450 °C the forward reaction becomes endothermic
The value of K increases as the temperature rises
questions.e: A low temperature would give a higher equilibrium yield, but the rate would be far too slow even with an iron catalyst, so about 450 °C is a compromise between rate and yield. For an exothermic reaction K decreases as temperature rises, and the sign of ΔH does not change with temperature.

questions.s: 3.0 mol of SO₂ and 2.0 mol of O₂ are placed in a 1.0 L sealed vessel. At equilibrium, 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), the vessel contains 2.0 mol of SO₃. What is K at this temperature?
questions.e: Forming 2.0 mol SO₃ uses 2.0 mol SO₂ and 1.0 mol O₂, leaving c(SO₂) = 1.0 and c(O₂) = 1.0 mol/L. K = c(SO₃)²/[c(SO₂)²·c(O₂)] = 2.0²/(1.0² × 1.0) = 4. Forgetting to square c(SO₃) gives 2, and 0.25 is K for the reverse reaction.

questions.s: Dilute FeCl₃ and KSCN solutions are mixed, giving the equilibrium Fe³⁺(aq) + 3SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ Fe(SCN)₃(aq), which is blood-red. Which addition makes the red colour deeper?
o: A few drops of concentrated KSCN solution
A few crystals of solid KCl
A few drops of NaOH solution
questions.e: Extra SCN⁻ raises a reactant concentration, so the equilibrium shifts right and more red Fe(SCN)₃ forms. K⁺ and Cl⁻ take no part in the equilibrium; iron powder reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ and NaOH precipitates Fe(OH)₃, both of which remove Fe³⁺ and make the colour paler.

questions.s: In potassium dichromate solution the equilibrium Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange) + H₂O ⇌ 2CrO₄²⁻ (yellow) + 2H⁺ exists. What happens when a few drops of NaOH solution are added?
o: It turns more orange as the equilibrium shifts left
It turns more orange as the equilibrium shifts right
It turns more yellow as the equilibrium shifts right
Its colour does not change because K is constant
questions.e: OH⁻ reacts with H⁺, lowering c(H⁺), so the equilibrium shifts right to replace it and more yellow CrO₄²⁻ forms. Adding acid would do the opposite and turn the solution more orange. K is constant, but the position of equilibrium still changes.

questions.s: The equilibrium 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) is established in a sealed rigid container. Argon is then pumped in at constant temperature, so the total pressure rises. What happens to the equilibrium?
o: It shifts right because the total pressure rises
It shifts left because the total pressure rises
Its position does not change because the concentrations are unchanged
K increases because more gas particles collide
questions.e: At constant volume, adding an inert gas does not change the amount per litre of SO₂, O₂ or SO₃, so Q still equals K and nothing shifts. A pressure increase shifts equilibrium only when it changes the concentrations (partial pressures) of the reacting gases, for example by compression. K depends only on temperature.

questions.s: The equilibrium N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) is held in a cylinder with a movable piston at constant temperature and constant total pressure. Helium is then added. How does the equilibrium respond?
o: It does not shift, because helium is inert
It does not shift, but K increases
questions.e: At constant total pressure the volume must increase when helium is added, so the concentrations of N₂O₄ and NO₂ both fall. The system responds like a pressure decrease and shifts towards the side with more gas molecules, the NO₂ side. Helium being unreactive matters only at constant volume, where nothing shifts.

questions.s: The equilibrium constant for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) at a certain temperature is K₁. At the same temperature, what is the equilibrium constant for NH₃(g) ⇌ ½N₂(g) + 3/2 H₂(g)?
questions.e: Reversing an equation inverts K, giving 1/K₁ for 2NH₃ ⇌ N₂ + 3H₂. Halving all coefficients takes the square root, so K = 1/√K₁. Answering 1/K₁ forgets the halving, and √K₁ forgets the reversal.

questions.s: For dilute strong acids and bases, H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), ΔH = −57.3 kJ/mol. 500 mL of 0.20 mol/L HCl is mixed with 500 mL of 0.10 mol/L NaOH. How much heat is released?
questions.e: n(HCl) = 0.10 mol and n(NaOH) = 0.050 mol, so NaOH is limiting and only 0.050 mol of water forms. Heat = 0.050 × 57.3 = 2.865 kJ. Using the HCl amount (0.10 mol) gives 5.73 kJ, but the excess acid has nothing to react with.

questions.s: When dilute acetic acid is neutralised by dilute NaOH, the heat released per mole of water formed is less than 57.3 kJ. Why?
o: Acetic acid has more H atoms per molecule than HCl
Some of the water evaporates during the reaction
Sodium acetate precipitates and absorbs heat
Ionisation of the weak acid absorbs some heat
questions.e: Acetic acid is a weak acid and is mostly un-ionised; as it is neutralised it must ionise further, and this ionisation is endothermic, so the net heat released is smaller. Only one H atom is acidic, sodium acetate is soluble, and evaporation is not the reason for the systematic difference.

questions.s: Burning 0.10 mol of a liquid fuel heats 500 g of water from 20 °C to 40 °C. Assume all the heat goes into the water (c = 4.2 J/(g·°C)). What is ΔH of combustion of the fuel?
questions.e: q = mcΔT = 500 × 4.2 × 20 = 42 000 J = 42 kJ, released by 0.10 mol of fuel, so 420 kJ per mole. Combustion releases heat, so ΔH = −420 kJ/mol. −42 kJ/mol forgets to divide by 0.10 mol, and the positive sign would mean heat absorbed.

questions.s: C(graphite) → C(diamond), ΔH = +1.9 kJ/mol. Which statement is correct?
o: Diamond is more stable than graphite
Converting diamond into graphite absorbs heat
Equal masses of each give out the same heat on burning
Graphite has the lower energy and is more stable
questions.e: The positive ΔH means diamond lies 1.9 kJ/mol above graphite, so graphite has lower energy and is the more stable form. The reverse change, diamond to graphite, releases 1.9 kJ/mol, and diamond releases more heat than graphite when equal masses burn to the same CO₂.

questions.s: Zinc granules react with dilute sulfuric acid in an open beaker. The rate of hydrogen evolution increases at first and later decreases. What causes the initial increase?
o: The reaction is exothermic, so the solution warms up
The acid concentration rises as the reaction proceeds
A catalyst is formed by the reaction
The surface area of the zinc grows as it dissolves
questions.e: The reaction releases heat, and the rising temperature at first outweighs the falling acid concentration, so the rate increases. Later the acid is used up and the concentration effect dominates, so the rate falls. The acid concentration only ever decreases during the reaction.

questions.s: According to collision theory, why does increasing the concentration of a reactant in solution increase the rate of reaction?
o: Each particle gains more kinetic energy
Particles collide more often per unit time
The enthalpy change becomes more negative
questions.e: More particles per unit volume means more collisions per second, and therefore more successful collisions per second. Concentration does not change Ea, particle energy (that depends on temperature) or ΔH.

questions.s: How does adding a catalyst change the energy profile of an exothermic reaction?
o: It lowers the peak and leaves ΔH unchanged
It lowers the peak and makes ΔH more negative
It raises the energy level of the reactants
It lowers the energy level of the products
questions.e: A catalyst provides a route with a lower energy barrier, so the peak is lower, but the reactant and product energy levels are unchanged and so is ΔH. Changing either level would change ΔH, which a catalyst cannot do.

questions.s: A sealed flask containing the equilibrium mixture 2NO₂(g) (brown) ⇌ N₂O₄(g) (colourless) is put into ice water, and the brown colour becomes paler. What can be concluded?
o: The forward reaction is endothermic, ΔH > 0
K becomes smaller when the flask is cooled
Cooling slows only the reverse reaction, not the forward one
The forward reaction is exothermic, ΔH < 0
questions.e: A paler colour means less NO₂, so cooling shifts the equilibrium right. Lowering the temperature favours the exothermic direction, so the forward reaction is exothermic and K increases on cooling. Cooling slows both reactions; the reverse simply slows more.

questions.s: What is the equilibrium constant expression for 2NO(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g)?
questions.e: Each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient: products on top, reactants below, giving c²(NO₂)/[c²(NO)·c(O₂)]. Coefficients are powers, not multipliers, and the last expression is K for the reverse reaction.

questions.s: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ/mol. Bond enthalpies: N≡N 946 kJ/mol, H–H 436 kJ/mol. What is the mean N–H bond enthalpy?
questions.e: Bonds broken: 946 + 3 × 436 = 2254 kJ. ΔH = broken − formed, so formed = 2254 + 92 = 2346 kJ, and two NH₃ molecules contain 6 N–H bonds: 2346 ÷ 6 = 391 kJ/mol. Dividing by 3 (one NH₃ only) gives 782.

questions.s: Which statement about reversible reactions is correct?
o: In a closed system a reversible reaction cannot reach 100 % conversion
Burning H₂ and electrolysing water form a pair of reversible reactions
A reversible reaction at equilibrium always has K = 1
A catalyst lets a reversible reaction go to completion
questions.e: In a closed system the reverse reaction always runs alongside the forward one, so the reactants are never completely converted. Burning hydrogen and electrolysing water happen under different conditions, so they are not one reversible reaction; K can have any value, and a catalyst does not change the equilibrium composition.

questions.s: Calcium carbonate reacts with excess dilute HCl and the total volume of CO₂ collected is recorded in the table. What is the average rate of CO₂ production over the first 2 min?
questions.e: Average rate = 50 mL ÷ 2 min = 25 mL/min. 30 mL/min is the rate in the first minute only and 20 mL/min is the rate in the second minute only; the average over both minutes lies between them.

questions.s: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), K = 64 at a certain temperature. 1.0 mol of H₂ and 1.0 mol of I₂ are sealed in a 1.0 L vessel at this temperature. What is c(HI) at equilibrium?
questions.e: If x mol/L of H₂ reacts, (2x)²/(1 − x)² = 64, so 2x/(1 − x) = 8, giving 2x = 8 − 8x and x = 0.8. Then c(HI) = 2x = 1.6 mol/L. 0.8 mol/L is x itself (forgetting the coefficient 2), and 0.2 mol/L is the H₂ left over.

questions.s: For which equilibrium does increasing the pressure (by compression at constant temperature) increase the equilibrium yield of the products?
questions.e: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules. For SO₃ synthesis, 3 mol of gas becomes 2 mol, so the yield rises. CaCO₃ decomposition and N₂O₄ dissociation produce more gas, so compression lowers their yield, and the HI reaction has 2 mol of gas on each side.

questions.s: Which statement about energy changes in chemical reactions is correct?
o: Every reaction that needs heating to start is endothermic
An endothermic reaction can never happen on its own
questions.e: Bond formation releases energy and bond breaking absorbs it; ΔH is the balance of the two. Many exothermic reactions, such as burning coal, still need heating to start because of their activation energy, and some endothermic processes, such as dissolving NH₄NO₃ in water, happen on their own.

questions.s: The gas reaction 2HI(g) → H₂(g) + I₂(g) takes place in a sealed rigid vessel at constant temperature. Nitrogen gas is pumped in, raising the total pressure. What happens to the rate of reaction?
o: It stays the same because the concentration of HI is unchanged
It increases because the total pressure is higher
It decreases because the HI is diluted by nitrogen
It increases because the collisions become more energetic
questions.e: In a rigid vessel the amount of HI per litre is unchanged when nitrogen is added, and the temperature is constant, so the rate does not change. Pressure affects rate only through the concentrations of the reacting gases; nitrogen does not dilute HI unless the volume increases.

questions.s: For the gas-phase reaction 2A(g) ⇌ B(g), ΔH < 0, which single change increases both the rate of reaction and the equilibrium conversion of A?
o: Compressing the mixture into a smaller volume
questions.e: Compression raises the concentration of A, which speeds up the reaction, and shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer gas molecules (B), raising the conversion. Raising the temperature speeds things up but lowers the conversion for an exothermic reaction; a catalyst does not change conversion; argon at constant volume changes nothing.

questions.s: Which is a correct unit for the rate of a reaction in solution?
questions.e: Rate is the change in concentration per unit time, so its unit is (mol/L) ÷ s = mol/(L·s), often written mol·L⁻¹·s⁻¹. mol/L is the unit of concentration alone, and the other two units are inverted.

questions.s: The red equilibrium mixture Fe³⁺(aq) + 3SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ Fe(SCN)₃(aq) is diluted with an equal volume of water. Which statement is correct?
o: The colour becomes lighter and the equilibrium shifts left
The colour becomes lighter and the equilibrium does not shift
The colour becomes darker and the equilibrium shifts right
The colour is unchanged because K is unchanged
questions.e: Halving every concentration multiplies Q = c(Fe(SCN)₃)/[c(Fe³⁺)·c³(SCN⁻)] by 2³/2 = 8 at the moment of dilution, so Q > K and the equilibrium shifts left, towards the side with more dissolved particles. Both the dilution and the shift make the red colour lighter.

questions.s: Why does food stay fresh for longer in a refrigerator?
o: Cold air in the refrigerator contains no oxygen
Lower temperature slows the reactions that spoil food
Low temperature raises the activation energy of spoilage
Cooling makes the spoilage reactions endothermic
questions.e: At a lower temperature fewer collisions have energy equal to or above the activation energy, so the chemical and microbial reactions that spoil food are slower. The activation energy itself does not change with temperature, and the air inside still contains oxygen.

questions.s: In the laboratory, chlorine gas is often collected over saturated sodium chloride solution instead of over water. Why?
o: NaCl reacts with chlorine to form a stable compound
Saturated brine is too dense for chlorine to dissolve in
High c(Cl⁻) shifts Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + Cl⁻ + HClO to the left
NaCl catalyses the decomposition of HClO in the water
questions.e: Chlorine dissolves in water partly by the equilibrium Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + Cl⁻ + HClO. A high chloride concentration shifts this equilibrium to the left, so much less chlorine dissolves and is lost. NaCl does not react with chlorine, and density is not the reason.

questions.s: Ethyl ethanoate is made by the reaction CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O with a sulfuric acid catalyst. Which change increases the equilibrium yield of ester based on the acetic acid used?
o: Adding water to the reaction mixture
Adding a little ethyl ethanoate at the start
questions.e: Excess ethanol raises a reactant concentration, so the equilibrium shifts right and a larger fraction of the acetic acid is converted into ester. Adding water or ester shifts the equilibrium left, and the size of the flask does not affect an equilibrium in solution.

questions.s: CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) is at equilibrium in a sealed vessel. The volume of the vessel is halved at constant temperature. When equilibrium is re-established, how does c(CO₂) compare with its original value?
o: It is twice the original value
It is between the original value and twice it
It is equal to the original value
It is half the original value
questions.e: For this equilibrium K = c(CO₂), because the solids are omitted. At constant temperature K is fixed, so after compression CO₂ reacts with CaO until c(CO₂) is back to exactly its original value. The answer 'between' applies to equilibria with gases on both sides, not to this one.

questions.s: What is the equilibrium constant expression for Fe₃O₄(s) + 4H₂(g) ⇌ 3Fe(s) + 4H₂O(g)?
questions.e: The solids Fe₃O₄ and Fe are omitted, and each gas concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient, so K = c⁴(H₂O)/c⁴(H₂). Leaving out the powers gives a different constant, and including the solids is incorrect.

questions.s: A sealed bottle of fizzy drink contains the equilibrium CO₂(aq) ⇌ CO₂(g). Why do bubbles form as soon as the bottle is opened?
o: The drink warms up at once, so dissolving CO₂ becomes endothermic
Air entering the bottle reacts with the dissolved CO₂
Opening the bottle introduces a catalyst for releasing CO₂
The pressure above the drink falls, so the equilibrium shifts towards CO₂(g)
questions.e: Opening the bottle lowers the pressure of CO₂ above the liquid, so the equilibrium shifts to the right, towards the gas, and dissolved CO₂ escapes as bubbles. The sign of ΔH does not change, and air does not react with CO₂.

questions.s: For CO(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO₂(g) + H₂(g), K = 1.0 at a certain temperature. 1.0 mol of CO and 3.0 mol of H₂O are placed in a 1.0 L vessel at this temperature. What percentage of the CO is converted at equilibrium?
questions.e: If x mol/L of CO reacts, x²/[(1.0 − x)(3.0 − x)] = 1, so x² = 3.0 − 4.0x + x², giving x = 0.75. The conversion of CO is 0.75/1.0 = 75 %. 25 % is the conversion of the water (0.75/3.0), and 50 % would be the result for equal starting amounts.

questions.s: Gases X and Y react in a 1.0 L sealed vessel to form Z. The concentrations (mol/L) at the start and once they have stopped changing are shown. Which equation describes the reaction?
questions.e: The changes are X −0.6, Y −0.2 and Z +0.4 mol/L, in the ratio 3 : 1 : 2, so X and Y are reactants in the ratio 3 : 1 and Z is the product. The amounts then stop changing while X and Y remain, so the reaction is reversible: 3X + Y ⇌ 2Z. Swapping the coefficients of X and Y is the common slip.

questions.s: Which thermochemical equation correctly shows the enthalpy of combustion of hydrogen?
questions.e: The enthalpy of combustion refers to 1 mol of fuel burning completely to its stable products under standard conditions, and water is stable as a liquid, so H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O(l), ΔH = −286 kJ/mol. The first equation burns 2 mol of H₂, the second forms steam, and combustion cannot have a positive ΔH.

questions.s: Using the enthalpies of combustion in the table, which fuel releases the most heat per gram when burned completely? (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.e: Divide by molar mass: carbon 393/12 ≈ 33, methane 890/16 ≈ 56, ethanol 1367/46 ≈ 30, hydrogen 286/2 = 143 kJ/g. Hydrogen releases by far the most per gram even though its value per mole is the smallest; ethanol only looks best per mole.

questions.s: H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(g), ΔH₁; H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l), ΔH₂. Which relation is correct?
questions.e: Both reactions are exothermic. Condensing steam to liquid water releases more heat, so ΔH₂ is more negative than ΔH₁, which means ΔH₁ > ΔH₂. Comparing only the amounts of heat released (more for liquid water) and forgetting the negative signs leads to the wrong choice ΔH₁ < ΔH₂.

questions.s: Given N₂(g) + 2O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g), ΔH = +68 kJ/mol, and N₂H₄(l) + O₂(g) → N₂(g) + 2H₂O(g), ΔH = −534 kJ/mol. What is ΔH for 2N₂H₄(l) + 2NO₂(g) → 3N₂(g) + 4H₂O(g)?
questions.e: Take 2 × the second equation (ΔH = −1068) and add the reverse of the first (ΔH = −68): the O₂ cancels and the target equation remains, with ΔH = −1068 − 68 = −1136 kJ/mol. Adding +68 instead of reversing gives −1000, and forgetting to double the hydrazine equation gives −602.

questions.s: For 4NH₃(g) + 5O₂(g) → 4NO(g) + 6H₂O(g), which relation between the rates of reaction is correct?
questions.e: Each rate divided by its coefficient is the same: v(O₂)/5 = v(H₂O)/6, so 6v(O₂) = 5v(H₂O). The first and third relations put the coefficients on the wrong side (correct forms are 5v(NH₃) = 4v(O₂) and 3v(NH₃) = 2v(H₂O)), and v(O₂) is 5/4 of v(NO).

questions.s: In a cobalt chloride solution, CoCl₄²⁻ (blue) + 6H₂O ⇌ [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (pink) + 4Cl⁻, ΔH < 0. What happens when the solution is heated?
o: It turns more pink as the equilibrium shifts right
It turns more blue as the equilibrium shifts left
It turns more blue because K increases
Its colour is unchanged because water is in excess
questions.e: Heating favours the endothermic direction. The forward reaction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts left and more blue CoCl₄²⁻ forms. Because the forward reaction is exothermic, K decreases on heating rather than increases.

questions.s: Which catalyst is used industrially in the contact process, 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)?
questions.e: The oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃ in sulfuric acid manufacture uses vanadium(V) oxide at about 450 °C. Iron is the catalyst for ammonia synthesis, nickel for hydrogenation, and MnO₂ for decomposing H₂O₂ in the laboratory.

questions.s: A little MnO₂ is added to hydrogen peroxide solution, and oxygen is given off rapidly. Which statement about the MnO₂ is correct?
o: Its mass and chemical properties are unchanged at the end
It increases the total volume of O₂ that can be formed
It is gradually used up as the reaction proceeds
It makes the decomposition more exothermic
